lessons.title: Rendering, reconciliation and component identity
lessons.summary: Rendering is a pure calculation of UI from props and state. React keeps or discards state based on a component's type and position in the tree, and keys give list items a stable identity.

sections.heading: Rendering is a calculation
How React decides what to keep
sections.body:
State is not stored inside the component function. React holds it and ties it to the component's **position in the UI tree**. Between renders, React compares the new tree with the previous one: - **Same component type at the same position:** React keeps the state, even if the props changed. - **Different type at that position** (for example `` replaced by `

`, or a `

` wrapper replaced by a `
` wrapper): React destroys the old subtree and its state. - **Removed and later re-added:** the state is gone; a fresh instance starts from its initial state. A trap that follows from this: never *define* a component inside another component. Each render of the parent creates a new function, so React sees a new component type at that position and resets the child's state (and DOM) on every parent render. Declare components at the top level.

sections.heading: Keys give list items identity
sections.body:
When you render a list, each item needs a `key` that is unique **among its siblings** and **stable across renders**. The key tells React which item is which when items are inserted, removed or reordered.

- Use an ID from your data (a database ID), or generate one when the item is created, not during render.
- Using the array **index** as a key works only when the list never reorders, inserts or deletes. Otherwise state and DOM (such as an uncontrolled input's text) stay attached to a position, not to the item.
- Never use `key={Math.random()}` or anything generated during render: keys then never match between renders, so every item and its state is recreated each time.
- `key` is not passed to your component as a prop. If the child needs the ID, pass it separately.

sections.heading: Resetting state on purpose with a key
sections.body:
Keys are not only for lists. Giving a component a different `key` tells React it is a different instance, so React discards its state and mounts a new one:

```jsx
<Chat key={contact.id} contact={contact} />
```

This is the recommended way to reset a whole subtree when an identity changes (switching chat recipient, switching the edited record). It is simpler and cheaper than an Effect that copies props into state, which renders once with stale values and then again.

keyPoints: Render is a pure function of props, state and context; commit only touches DOM that changed.
State lives with React and is tied to the component's type and position in the tree.
A different type at the same position, or a different key, resets the whole subtree.
Keys must be stable and unique among siblings; index keys break on reorder, random keys break always.
Never declare a component inside another component.

gotchas.trap: Use the array index as the key for a list that users can reorder or delete from.
gotchas.correct: Use a stable ID from the data so state and DOM follow the item, not the position.

gotchas.trap: Reset a form when a prop changes by copying the prop into state in a useEffect.
gotchas.correct: Give the component key={id}; React remounts it with fresh state.

gotchas.trap: Strict Mode rendering twice is a bug to work around.
gotchas.correct: It is development-only and exists to expose impure render logic.

lessons.lab: Build a list of editable rows (each with an uncontrolled <input>) keyed by index. Delete the first row and observe the text shift. Switch to key={item.id} and repeat. Then add <Profile key={userId} /> and confirm switching users clears its local state.

lessons.title: State: snapshots, batching and where state lives
lessons.summary: Each render sees a fixed snapshot of state. Setters queue updates that React batches and applies on the next render; updater functions chain off the latest queued value. Keep state minimal, derived values computed, and state owned by the closest common parent.

sections.heading: State as a snapshot
Batching and the update queue
sections.body:
React waits until all code in an event handler has run before re-rendering, so several `set` calls produce one render (**batching**). Each call adds an entry to a queue that React processes in order during the next render:

| Handler | Result from 0 |
|---|---|
| `setNumber(number + 1)` three times | 1 |
| `setNumber(n => n + 1)` three times | 3 |
| `setNumber(number + 5); setNumber(n => n + 1); setNumber(42)` | 42 |

A plain value means "replace with this"; a function means "compute from the previous queued value". The last entry in the example replaces everything before it.

sections.heading: Updater functions
sections.body:
Use the updater form `setX(prev => next)` when the next state depends on the previous one and several updates can happen before the next render. By convention, name the argument after the variable's first letter (`n`, `prev`).

Updaters run during rendering, so they must be **pure**: return the next state and do nothing else. In Strict Mode, React calls them twice in development to catch mistakes.

sections.heading: Updating objects and arrays
sections.body:
React compares old and new state with `Object.is`. Mutating an object in place and passing the same reference back does not trigger a re-render:

```jsx
user.name = 'Ada';
setUser(user);            // same object: no re-render
setUser({ ...user, name: 'Ada' }); // new object: re-renders
```

Treat state as read-only. Create new objects and arrays with spread, `map` and `filter`.

sections.heading: Choosing the state structure
sections.body:
Keep state minimal:

- **Avoid redundant state.** If a value can be computed from props or other state (a `fullName` from `firstName` and `lastName`, a filtered list), compute it during render instead of storing and syncing it.
- **Avoid duplication.** Store a `selectedId`, not a copy of the selected object.
- **Avoid contradictions.** Replace several booleans that can disagree with one status value.
- Don't mirror props in state unless you deliberately want only the initial value (name it `initialColor`).

sections.heading: Lifting state up and colocation
sections.body:
When two components must change together, remove the state from both, move it to their **closest common parent**, and pass it down with callbacks. That parent becomes the single source of truth, and the children become controlled.

The opposite also matters: keep state as **close as possible** to the components that use it. State that only one subtree needs should not live at the top of the app, where every change re-renders unrelated parts.

keyPoints: A state variable is fixed for the whole render; handlers and timeouts see that render's value.
React batches setter calls in a handler and processes the queue in order on the next render.
Updater functions compute from the previous queued value and must be pure.
Mutating state in place and setting the same reference does not re-render.
Derive what you can; lift shared state to the closest common parent; keep the rest local.

gotchas.trap: Calling setCount(count + 1) three times increments by three.
gotchas.correct: It increments by one; use setCount(c => c + 1) to chain updates.

gotchas.trap: Store fullName in state and update it in an Effect when the name parts change.
gotchas.correct: Compute fullName during render; it is redundant state.

gotchas.trap: Push to the state array and call setItems(items).
gotchas.correct: Create a new array, for example setItems([...items, item]).

lessons.lab: Write a counter button that calls the setter three times with a value, then with an updater, and log the result. Then build two accordion panels where opening one closes the other by lifting activeIndex into the parent.

lessons.title: Effects: synchronising with external systems
lessons.summary: Effects synchronise a component with something outside React. Declare every reactive value as a dependency, always return a cleanup when setup creates something, expect Strict Mode to run setup twice in development, and remove Effects that only transform data or respond to events.

sections.heading: What an Effect is for
sections.body:
Rendering must stay pure, and event handlers handle specific user actions. Effects cover the remaining case: side effects caused by **rendering itself**, typically keeping a component in sync with an external system such as a network connection, a browser API, a non-React widget or an analytics call when a page is shown.

Effects run after the commit. Think of each Effect as "start synchronising" (setup) and "stop synchronising" (cleanup), not as lifecycle events.

sections.heading: Dependencies
sections.body:
Every reactive value the Effect reads (props, state and anything computed from them in the component body) must be in the dependency array. The React hooks lint rule checks this; you change dependencies by changing the code, not by suppressing the linter.

- No array: runs after every render. `[]`: runs after mount only. `[a, b]`: runs when `a` or `b` changes (compared with `Object.is`).
- Objects and functions created during render are new on every render, so using them as dependencies re-runs the Effect every time. Move the object or function *inside* the Effect, or depend on the primitive values it is built from.

sections.heading: Cleanup and Strict Mode
Fetching data without race conditions
When you do not need an Effect
sections.body:
- **Transforming data for rendering:** compute it in the body; wrap genuinely expensive work in `useMemo`.
- **Resetting state when a prop changes:** pass a `key`.
- **Responding to a user action** (submitting, buying, showing a toast after a click): do it in the event handler. Ask *why* the code runs: because the component was displayed (Effect) or because the user did something (handler).
- **Chains of Effects** that set state to trigger other Effects: compute the next state in the handler.
- **Notifying a parent** of a change: call the parent's callback in the same handler that updates state.
- **Subscribing to an external store:** prefer `useSyncExternalStore`.

sections.heading: Separating events from Effects with useEffectEvent

keyPoints: Effects synchronise with external systems; they are not a general 'run after something changes' tool.
List every reactive value as a dependency; fix unwanted re-runs by changing the code.
Return a cleanup for anything setup creates; Strict Mode runs an extra setup/cleanup cycle in development.
Guard Effect-based fetches with an ignore flag to avoid race conditions.
Derive data in render, reset with key, and handle user actions in event handlers.

gotchas.trap: Use a ref flag to stop the Effect running twice in development.
gotchas.correct: Implement cleanup so setup → cleanup → setup behaves like a single setup.

gotchas.trap: Disable the exhaustive-deps lint rule to stop an Effect re-running.
gotchas.correct: Move non-reactive logic into useEffectEvent or move objects inside the Effect.

gotchas.trap: Send the purchase POST in an Effect that watches a 'submitted' state flag.
gotchas.correct: Send it from the submit event handler.

lessons.lab: Write a chat-room component that connects in an Effect without cleanup, wrap it in <StrictMode>, and watch the double 'Connecting' log with no disconnect. Add cleanup, then add a theme-colored notification through useEffectEvent and confirm theme changes no longer reconnect.

lessons.title: Refs, context and reducers
lessons.summary: Refs hold mutable values that don't drive rendering; context passes data deeply but re-renders every consumer when its value changes; reducers centralise complex update logic in pure functions.

sections.heading: Refs as an escape hatch
sections.body:
`useRef(initial)` returns an object whose `current` property you can read and write. Changing it does **not** trigger a re-render, and the value persists across renders. Use it for values that rendering doesn't depend on: interval IDs, DOM nodes, the latest value for a callback.

Don't read or write `ref.current` during rendering (except lazy one-time initialisation). If the value is shown on screen, it belongs in state. A module-level variable is not a substitute: it is shared by every instance of the component.

sections.heading: DOM refs and ref as a prop
Context and the nearest provider
sections.body:
Context lets a parent provide data to any component below it without passing props through every level. Try passing props or `children` first; reach for context for genuinely global concerns such as theme, current user or routing.

In React 19 you can render the context itself as the provider: `<ThemeContext value="dark">`. A component calling `useContext` reads the value from the **closest provider above it**; a provider rendered inside the same component does not count.

sections.heading: Avoiding context re-render storms
useReducer for complex state
sections.body:
When many handlers update the same state in related ways, move the logic into a reducer: `const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialArg)`. Handlers `dispatch` actions that describe *what happened* (`{ type: 'added', text }`), and the reducer computes the next state.

Reducers must be **pure**: no requests, timers or mutation; return a new object. Like setters, `dispatch` doesn't change the value in the currently running code. Combining a reducer with context (state in one context, `dispatch` in another) scales well for deep trees, because `dispatch` is stable.

keyPoints: Refs persist values without re-rendering; don't read or write them during render.
React 19: ref is a prop on function components, and ref callbacks can return cleanup.
useContext reads the closest provider above the calling component.
A new provider value re-renders all consumers, including memo-wrapped ones; memoize and split.
Reducers are pure functions of (state, action); actions describe what happened.

gotchas.trap: Wrap consumers in memo to stop them re-rendering when context changes.
gotchas.correct: memo doesn't block context updates; stabilise the value or split the context.

gotchas.trap: Render a value from ref.current in JSX and expect it to update.
gotchas.correct: Use state for anything displayed; refs don't trigger renders.

gotchas.trap: Call fetch inside the reducer to persist the new state.
gotchas.correct: Keep reducers pure; do side effects in handlers or Effects.

lessons.lab: Create an AuthContext whose value is an inline object, add a frequently ticking clock state to the provider's parent, and use React DevTools to see every consumer re-render. Fix it with useMemo/useCallback, then refactor task state into useReducer with state and dispatch in separate contexts.

lessons.title: React 19: Actions, optimistic UI, use() and the Compiler
lessons.summary: React 19 adds Actions (async transitions with built-in pending and error handling), useActionState and useOptimistic for forms, use() for reading promises and context, and the React Compiler, which memoizes components and hooks automatically.

sections.heading: Actions and transitions
sections.body:
An **Action** is a function, often async, run inside a Transition. React tracks its pending state, keeps showing the current UI while it runs, and sends thrown errors to the nearest error boundary. You can pass Actions to `<form action={fn}>`, `useActionState` and `startTransition`.

A known limitation: state updates made **after an `await`** inside a Transition are not marked as part of it. Wrap them in another `startTransition`. A Transition also cannot control a text input's value.

sections.heading: useActionState
sections.body:
```jsx
const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(action, initialState, permalink?);
```

- The action receives **`(previousState, formData)`**, not just `formData`, and returns the next state (such as field errors).
- Pass `formAction` to `<form action>` or a button's `formAction`. Calling it elsewhere needs `startTransition`.
- Calls are queued and run one after another; if one throws, the queued calls are cancelled.
- Uncontrolled forms reset automatically after a successful form action.

sections.heading: useOptimistic
sections.body:
`useOptimistic(value, reducer?)` returns `[optimisticValue, setOptimistic]`. It shows a temporary value while an Action is in flight; when the Action finishes, the optimistic value converges with the real `value` in the same commit.

The setter must be called **inside an Action or Transition** (a form action or `startTransition`). Called from a plain event handler, React warns and the optimistic value snaps back.

sections.heading: Reading resources with use()
sections.body:
`use(resource)` reads a promise or a context. When reading a promise it suspends to the nearest `<Suspense>` boundary, and rejections go to the nearest error boundary. You cannot wrap `use` in `try/catch`.

Unlike other hooks, `use` may appear inside conditions and loops. Promises must be **stable**: create them in a Server Component (or a cache) and pass them down. A promise created during a Client Component render is new on every render.

sections.heading: Other React 19 changes
sections.body:
- `ref` as a prop for function components; ref callbacks can return cleanup.
- `<Context value>` works as a provider.
- `<title>`, `<meta>` and `<link>` rendered anywhere are hoisted to the document head; stylesheets support `precedence`.
- Resource hints: `preload`, `preinit`, `prefetchDNS`, `preconnect`.
- React 19.3 is the current line, with stable `<ViewTransition>` and Fragment Refs.

sections.heading: The React Compiler
sections.body:
React Compiler 1.0 is a build-time tool that automatically memoizes **components and hooks**, reducing the need for hand-written `useMemo`, `useCallback` and `memo`. It assumes your code follows the Rules of React (pure render, immutable props and state, hooks called unconditionally); its lint rules ship in `eslint-plugin-react-hooks`.

Guidance for adopters: keep existing manual memoization (removing it can change compiled output), pin an exact compiler version, and expect a "Memo ✨" badge in DevTools. In Next.js, `reactCompiler: true` is a stable option but not on by default, and it requires `babel-plugin-react-compiler`.

keyPoints: Actions are async functions in Transitions with built-in pending and error handling.
useActionState actions receive (previousState, formData) and return the next state.
useOptimistic setters must run inside an Action or Transition.
use() needs a stable promise, a Suspense boundary and an error boundary (not try/catch).
The React Compiler auto-memoizes components and hooks; keep existing memoization when adopting.

gotchas.trap: Write the useActionState action as async (formData) => {...}.
gotchas.correct: The first argument is the previous state: async (prevState, formData) => {...}.

gotchas.trap: Call use(fetch(url)) directly in a Client Component.
gotchas.correct: Create the promise in a Server Component or cache and pass it down, inside Suspense.

gotchas.trap: After enabling the compiler, delete every useMemo and useCallback.
gotchas.correct: Keep them; removing them can change compiler output. Write new code without them.

lessons.lab: Build a 'like' button with useOptimistic driven from a form action, then move the setter call into a plain onClick and observe the warning. Add an error to the action and wire an error boundary. Finally, enable the compiler in a sample project and look for the Memo ✨ badge.

lessons.title: Server and Client Components
lessons.summary: Where the server/client boundary sits, what may cross it, and how to keep client bundles small.

sections.heading: Two environments, one tree
sections.body: In the App Router every component is a **Server Component** unless it, or a module that imports it, sits below a `'use client'` directive. Server Components run only on the server: they can be `async`, read databases and secrets directly, and ship **no JavaScript** for themselves to the browser. Client Components are pre-rendered to HTML and then hydrated, so they can use state, effects, event handlers and browser APIs.

sections.heading: The boundary lives in the module graph
What can cross the boundary
sections.body:
Props passed from a Server Component to a Client Component must be **serializable by React**:

| Allowed | Not allowed |
|---|---|
| primitives, bigint, `Symbol.for` symbols | ordinary functions (except Server Functions) |
| plain objects, Array, Map, Set, TypedArray, ArrayBuffer | class instances, classes |
| Date | null-prototype objects |
| JSX elements, Promises, Server Functions | unregistered Symbols |

Passing `onClick={() => ...}` from a Server Component fails. Either move the handler into the Client Component or pass a Server Function (`'use server'`).

sections.heading: Bundle impact and leaf boundaries
sections.body: Because everything under `'use client'` ships to the browser, put the directive on the **smallest interactive leaf** (a like button, a search box), not on a layout or page. A large markdown parser or date library used only in a Server Component never reaches the client bundle.

sections.heading: Keeping secrets on the right side
sections.body:
- Variables without the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix are not exposed to the client.
- `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` values are **inlined at build time** and frozen; dynamic lookups such as `process.env[name]` are not inlined.
- `import 'server-only'` in a data module turns an accidental client import into a **build error**; `client-only` does the reverse.

keyPoints: Components are Server Components by default; 'use client' opts a module and its imports into the client bundle.
The boundary is in the module graph: imports below it become client code.
Client Components can render Server Components received as children or props.
Props crossing the boundary must be serializable; functions only as Server Functions.
Push the boundary to interactive leaves to keep bundles small.
Use the server-only package to make leaking server modules a build error.

gotchas.trap: Adding 'use client' to every component that renders a Client Component.
gotchas.correct: Only the module that needs interactivity needs the directive; its importers can stay Server Components.

gotchas.trap: Passing a class instance (for example an ORM model) as a prop to a Client Component.
gotchas.correct: Map it to a plain object first; class instances are not serializable.

gotchas.trap: Expecting NEXT_PUBLIC_ values to change after redeploying with new env only at runtime.
gotchas.correct: They are inlined at build time; rebuild, or read the value on the server.

lessons.lab: Take a page with a "use client" layout. Move the directive down to a single interactive component, pass the server-rendered content as children, then compare the client bundle with the bundle analyzer.

lessons.title: App Router File Conventions
lessons.summary: Layouts, pages, templates, route groups, dynamic segments and the special loading, error and not-found files.

sections.heading: Folders define routes, files define UI
sections.body:
In `app/`, each folder is a route segment and a `page` file makes it publicly reachable. Special files in a segment nest in a fixed hierarchy:

`layout` > `template` > `error` > `loading` > `not-found` > `page`

So `loading` wraps the page in a Suspense boundary, and `error` wraps loading and the page, but not the layout of the same segment.

sections.heading: Layouts versus templates
sections.body: A **layout** wraps its children and is preserved across navigations between its child routes: it keeps state and **does not re-render on navigation**. That is why the Next.js auth guide warns against relying on a layout for auth checks. A **template** is similar, but it gets a fresh instance on each navigation, so state resets and effects re-run.

sections.heading: Organizing without changing URLs
sections.body:
- `(marketing)`: a **route group**, omitted from the URL; useful for separate root layouts or grouping.
- `_components`: a **private folder**, opted out of routing.
- `@slot`: a **parallel route** slot rendered by the parent layout; in v16 each slot needs a `default` file.
- `(.)`, `(..)`, `(...)`: **intercepting routes**, for example a photo opening in a modal.

sections.heading: Dynamic segments and async params
Error and not-found boundaries
sections.body:
- `error` must be a **Client Component** and receives `{ error, retry }` (`retry` is stable since 16.3 and refetches; the older `reset` re-renders without refetching).
- Because `error` does not wrap the same segment's layout, errors thrown in a layout are caught by the parent segment's boundary; `global-error` handles the root and must render its own `<html>` and `<body>`.
- Calling `notFound()` renders the nearest `not-found` file.

keyPoints: A page file makes a segment routable; layout, template, error, loading and not-found nest in a fixed order.
Layouts persist and do not re-render on navigation; templates remount.
Route groups and private folders organize code without affecting the URL.
[[...slug]] also matches the base path; [...slug] does not.
params and searchParams must be awaited in Next 16.
error files are Client Components and do not catch errors from the same segment's layout.

gotchas.trap: Putting the session check in a layout so every child page is protected.
gotchas.correct: Layouts do not re-render on navigation; check auth close to the data (a Data Access Layer) and in each page or action.

gotchas.trap: Expecting app/dashboard/error.tsx to catch an error thrown in app/dashboard/layout.tsx.
gotchas.correct: Place the boundary in the parent segment (or global-error for the root layout).

gotchas.trap: Reading params.slug synchronously in Next 16.
gotchas.correct: await props.params first.

lessons.lab: Build app/(shop)/products/[[...filters]]/page.tsx with its own loading.tsx and error.tsx. Throw in the page, then in the layout, and observe which boundary catches each.

lessons.title: Server Data Fetching and Streaming
lessons.summary: Async Server Components, avoiding waterfalls, request-scoped deduplication, Suspense streaming and Partial Prerendering.

sections.heading: Fetching in async Server Components
sections.body: A Server Component can be `async` and `await` data directly: `fetch`, an ORM or a database client. No API route or client effect is needed for reads. Within one render pass, identical `fetch` calls are **memoized**; for non-fetch work (for example a DB query called from several components) wrap the function in **`React.cache`** to dedupe it per request.

sections.heading: Sequential versus parallel
Passing promises to the client
sections.body: A Server Component can start a fetch **without awaiting** and pass the Promise to a Client Component, which reads it with `use(promise)`. The client suspends to the nearest Suspense boundary. Create the promise on the server (stable), not during a client render, and handle rejection with an error boundary, since `use` cannot be called inside try/catch.

sections.heading: Streaming with Suspense and loading files
sections.body:
Streaming sends HTML in chunks: the parts that are ready render first and each `<Suspense>` fallback is replaced when its data arrives. `loading` wraps the whole page in a boundary; finer `<Suspense>` boundaries let fast parts show while slow ones load.

- Once streaming starts, the HTTP status is already **200**. `notFound()` mid-stream injects `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">`, and `redirect()` mid-stream becomes a client-side redirect.
- Intermediaries can buffer the stream: Nginx (send `X-Accel-Buffering: no`), compression proxies, Lambda without response streaming, or `curl` without `-N`.

sections.heading: Where Partial Prerendering fits
sections.body: **Partial Prerendering (PPR)** combines a static shell, prerendered at build time, with dynamic holes that stream in through Suspense. In Next 16 the `experimental.ppr` flag and `experimental_ppr` segment config were removed; PPR comes with **`cacheComponents: true`**, which create-next-app enables by default since 16.4. Content outside Suspense that needs request data, or that is not cached with `'use cache'`, has to be wrapped in Suspense so the shell can still be prerendered.

keyPoints: Async Server Components await data directly; fetch is memoized per render pass, React.cache dedupes other work per request.
Use Promise.all or start promises early to avoid waterfalls.
Pass an unawaited server promise to a Client Component and read it with use().
loading wraps the page in Suspense; finer Suspense boundaries stream independently.
Streaming commits a 200 status; later notFound/redirect are handled in-page.
PPR = static shell + streamed dynamic holes, enabled via cacheComponents in Next 16.

gotchas.trap: await getUser(); await getPosts(); for independent data.
gotchas.correct: Start both and await Promise.all, or split into Suspense-wrapped siblings.

gotchas.trap: Creating a new promise inside a Client Component render and passing it to use().
gotchas.correct: Create the promise on the server (or cache it) and pass it down.

gotchas.trap: Enabling experimental.ppr in Next 16.
gotchas.correct: The flag was removed; set cacheComponents: true.

lessons.lab: Build a dashboard page with three slow fetches. Measure time to first byte with sequential awaits, then with Promise.all, then with three Suspense boundaries and fallbacks.

lessons.title: Route Handlers, Proxy and Runtimes
lessons.summary: What runs where: route.ts endpoints, proxy.ts on every matched request, and why Node is the default runtime.

sections.heading: Route Handlers
sections.body: A `route.ts` file in `app/` exports functions named after HTTP methods (`GET`, `POST`, ...) that take a Web `Request` and return a `Response`. They are for custom endpoints such as webhooks, feeds or public APIs. A `route` file cannot sit in the same segment as a `page` file. Without Cache Components, GET handlers are not cached by default (opt in with `export const dynamic = 'force-static'`); with Cache Components they follow the same prerendering model as pages.

sections.heading: proxy.ts replaces middleware.ts
sections.body:
In Next 16 the `middleware` file and export are deprecated; use `proxy.ts` exporting `proxy`. Proxy runs **before** routes are matched: after `headers` and `redirects` from config, and before `beforeFiles` rewrites and the filesystem. Without a `matcher` it runs on **every** request, including assets, so scope it.

Use it for lightweight work: redirects, rewrites, headers, and **optimistic** auth checks such as reading a session cookie. Do not do database-backed authorization there; re-check in the page, Data Access Layer and every Server Action.

sections.heading: Runtimes: Node.js by default
sections.body:
- Proxy runs on the **Node.js runtime only**; setting a `runtime` in proxy config throws. If you must stay on Edge, keep using the deprecated `middleware` file.
- The Edge runtime is **deprecated**; the adapter docs say new routes should use Node.js.
- Cache Components requires the Node runtime, so remove `export const runtime = 'edge'` when you enable it.

sections.heading: Choosing the right tool
sections.body:
| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Read data for a page | async Server Component |
| Mutation from your own UI | Server Function / Server Action |
| Endpoint for third parties, webhooks, non-HTML responses | Route Handler |
| Redirect / rewrite / header logic before routing | proxy.ts |

Calling your own Route Handler from a Server Component adds an unnecessary HTTP hop; call the data function directly.

keyPoints: route.ts exports HTTP-method functions using Web Request/Response; it cannot coexist with page in one segment.
proxy.ts (Next 16) replaces middleware.ts and runs before filesystem routing.
Proxy runs on Node.js only; scope it with a matcher.
Proxy is for optimistic checks; authorize again near the data.
The Edge runtime is deprecated; Cache Components needs Node.

gotchas.trap: Fetching /api/products from a Server Component to render a page.
gotchas.correct: Call the data function directly; the extra HTTP round trip adds latency.

gotchas.trap: Adding export const config = { runtime: "edge" } to proxy.ts.
gotchas.correct: Proxy is Node-only and setting runtime throws.

gotchas.trap: Treating proxy as the only authorization layer.
gotchas.correct: A matcher that excludes a path skips it; check auth in the DAL and in actions too.

lessons.lab: Rename middleware.ts to proxy.ts and its export to proxy, add a matcher that excludes static assets, and add a Route Handler that verifies a webhook signature before parsing the body.

lessons.title: Server Functions and Forms
lessons.summary: How to define Server Functions with 'use server', call them from forms and event handlers, and keep forms working before hydration.

sections.heading: What a Server Function is
sections.body:
A **Server Function** is an async function that runs on the server and that the client can call through a reference. In Next.js, a Server Function used for a mutation is called a **Server Action**.

- Mark one function with `'use server'` at the top of its body, or mark a whole module with `'use server'` at the top of the file. Then every export of that module becomes a Server Function.
- An inline `'use server'` function can be defined inside a **Server Component**. A **Client Component** cannot define one inline. It imports the function from a `'use server'` module or receives it as a prop.
- Arguments and return values cross the network, so they must be serializable.
- Under the hood, a call is sent as a **POST** request to the current page route.

sections.heading: Calling from a form
Calling from event handlers
Pending state and ordering
sections.body:
- `useFormStatus()` from `react-dom` reads the pending state of the **parent** `<form>`. It must be called from a component rendered **inside** that form, such as a submit button. It does not work in the component that renders the form.
- Next.js dispatches Server Actions **one at a time per client**. Wrapping several action calls in `Promise.all` does not make them run in parallel. For parallel reads, fetch data in Server Components or use Route Handlers.
- After a successful action, React 19 resets **uncontrolled** form fields automatically.

keyPoints: 'use server' marks a function or a whole module as callable from the client; Client Components import Server Functions, they never define them inline.
A Server Action is invoked through a POST to the page route; arguments and return values must be serializable.
A form rendered by a Server Component with action={fn} works before JavaScript loads (progressive enhancement).
Call actions from event handlers inside startTransition to get a pending state.
useFormStatus must be rendered inside the form whose status it reads.
Actions run sequentially per client, so they are not a tool for parallel data fetching.

gotchas.trap: Using Server Actions to fetch several data sets in parallel with Promise.all.
gotchas.correct: Actions are dispatched sequentially per client. Fetch data in Server Components, which can run requests in parallel.

gotchas.trap: Calling useFormStatus in the same component that renders the <form>.
gotchas.correct: Move it into a child component rendered inside the form, such as a SubmitButton.

gotchas.trap: Writing an inline 'use server' function inside a Client Component.
gotchas.correct: Put the function in a separate 'use server' module and import it, or pass it down from a Server Component.

lessons.lab: Build a "new post" page whose form is rendered by a Server Component and posts to a createPost action. Disable JavaScript in the browser and confirm the form still submits. Then add a SubmitButton that uses useFormStatus to show "Saving..." while the action runs.

lessons.title: Validation, Field Errors and Error Boundaries
lessons.summary: Parse FormData with Zod, return expected errors as state through useActionState, and leave unexpected failures to error boundaries.

sections.heading: Never trust FormData
Returning field errors with useActionState
Expected errors versus exceptions
sections.body:
The Next.js docs split errors into two kinds:

- **Expected errors**, such as invalid input or a duplicate email. Model them as **return values** and show them with `useActionState`. Do not throw them.
- **Uncaught exceptions**, which are bugs or outages. Let them throw; the nearest `error.js` boundary catches them. In production, the message of a server error is replaced by a generic one plus an `error.digest`, so you never leak internals.

Throwing inside an action called through `useActionState` also cancels any calls still in its queue.

sections.heading: Error boundaries in the App Router
sections.body:
- `error.js` must be a Client Component. In Next 16.3 and later it receives `{ error, retry }`; the older `reset` re-renders without refetching.
- An `error.js` file does not wrap the `layout` of its own segment, so put it one level higher to catch layout errors.
- Error boundaries do not catch errors thrown in event handlers. Handle those with `try/catch` and state.

keyPoints: Validate every field on the server inside the action; client checks are only for UX.
safeParse returns a result object instead of throwing, which suits returning field errors.
useActionState passes (prevState, formData) to the action and returns [state, formAction, isPending].
Expected errors are returned as values; unexpected errors throw to error.js.
Production replaces server error messages with a generic message and a digest.

gotchas.trap: Throwing a validation error from the action so error.js shows it.
gotchas.correct: Return the field errors as state and render them inline; error.js replaces the whole segment and loses the form.

gotchas.trap: Relying on the input's required attribute as validation.
gotchas.correct: Anyone can POST to an action directly. Validate on the server every time.

gotchas.trap: Keeping the (formData) signature after switching to useActionState.
gotchas.correct: The action now receives prevState first and formData second.

lessons.title: Revalidation, Redirects and Optimistic UI
lessons.summary: Keep data consistent after a mutation with updateTag, revalidateTag, revalidatePath, refresh and redirect, and show instant feedback with useOptimistic.

sections.heading: Choosing a revalidation API
sections.body:
After a write, cached reads must be updated. Next 16 offers several APIs:

| API | Where it can run | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `updateTag(tag)` | Server Actions only | Expires the tag and refreshes it in the same request, so the user reads their own write |
| `revalidateTag(tag, 'max')` | Server Functions and Route Handlers | Stale-while-revalidate: the next visitor may get stale data while it refreshes in the background |
| `revalidatePath(path, type?)` | Server Functions and Route Handlers | Invalidates a route. Pass `'page'` or `'layout'` for dynamic patterns |
| `refresh()` | Server Actions | Refreshes uncached data and the client router |

`revalidateTag(tag)` with a single argument is deprecated in Next 16. Pass a profile such as `'max'`.

sections.heading: Read-your-own-writes
sections.body:
When a user edits their profile and the page reloads with the old value, the feedback is wrong. Inside a Server Action, `updateTag` fixes it, because the response already contains the fresh data.

For writes that come from outside the app, such as a CMS webhook hitting a Route Handler, use `revalidateTag(tag, 'max')`. `updateTag` is not allowed there, and stale-while-revalidate is acceptable for those readers.

Revalidating inside a Server Action also clears the client router cache. The action's response carries the new RSC payload, so the UI updates in a single round trip.

sections.heading: redirect after a mutation
Optimistic UI with useOptimistic
sections.body:
`useOptimistic(value, reducer?)` returns `[optimisticValue, setOptimistic]`. It shows a temporary value while an Action is in flight:

- Call the setter **inside an Action or Transition**, for example inside a form action or `startTransition`. Outside one, React warns and the value flips straight back.
- When the Action finishes, the optimistic value converges with the real `value` prop. If the server rejects the write, the UI falls back to the real data, so no manual rollback is needed.
- Optimistic UI changes only what the user sees. You still revalidate on the server so every other reader gets the truth.

keyPoints: updateTag is for Server Actions and gives read-your-own-writes; revalidateTag(tag, "max") is stale-while-revalidate and also works in Route Handlers.
Single-argument revalidateTag is deprecated in Next 16.
redirect() throws: revalidate first, and keep it out of catch-all try blocks.
useOptimistic setters must run inside an Action or Transition.
The optimistic value converges with the real value when the Action ends, which also handles failures.

gotchas.trap: Calling redirect() and then revalidatePath() on the next line.
gotchas.correct: redirect throws, so the revalidation never runs. Revalidate first.

gotchas.trap: Using updateTag in a webhook Route Handler.
gotchas.correct: updateTag is for Server Actions only; use revalidateTag(tag, "max") in Route Handlers.

gotchas.trap: Calling setOptimistic in a plain onClick without a Transition.
gotchas.correct: Wrap it in startTransition together with the action call, or call it from a form action.

lessons.lab: Build a todo list where adding an item uses useOptimistic to show it immediately, then calls a Server Action that inserts the row and calls updateTag("todos"). Make the action fail randomly and watch the optimistic item disappear.

lessons.title: Securing Server Functions and Client-Side Data
lessons.summary: Treat every Server Function as a public endpoint, check auth, authorization and input in each one, and choose between server rendering and a client cache without race conditions.

sections.heading: Every action is a public endpoint
sections.body:
The Next.js data security guide is explicit: a Server Action can be called directly with a POST request, not only through your UI. Hiding a button does not protect the action behind it.

Next.js adds some built-in protection:

- **CSRF:** it compares the `Origin` header with `Host` (or `X-Forwarded-Host`). Behind a reverse proxy, list trusted origins in `serverActions.allowedOrigins`.
- **Body size:** a default request body limit applies, configurable with `serverActions.bodySizeLimit`.
- **IDs:** action IDs are encrypted and non-deterministic, and unused actions are removed from the client bundle.
- **Closures:** variables a closure captures are encrypted. Multi-instance deployments need one shared `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.

None of this checks **who** is calling or **what** they may touch.

sections.heading: The checks every action needs
sections.body:
Inside every action, before any write:

1. **Authenticate:** verify the session, for example through a Data Access Layer `verifySession()`.
2. **Authorize the specific resource:** confirm this user owns or may edit the given id. Skipping this is an IDOR (insecure direct object reference) bug.
3. **Validate input** with a schema; ids, hidden fields and enums all count as input.
4. **Return minimal data:** never return whole database rows to the client.

Do not rely on a layout or on Proxy for this. Layouts do not re-render on navigation, and a Proxy `matcher` that excludes a path also skips the actions posted to that path. Treat Proxy as an optimistic check only.

sections.heading: Server rendering or a client cache
Race conditions and cancellation

keyPoints: A Server Action is reachable by direct POST; UI hiding is not access control.
Built-in CSRF, ID encryption and body limits do not replace authentication and authorization.
Every action: authenticate, authorize the specific resource, validate input, return minimal data.
Proxy and layouts are not authorization boundaries for actions.
Prefer Server Component fetching; use a client cache for live, interactive or shared client data.
Guard client fetches against out-of-order responses with an ignore flag and AbortController.

gotchas.trap: "The action is only reachable from the admin page, so it is safe."
gotchas.correct: Anyone can POST to it. Check the session and role inside the action.

gotchas.trap: Checking that the user is logged in but not that they own the record.
gotchas.correct: Authorize the specific resource id against the session user to prevent IDOR.

gotchas.trap: Fetching in useEffect without cleanup when the query changes.
gotchas.correct: Set an ignore flag (and abort) in cleanup so stale responses are dropped.

lessons.lab: Write a deletePost(id) action. First call it with curl or a script for a post owned by another user and observe it succeed. Then add verifySession, an ownership check and a Zod schema for id, and confirm the same request is rejected.

lessons.title: Static vs dynamic rendering and choosing a strategy per page
lessons.summary: How Next.js 16 decides what is prerendered and what waits for a request, what makes part of a route dynamic, and how to pick a rendering strategy for each kind of page in a SaaS app.

sections.heading: Two models, one goal
sections.body:
Next.js 16 supports two rendering and caching models:

- **Cache Components** (`cacheComponents: true` in `next.config`), the recommended model. It is on by default in new create-next-app projects since 16.4 and is planned as the framework default in Next 17.
- **The previous model**, documented as "caching without Cache Components", where whole routes are classified as static or dynamic and segment configs such as `dynamic` and `revalidate` control them.

Both answer the same question: which parts of a page can be produced ahead of time and reused, and which must be computed per request.

sections.heading: What makes rendering dynamic
sections.body:
Data that only exists at request time forces work to wait for the request:

- `cookies()` and `headers()`
- `searchParams` (and `params` for paths not generated ahead of time)
- `draftMode()`
- non-deterministic values such as `Math.random()`, `Date.now()` or `crypto.randomUUID()`

In Next 16 the request APIs are **async** and must be awaited; synchronous access was removed. In the previous model, touching any of them makes the **whole route** dynamic. With Cache Components the unit is smaller: the static parts become a prerendered **shell** and the request-dependent parts become **dynamic holes** that stream in.

sections.heading: Cache Components: shell plus holes
Choosing a strategy per page
sections.body:
A typical SaaS app has four kinds of pages:

| Page | Strategy |
|---|---|
| **Marketing / docs / pricing** | Fully cached: `'use cache'` with a long `cacheLife` and a `cacheTag`, refreshed on demand by a CMS webhook calling `revalidateTag(tag, 'max')`. |
| **Dashboard (shared chrome, per-user data)** | Static shell (nav, layout, skeletons) with user data in Suspense holes that read the session. |
| **User-specific but cacheable** | Read cookies outside the cache, pass the user or tenant id as an **argument** to a `'use cache'` function so it is part of the key; or use `'use cache: private'`, which is cached in the browser only. |
| **Real-time (live feeds, prices, presence)** | Not cached on the server: `await connection()` inside Suspense, with client-side updates (polling or a subscription) on top. |

The rule of thumb is to cache the most you safely can and to keep the per-request work as small as possible.

sections.heading: Streaming details that affect behaviour
sections.body:
- `loading.js` wraps the page in a Suspense boundary.
- Once streaming starts, the status code is already 200. A `notFound()` thrown mid-stream adds `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">`, and a `redirect()` mid-stream becomes a client-side redirect.
- Intermediaries can buffer streams: Nginx (fix with `X-Accel-Buffering: no`), compression proxies, AWS Lambda without response streaming, and `curl` without `-N`.

keyPoints: cookies(), headers(), searchParams and draftMode() are request-time data; in Next 16 they must be awaited.
In the previous model one request API makes the whole route dynamic; with Cache Components only the Suspense-wrapped hole is dynamic.
Non-deterministic values need await connection() plus Suspense, or a cache boundary.
Pick per page: cached marketing, shell plus holes for dashboards, keyed or private caches for per-user data, uncached for real-time.

gotchas.trap: Reading cookies() in the root layout to show the user name is harmless.
gotchas.correct: A request API high in the tree makes far more of the output request-dependent. Read it in a small component inside Suspense.

gotchas.trap: A route can return a 404 status after it has started streaming.
gotchas.correct: The status is already 200 once streaming starts; notFound() mid-stream injects a noindex meta tag instead.

lessons.lab: Enable cacheComponents in a sample app, build a page with a static hero and a component that reads cookies(), and run next build. Note the error you get without Suspense, then add a Suspense boundary and compare the build output.

lessons.title: The caching layers: 'use cache', cacheLife and cacheTag
lessons.summary: What the 'use cache' directive caches, how its key is built, where entries are stored, how cacheLife profiles work, and how the previous fetch-based caching model differs.

sections.heading: The 'use cache' directive
sections.body:
`'use cache'` marks a file, a component or a function as cacheable. It only applies to **async** functions.

```ts
import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function getPlans() {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('days')
  cacheTag('plans')
  return db.plan.findMany()
}
```

The **cache key** is made from the build ID (or `deploymentId`), the function ID, the serialized arguments and any closed-over values. Children and Server Actions passed in are not introspected; they pass through. `cacheLife` and `cacheTag` are stable (no `unstable_` prefix).

sections.heading: What is not allowed inside a cache
sections.body:
- `cookies()`, `headers()` and `searchParams` cannot be read inside a `'use cache'` scope (error `next-request-in-use-cache`). Read them outside and pass the **values** in as arguments, so they become part of the key.
- Do not pass promises of runtime data into the scope: prerendering hangs and eventually fails with a "Filling a cache during prerender timed out" error.
- `React.cache` is isolated inside `'use cache'`.
- `'use cache'` has no effect in Proxy.

Forgetting to put the tenant or user id in the arguments is the classic way to serve one customer's data to another.

sections.heading: Where entries live
sections.body:
| Variant | Storage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `'use cache'` | In-memory LRU on the server instance | Does not persist across serverless invocations and does not survive deploys. |
| `'use cache: remote'` | A durable, shared cache handler | Use when instances must share entries. |
| `'use cache: private'` | The browser only | May read `cookies()`, `headers()` and `searchParams` (not `connection()`); excluded from the static shell; no custom handlers. |

Self-hosted multi-instance deployments configure a shared `cacheHandler` / `cacheHandlers` implementation.

sections.heading: cacheLife profiles
sections.body:
Each profile has three values:

- **stale**: how long the client may use the entry without asking the server;
- **revalidate**: after this, the next request is served the cached value while it refreshes in the background;
- **expire**: after this with no traffic, the entry must be regenerated before it is served.

| Profile | stale | revalidate | expire |
|---|---|---|---|
| default | 5m | 15m | never |
| seconds | 30s | 1s | 60s |
| minutes | 5m | 1m | 1h |
| hours | 5m | 1h | 1d |
| days | 5m | 1d | 1w |
| weeks | 5m | 1w | 30d |
| max | 5m | 30d | 1y |

- The client enforces a minimum stale time of 30 seconds.
- An entry with `revalidate: 0` or an `expire` under 5 minutes is treated as a **dynamic hole** rather than being prerendered, and a stale time under 30s is excluded from prerendering.
- Nested caches: an outer cache without an explicit `cacheLife` uses the `default` profile; shorter inner lifetimes reduce it, longer ones cannot extend it. An explicit outer `cacheLife` always takes precedence.
- If a short-lived cache (`revalidate: 0` or `expire` under 5 minutes, such as the `seconds` profile) is nested in an outer cache with no explicit `cacheLife`, Next.js throws an error during prerendering; set an explicit lifetime on the outer cache.

sections.heading: The previous model
sections.body:
Without Cache Components:

- `fetch` is **not** cached by default; opt in with `cache: 'force-cache'` or `next: { revalidate: n }`.
- `unstable_cache` caches non-fetch work.
- Segment configs `dynamic`, `revalidate` (must be statically analyzable) and `fetchCache` control whole routes.
- GET Route Handlers are not cached by default; opt in with `export const dynamic = 'force-static'`. With Cache Components, GET handlers follow the same prerender model as pages.

The old `experimental.ppr`, `experimental.dynamicIO` and `experimental.useCache` flags were removed in favour of the top-level `cacheComponents` option.

keyPoints: 'use cache' works only on async functions; its key includes arguments and closed-over values.
Request APIs are forbidden inside a cache; pass their values in as arguments.
Default storage is a per-instance in-memory LRU; use 'use cache: remote' or a shared handler for durability.
cacheLife profiles set stale, revalidate and expire; very short lifetimes turn the entry into a dynamic hole.
In the previous model fetch is uncached by default; opt in with force-cache or next.revalidate.

gotchas.trap: Adding 'use cache' to a function that fetches the current user's invoices is fine as long as it reads the session inside.
gotchas.correct: Request APIs cannot be read inside the cache. Read the session outside and pass the user id as an argument so it is part of the key.

gotchas.trap: Plain 'use cache' entries are shared across all serverless instances and survive a redeploy.
gotchas.correct: The default is an in-memory LRU per instance; entries do not survive deploys. Use 'use cache: remote' or a shared cache handler.

gotchas.trap: fetch calls are cached by default in the App Router.
gotchas.correct: Without Cache Components, fetch is not cached unless you opt in; with Cache Components, caching is opted into with use cache.

lessons.lab: Write a cached getPlans() with cacheLife('hours') and cacheTag('plans'), then a second function that takes a tenantId argument. Log inside each and confirm when the body re-runs for the same and different arguments.
