lessons.title: Revalidation: time-based, on-demand and CDN headers
lessons.summary: Keeping cached content fresh with cacheLife timers and tag-based invalidation, picking between revalidateTag, updateTag, revalidatePath and refresh, and what HTTP caching headers Next.js sends.

sections.heading: Time-based revalidation
sections.body: Time-based revalidation comes from the `revalidate` value of the entry's `cacheLife` profile (or `next: { revalidate }` / the `revalidate` segment config in the previous model). It behaves as **stale-while-revalidate**: after the window passes, the next visitor still gets the cached value while a fresh one is generated in the background. It suits content that changes on a predictable rhythm and where a little staleness is acceptable.

sections.heading: On-demand, tag-based revalidation
Time-based or tag-based?
sections.body:
- Use **tags** when you know exactly when the data changes (a CMS publish, an admin edit): content stays cached for a long time and refreshes right after the change.
- Use **time** when changes are frequent, external or not observable (a third-party price feed).
- Combine them: a long `cacheLife` as a safety net plus tag invalidation for known changes.
- After a user's own mutation in a Server Action, prefer `updateTag` so the response shows the new data instead of a stale copy.

sections.heading: CDN and HTTP caching headers
sections.body:
When self-hosting, Next.js sets:

- hashed static assets (`/_next/static`): `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, safe to cache forever because the file name changes with the content;
- dynamically rendered pages: `private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate`, so shared caches must not store them.

Do not override these headers to make per-user pages cacheable at a CDN; a shared cache keyed only by URL would serve one user's page to another. Multi-instance deployments also need a shared cache handler that implements tag refresh, plus a `deploymentId`, so that revalidation reaches every instance.

keyPoints: Time-based revalidation is stale-while-revalidate: the first visitor after the window gets the old value.
revalidateTag(tag, 'max') is for webhooks and Route Handlers; updateTag is Server Actions only, for read-your-own-writes.
One-argument revalidateTag is deprecated in Next 16.
Hashed static assets are immutable for a year; dynamic pages are sent as private, no-store.

gotchas.trap: Call updateTag from the CMS webhook Route Handler.
gotchas.correct: updateTag only works in Server Actions. In a Route Handler use revalidateTag(tag, 'max').

gotchas.trap: revalidateTag(tag, 'max') makes the very next request wait for fresh data.
gotchas.correct: It is stale-while-revalidate: the next request can still get the stale entry while a fresh one is generated. Use updateTag in a Server Action, or expire: 0, for immediate expiry.

lessons.lab: Build a Route Handler that verifies a shared secret and calls revalidateTag(tag, 'max') on a tagged cached function. Trigger it with curl and observe that the next page load can still return the old value while a fresh one is generated in the background, and a later load returns the new value.

lessons.title: Images, fonts and scripts
lessons.summary: How next/image, next/font and next/script affect LCP, CLS and main-thread time, and the Next 16 defaults to know.

sections.heading: next/image
sections.body:
The Image component optimizes, resizes and serves modern formats, and it **lazy-loads by default**.

- Give it `width` and `height` (or use `fill` inside a sized container, or a static import) so the browser reserves space and the layout does not shift.
- For the **LCP image**, do not leave it lazy: use `loading="eager"` or `fetchPriority="high"`, or the `preload` prop. The `priority` prop is deprecated in Next 16 in favour of `preload`.
- Next 16 defaults: `minimumCacheTTL` of 14400 seconds (was 60), `qualities: [75]`, `maximumRedirects: 3`, local IPs blocked unless explicitly allowed, and `images.domains` deprecated in favour of `remotePatterns`.

```tsx
import Image from 'next/image'

<Image src="/hero.jpg" alt="Product dashboard" width={1200} height={630} fetchPriority="high" loading="eager" />
```

sections.heading: next/font
next/script
sections.body:
`next/script` controls when third-party scripts load:

| Strategy | When it loads | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `beforeInteractive` | Before hydration; must be in the root layout | Rare, truly critical scripts (bot detection, consent) |
| `afterInteractive` (default) | After some hydration | Tag managers, analytics |
| `lazyOnload` | During browser idle time | Chat widgets, social embeds |
| `worker` | Off the main thread (experimental) | Not supported with the App Router |

Moving non-critical scripts to `lazyOnload` frees the main thread during load and helps interaction responsiveness.

keyPoints: next/image is lazy by default; mark the LCP image eager or high priority, using preload instead of the deprecated priority prop.
Always reserve image space with width/height or fill to avoid CLS.
next/font self-hosts at build time; no runtime requests to Google, display swap by default.
next/script: beforeInteractive only in the root layout, afterInteractive is the default, lazyOnload for non-critical widgets, worker is not for the App Router.

gotchas.trap: Keep the hero image on default settings; next/image makes it fast automatically.
gotchas.correct: The default is lazy loading, which delays the LCP image. Set loading="eager" or fetchPriority="high" (or preload).

gotchas.trap: Use the priority prop on the hero image in Next 16.
gotchas.correct: priority is deprecated in v16; use preload, or loading="eager" / fetchPriority="high".

gotchas.trap: Load a chat widget with beforeInteractive so it is ready sooner.
gotchas.correct: beforeInteractive is for critical scripts and belongs in the root layout; a chat widget should use lazyOnload.

lessons.lab: Run Lighthouse on a page with a lazy hero image, a Google font loaded by a link tag and a chat script in the head. Switch to next/image with fetchPriority="high", next/font and next/script lazyOnload, and compare LCP, CLS and Total Blocking Time.

lessons.title: Core Web Vitals in a Next.js app
lessons.summary: What LCP, INP and CLS measure, how they are scored at the 75th percentile in the field, and the usual causes and fixes for each in a React and Next.js app.

sections.heading: Thresholds and measurement
sections.body:
Core Web Vitals are three field metrics. Each one is judged at the **75th percentile** of page loads, with mobile and desktop segmented separately, so a page passes only if at least 75% of real visits meet the "good" threshold.

| Metric | Measures | Good | Poor |
|---|---|---|---|
| LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) | loading | ≤ 2.5 s | > 4 s |
| INP (Interaction to Next Paint) | responsiveness | ≤ 200 ms | > 500 ms |
| CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) | visual stability | ≤ 0.1 | > 0.25 |

Values between the two thresholds are "needs improvement". Field data (real users) is the source of truth. Lab tools such as Lighthouse cannot measure INP because there is no real user interacting, so they report **Total Blocking Time (TBT)** as a proxy.

sections.heading: LCP: the hero element
sections.body:
LCP is the render time of the largest image or text block in the viewport. web.dev splits it into four subparts, with an approximate target split for a good LCP:

- **TTFB**: about 40%
- **Resource load delay**: under 10% (how late the browser discovers the image)
- **Resource load duration**: about 40%
- **Element render delay**: under 10%

Common causes in Next.js:

- The LCP image uses `next/image`, which is **lazy by default**, so its fetch starts late. Mark the hero image with `preload` (which replaces the deprecated `priority` in v16), or `loading="eager"` / `fetchPriority="high"`.
- The LCP element sits **inside a Suspense fallback** or behind a slow data await, so it only appears when that boundary streams in. Keep the LCP element in the shell, outside the boundary.
- Slow TTFB from blocking server work that could have been cached or streamed.

```tsx
import Image from 'next/image';

export function Hero() {
  return <Image src="/hero.jpg" alt="Mountain lake at dawn" width={1200} height={600} preload />;
}
```

sections.heading: INP: responsiveness to input
sections.body:
INP observes click, tap and keyboard interactions (not hover or scroll) across the whole visit and reports one of the slowest. It ignores the single highest interaction for every 50, so one outlier does not dominate a long session.

Each interaction has three phases:

1. **Input delay**: the main thread is busy with something else (hydration, a long task from a third-party script).
2. **Processing duration**: your event handlers run. In React this includes the synchronous re-render they trigger.
3. **Presentation delay**: layout, paint and the work of rendering a large DOM.

React-specific fixes: mark non-urgent updates as Transitions so the urgent update paints first, defer expensive derived UI with `useDeferredValue`, avoid re-rendering huge trees on every keystroke, and keep the DOM small (virtualize long lists).

sections.heading: CLS: unexpected layout shifts
sections.body:
Each layout shift scores **impact fraction × distance fraction**. The impact fraction is the union of the unstable element's area before and after the shift, so an element covering half the viewport that moves down by 25% of it has an impact fraction of 0.75 and scores 0.75 × 0.25 = 0.1875. Shifts are grouped into **session windows** (gaps under 1 s, at most 5 s per window), and the worst window is the page's CLS. Shifts within 500 ms of user input are excluded, because the user expected them.

Common causes and fixes:

- Images and embeds without dimensions. `next/image` requires `width`/`height` (or `fill` in a sized container), which reserves space.
- Web fonts swapping in with different metrics. `next/font` self-hosts fonts at build time and uses `adjustFontFallback` to size the fallback font so the swap barely moves text.
- Content injected above existing content (banners, consent bars, late ads). Reserve the space or overlay it.
- Loading skeletons whose size differs from the final content.

keyPoints: Core Web Vitals are scored at the 75th percentile of field data, segmented by mobile and desktop.
Good thresholds: LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1; poor is above 4 s, 500 ms and 0.25.
Lighthouse cannot measure INP; it reports Total Blocking Time as a lab proxy.
next/image is lazy by default, so mark the LCP image with preload (or loading="eager" / fetchPriority="high"); priority is deprecated in v16.
A layout shift scores impact fraction × distance fraction; shifts within 500 ms of input do not count.

gotchas.trap: Wrapping the hero section in a Suspense boundary with a skeleton fallback improves LCP.
gotchas.correct: If the LCP element is inside the boundary it only paints when the boundary resolves. Keep the LCP element in the shell, outside Suspense fallbacks.

gotchas.trap: A great Lighthouse score proves INP is good.
gotchas.correct: INP needs real interactions and is a field metric. Lighthouse reports TBT as a proxy; confirm INP with field data.

gotchas.trap: Every layout shift counts against CLS.
gotchas.correct: Shifts within 500 ms of a user input are excluded, and only the worst session window counts.

lessons.lab: Run a production build of a Next.js page with a hero image. Record LCP in the browser performance panel, then change the hero from the default lazy next/image to one with preload and compare when the image request starts. Add a 300 px banner above the content after a 1 s timeout and watch the layout-shift entries appear; then reserve its space and confirm they disappear.

lessons.title: Rendering performance and bundle size
lessons.summary: Find and fix unnecessary re-renders, decide when memoization is still needed with the React Compiler, keep interactions responsive with Transitions and deferred values, and keep client JavaScript small.

sections.heading: Unnecessary re-renders and memoization
sections.body:
A component re-renders when its state changes, its parent re-renders, or a context it reads changes. Re-rendering is usually cheap; it becomes a problem when an expensive subtree re-renders on every keystroke or interaction and pushes INP up.

Manual tools:

- `memo(Component)` skips re-rendering when props are shallowly equal.
- `useMemo` caches an expensive computed value; `useCallback` caches a function so a memoized child receives a stable prop.
- Moving state down (colocation) or passing JSX as `children` keeps fast-changing state away from slow subtrees.

sections.heading: The React Compiler
sections.body:
React Compiler 1.0 (October 2025) is a build-time tool that **automatically memoizes components and hooks**, so most hand-written `memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` becomes unnecessary in new code. Key facts:

- It works with React 17 and later (below 19 via `react-compiler-runtime`).
- It memoizes components and hooks only, not arbitrary functions.
- **Keep existing `useMemo` / `useCallback`**: removing them can change the compiler's output. Use them in new code as escape hatches when you need precise control, such as a value used as an Effect dependency.
- Its lint rules live in `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` (recommended preset). Pin an exact compiler version.
- In Next.js 16, `reactCompiler: true` is stable but **not on by default**. It needs `babel-plugin-react-compiler`, and build times go up.
- React DevTools shows a "Memo ✨" badge on compiled components.

sections.heading: Transitions and deferred values
Virtualization
sections.body: A list of thousands of rows creates thousands of DOM nodes. A large DOM makes every render, style recalculation and layout slower, which shows up as presentation delay in INP. **Virtualization (windowing)** renders only the rows in or near the viewport and swaps them as the user scrolls. Memoization does not fix this: it skips React work but leaves the browser with the same huge DOM.

sections.heading: Bundle size: splitting and server-only code
sections.body:
Less client JavaScript means less to download, parse and hydrate, which helps both LCP and INP.

- **Server Components ship no component JavaScript.** Everything imported by a `'use client'` module joins the client bundle, so put the boundary as low in the tree as possible.
- **Code splitting:** load heavy client-only widgets on demand with `next/dynamic` or `React.lazy`. `dynamic(..., { ssr: false })` is only allowed inside a Client Component; using it in a Server Component is an error.
- **Keep secrets and heavy server libraries out of the client:** add `import 'server-only'` to modules that must never be bundled for the browser. A wrong-side import then fails the build.
- **Third-party scripts:** `next/script` defaults to `afterInteractive`; use `lazyOnload` for low-priority scripts so they do not compete with hydration.
- **Analysing bundles:** Next 16 removed the "size / First Load JS" build output. Use the bundle analyzer (added for Turbopack in 16.1) to see which modules end up in which chunk.

keyPoints: React Compiler auto-memoizes components and hooks; keep existing useMemo/useCallback rather than deleting them.
reactCompiler: true is stable in Next 16 but off by default and needs babel-plugin-react-compiler.
useDeferredValue has no fixed delay, and the slow child must be memoized to benefit.
useTransition cannot control a text input value; keep the input urgent and defer the expensive part.
Virtualize long lists: memoization does not shrink the DOM.
dynamic(..., { ssr: false }) must live in a Client Component; 'server-only' turns wrong-side imports into build errors.

gotchas.trap: With the React Compiler on, delete every useMemo and useCallback in the codebase.
gotchas.correct: Keep existing ones; removing them can change compiler output. Rely on the compiler for new code and use the hooks as escape hatches.

gotchas.trap: useDeferredValue delays rendering by a fixed debounce interval.
gotchas.correct: It has no fixed delay. React renders the deferred value in the background as soon as the urgent render finishes, and interrupts it if a newer value arrives.

gotchas.trap: Calling dynamic(() => import('./Chart'), { ssr: false }) directly in a Server Component page.
gotchas.correct: That is an error. Put the dynamic import in a Client Component and render that from the server page.

lessons.lab: Build a search page that filters 10,000 items on every keystroke and profile typing with React DevTools. Then: (1) wrap the list in memo and feed it useDeferredValue(query); (2) virtualize the list; (3) move the chart widget behind next/dynamic in a Client Component. Compare the profiler and the bundle analyzer output after each step.

lessons.title: Hydration and accessible React UIs
lessons.summary: What hydration does, why mismatches happen and how to fix them, how Suspense enables selective hydration, and the accessibility basics (semantic HTML, focus, forms, live regions) required by WCAG 2.2 AA.

sections.heading: What hydration is
sections.body:
Server rendering sends HTML so the page can be seen before JavaScript runs. **Hydration** is React attaching to that existing HTML on the client: it renders the same tree, attaches event handlers and takes over. For this to work, the first client render must produce the **same markup** as the server.

Each Suspense boundary hydrates independently (**selective hydration**), so a slow, data-heavy part of the page does not block the rest from becoming interactive. Hydration is main-thread work, so a large client tree also adds input delay to early interactions (INP).

sections.heading: Hydration mismatches: causes and fixes
sections.body:
Common causes listed in the Next.js docs: - **Invalid HTML nesting**, such as a `
` inside a `

`, or a `

` inside another `

`. The browser repairs the HTML so the DOM no longer matches. - Branches on `typeof window` or other browser-only APIs during render. - **Time and locale** values: `Date.now()`, `new Date().toLocaleString()`, random IDs. - Browser extensions that modify the HTML, CSS-in-JS misconfiguration, and CDN HTML minification. Fixes: - Render client-only values **after mount** in `useEffect` (render a stable placeholder on the server and the first client render). - Disable SSR for a client-only component with `dynamic(..., { ssr: false })` inside a Client Component. - `suppressHydrationWarning` for unavoidable differences such as a timestamp. It only works **one level deep** and is an escape hatch, not a fix. - Fix the HTML nesting.

sections.heading: Semantic HTML and focus on navigation
sections.body:
Prefer native elements: `<button>` for actions, `<a>`/`<Link>` for navigation, `<label>` tied to inputs, headings in order, and landmarks (`<nav>`, `<main>`). A clickable `<div>` has no role, no keyboard focus and no Enter/Space activation unless you rebuild them all.

In a single-page navigation the browser does not reload, so screen-reader users get no automatic signal. Next.js includes a **route announcer** that announces the new page, using the document title (then the first `<h1>`, then the pathname). Give every route a unique, descriptive title through metadata. For custom flows such as dialogs, move focus into the dialog on open and return it to the trigger on close.

WCAG 2.2 adds **2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)** (AA): a focused element must not be entirely hidden by author content such as a sticky header or cookie bar.

sections.heading: Forms, live regions and WCAG 2.2
sections.body:
- Every input needs a programmatic label; error messages should be associated with the field (for example via `aria-describedby`) and describe how to fix the problem.
- **4.1.3 Status Messages** (AA): messages such as "Saving…", "3 results" or "Saved" must be announced without moving focus. Use `role="status"` or `aria-live="polite"` on a region that exists in the DOM before the message is inserted.

New criteria in WCAG 2.2 (W3C Recommendation):

| Criterion | Level |
|---|---|
| 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) | AA |
| 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) | AAA |
| 2.4.13 Focus Appearance | AAA |
| 2.5.7 Dragging Movements | AA |
| 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), 24×24 CSS px | AA |
| 3.2.6 Consistent Help | A |
| 3.3.7 Redundant Entry | A |
| 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) | AA |
| 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) | AAA |

4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete and removed in 2.2.

keyPoints: Hydration requires the first client render to match the server HTML.
Typical mismatch causes: invalid nesting, typeof window branches, dates and locales, browser extensions.
suppressHydrationWarning works only one level deep and is an escape hatch.
Each Suspense boundary hydrates independently (selective hydration).
Next.js announces route changes using the page title; give each route a unique title.
WCAG 2.2 AA adds Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), Dragging Movements, Target Size (Minimum) and Accessible Authentication (Minimum); 4.1.1 Parsing is removed.

gotchas.trap: Put suppressHydrationWarning on <body> to silence every mismatch in the app.
gotchas.correct: It only applies one level deep, to the element it is on. Fix the cause or render client-only values after mount.

gotchas.trap: Render the "Saved" message into a brand-new aria-live element when the action finishes.
gotchas.correct: Live regions should already be in the DOM; update the content of an existing role="status" region so assistive tech announces it.

gotchas.trap: Target Size (Minimum) in WCAG 2.2 requires 44×44 px targets at AA.
gotchas.correct: 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) is AA at 24×24 CSS px; the stricter 44×44 criterion is AAA.

lessons.lab: Create a Client Component that renders new Date().toLocaleTimeString() and observe the hydration error in development. Fix it by rendering a placeholder and setting the time in useEffect. Then add a form whose submit shows "Saving…" and "Saved" in a role="status" region and check with a screen reader that both are announced without focus moving.

lessons.title: Authentication, cookies and web security in Next.js
lessons.summary: How sessions are carried in cookies, where authorization really belongs (the data layer, not layouts or proxy), how CSRF and XSS defenses fit together, and how to keep secrets on the server.

sections.heading: Sessions: stateless cookies vs database sessions
Cookie attributes that matter
sections.body:
From MDN `Set-Cookie`:

| Attribute | Effect |
|---|---|
| `HttpOnly` | Not readable from JavaScript (`document.cookie`), which limits what an XSS payload can steal |
| `Secure` | Sent only over HTTPS |
| `SameSite=Lax` | Not sent on most cross-site subrequests, but **still sent on top-level GET navigations** |
| `SameSite=None` | Sent cross-site; **requires `Secure`** |
| `__Host-` name prefix | Requires `Secure` and `Path=/` and forbids `Domain`, so a sibling subdomain cannot overwrite it |
| `Max-Age` vs `Expires` | If both are set, `Max-Age` wins |

Because Lax still allows top-level GET navigations, never perform state changes on GET.

sections.heading: Protect data at the data layer
sections.body:
The guide recommends a **Data Access Layer (DAL)**: a `server-only` module with a `verifySession()` helper (wrapped in `React.cache` to dedupe within a render) that every data function calls before reading or writing.

- **Layouts are not an auth boundary.** Layouts do not re-render on client navigation, so a check in a layout can be skipped; and a page or action can be reached without it.
- **Proxy (`proxy.ts`) is for optimistic checks only**, such as redirecting when no session cookie exists. It should not be the only gate, and a matcher that excludes a path also skips that path's Server Actions.
- **Server Actions are public POST endpoints.** Each one must authenticate, authorize the specific resource (to avoid IDOR), validate its input and return only what the UI needs.
- Note that `React.cache` has no effect inside Server Actions and Route Handlers, so it only dedupes during rendering.

sections.heading: CSRF
sections.body:
For Server Actions, Next.js only accepts POST and compares the `Origin` header with `Host` (or `X-Forwarded-Host`); behind a reverse proxy on a different host you configure `serverActions.allowedOrigins`. Custom Route Handlers do not get that action-specific check, so audit them yourself.

OWASP adds two points:

- Fetch Metadata headers (`Sec-Fetch-Site`) are a strong primary signal; `SameSite` cookies are defense in depth, not a complete defense.
- **Any XSS defeats CSRF defenses**, because script running on your origin can make same-origin requests.

sections.heading: XSS, dangerouslySetInnerHTML and CSP
sections.body:
React escapes text you render in JSX. The escape hatch `dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html }}` inserts raw HTML, so any untrusted input must be sanitized first (OWASP suggests a library such as DOMPurify).

A **Content-Security-Policy** is defense in depth, not the primary defense. In Next.js, a nonce-based CSP is generated **per request in proxy**, usually with `'strict-dynamic'`, and `'unsafe-eval'` is allowed only in development. Because the nonce changes per request, a nonce CSP **forces dynamic rendering** and does not work with static shells / Partial Prerendering. The alternative for static pages is hash-based Subresource Integrity (experimental `experimental.sri`).

sections.heading: Secrets and environment variables
sections.body:
- Variables prefixed `NEXT_PUBLIC_` are **inlined into the client bundle at build time** and frozen; changing them later requires a rebuild. Never put secrets behind that prefix.
- Non-prefixed variables stay on the server. Dynamic lookups like `process.env[name]` are not inlined.
- `import 'server-only'` turns an accidental client import of a module into a build error; `client-only` does the reverse.
- Keep the framework patched: treat the November 2026 security release (16.4.5 / 15.5.29) as the minimum, and React Server Components versions patched for CVE-2025-55182.

keyPoints: Session cookies: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax, an expiry and Path=/.
Authorize in a server-only Data Access Layer, never only in a layout or proxy.
Every Server Action is a public endpoint: authenticate, authorize, validate.
SameSite is defense in depth; XSS defeats CSRF defenses.
Sanitize before dangerouslySetInnerHTML; CSP is a second layer.
Nonce CSP forces dynamic rendering; NEXT_PUBLIC_ values ship to the browser.

gotchas.trap: Checking the session in the root layout protects every page below it.
gotchas.correct: Layouts do not re-render on navigation and do not guard actions; check in the data layer and in each action.

gotchas.trap: SameSite=Lax makes CSRF impossible.
gotchas.correct: Lax still sends cookies on top-level GET navigations and is only defense in depth; never mutate on GET.

gotchas.trap: NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables can be changed at runtime per environment.
gotchas.correct: They are inlined at build time; a different value needs a new build.

gotchas.trap: A CSP lets you safely render unsanitized HTML.
gotchas.correct: Sanitize first; CSP only limits the damage if something slips through.

lessons.lab: Build a small app with a login Server Action that sets an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax session cookie. Add a server-only `dal.ts` with `verifySession()` and call it from a page and from a `deletePost` action that also checks ownership. Then remove the layout check and confirm the page and action are still protected. Finally add a nonce CSP in `proxy.ts` and observe that the affected routes now render dynamically.

lessons.title: Testing Next.js apps and building streaming AI interfaces
lessons.summary: Which layer to test with Testing Library and which with Playwright, how to test Server Components and actions, and how to stream model output from a Route Handler with cancellation and backpressure.

sections.heading: Choosing the test layer
sections.body:
The Next.js testing guide splits the work:

- **Unit and component tests** with Vitest or Jest plus React Testing Library work for Client Components and synchronous Server Components.
- **Async Server Components** are not well supported by those tools yet, so the docs **recommend end-to-end tests (Playwright)** for them.
- Server Actions and data functions are ordinary async functions; you can unit-test their logic (validation, authorization decisions) directly, and cover the wiring with E2E.
- Run Playwright against a production build (`next build` then `next start`) so you test what ships. Next 16.3 added an `instant()` helper in `@next/playwright`.

sections.heading: Testing Library habits
Playwright habits
sections.body:
- Use user-facing **locators** (`page.getByRole(...)`) rather than CSS chains tied to markup.
- Use **web-first assertions** such as `await expect(locator).toBeVisible()`, which retry until the condition holds; avoid fixed `waitForTimeout` sleeps.
- Keep tests **isolated**: each test gets a fresh browser context, so log in through a setup step or stored auth state instead of depending on another test's leftovers.

sections.heading: Streaming a model response from a Route Handler
Rendering partial output and cancelling

keyPoints: Async Server Components: test with Playwright E2E, per the Next.js docs.
Testing Library: getByRole first, findBy for async, user-event over fireEvent.
Playwright: role locators, auto-retrying web-first assertions, isolated tests.
Stream from a Route Handler; keep the API key server-side.
Forward request.signal upstream; abort on Stop and on unmount.
Decode with { stream: true } and append with an updater function.

gotchas.trap: Render an async Server Component in Vitest like any other component.
gotchas.correct: The docs recommend E2E tests for async Server Components; unit-test the underlying functions instead.

gotchas.trap: Add waitForTimeout(2000) to make a flaky Playwright test pass.
gotchas.correct: Use web-first assertions that retry until the expected state appears.

gotchas.trap: Call the model API from the browser with a NEXT_PUBLIC_ key for lower latency.
gotchas.correct: That ships the key to every visitor; proxy the call through a Route Handler.

gotchas.trap: Streaming works locally, so it will work behind any proxy.
gotchas.correct: Nginx, compression and non-streaming serverless can buffer the whole response.

lessons.lab: Write a Route Handler that streams a fake model response from a pull-based ReadableStream (one word per pull, with a short delay). Build a client chat box that renders partial text, has a Stop button using AbortController, and aborts in Effect cleanup. Write a Testing Library test for the form and a Playwright test that asserts the streamed text eventually appears and that Stop halts it.

lessons.title: Deploying, caching behind a CDN and observing Next.js in production
lessons.summary: Managed platforms vs self-hosting, output modes (Node server, standalone, static export), the cache headers Next.js emits, what multi-instance deployments need, and how to report errors with instrumentation.

sections.heading: Deployment options
sections.body:
The deploying guide lists four ways to run a Next.js app:

| Option | Features | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Node.js server (`next build` + `next start`) | All | You run and scale the process |
| Docker container | All | Same as Node, packaged |
| Static export (`output: 'export'`) | Limited | HTML/CSS/JS only, any static host |
| Platform adapters | Depends on platform | Adapters went stable in 16.2 (`adapterPath`) |

Managed platforms handle scaling, shared caches and skew protection for you. Self-hosting gives control but makes those your job.

sections.heading: Output modes
sections.body:
- **`output: 'standalone'`** traces the files the server needs and writes `.next/standalone` with a minimal `server.js` and only the required `node_modules`. It is ideal for small Docker images. It does **not** copy `public/` or `.next/static` by default: copy them in, or serve them from a CDN.
- **`output: 'export'`** produces static files. Features that need a server are unavailable, for example Server Actions, cookies and other request-time APIs, rewrites/redirects/headers config, proxy, ISR/revalidation, the default image optimization loader, and dynamic routes without `generateStaticParams`.

sections.heading: Caching behind a CDN
sections.body:
From the self-hosting guide:

- Hashed build assets under `/_next/static` are sent with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, so a CDN can cache them indefinitely; new builds get new file names.
- Dynamically rendered pages get `private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate`, so a CDN does not cache them.
- Streaming responses must not be buffered by the proxy or CDN in front (for Nginx, `X-Accel-Buffering: no`).

**Multiple instances** need:

- a shared cache handler (`cacheHandler` / `cacheHandlers`, implementing `refreshTags`), because the default cache is in memory per instance;
- a `deploymentId`, for version-skew protection;
- the same `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` on every instance, or actions encrypted by one instance fail on another.

Skew between client and server builds surfaces as "Failed to find Server Action". `after()` callbacks need a graceful SIGTERM shutdown to finish.

sections.heading: Observability and error reporting

keyPoints: Four options: Node server, Docker, static export, adapters.
standalone output: minimal server; copy public and .next/static yourself.
Static export loses server features such as Server Actions and proxy.
Hashed assets are immutable for a year; dynamic pages are no-store.
Multi-instance: shared cache handler, deploymentId, same action encryption key.
instrumentation.ts: register() at startup, onRequestError() for reporting.

gotchas.trap: output: 'standalone' bundles everything, including public assets.
gotchas.correct: Copy public/ and .next/static into the image or serve them from a CDN.

gotchas.trap: Scaling to three replicas just works because each one has a cache.
gotchas.correct: Per-instance in-memory caches diverge; configure a shared cache handler and shared keys.

gotchas.trap: The error message users see in production is what to search for in logs.
gotchas.correct: Production shows a generic message; correlate using error.digest.

lessons.lab: Build the app with output: 'standalone' into a multi-stage Docker image, copy public/ and .next/static, and run two containers behind a local reverse proxy. Inspect Cache-Control on a /_next/static file and on a dynamic page. Add instrumentation.ts with onRequestError that logs the route and digest, then throw in a Server Component and match the digest the browser shows.

flashcards.front: What are the three steps of a React screen update?
flashcards.back: Trigger (initial mount or state update), render (React calls your components to compute JSX) and commit (React applies only the DOM changes that differ).

flashcards.front: What makes a React component pure?
flashcards.back: Given the same props, state and context it returns the same JSX, and it does not change objects or variables that existed before rendering.

flashcards.front: When does React preserve a component's state between renders?
flashcards.back: When the same component type renders at the same position in the UI tree. Changing props does not reset it; changing type, position or key does.

flashcards.front: Why should you never define a component inside another component?
flashcards.back: Each parent render creates a new function, so React sees a new component type at that position and resets the child's state and DOM every time.

flashcards.front: Why is the array index a risky key?
flashcards.back: If items are inserted, deleted or reordered, state and DOM stay with the position rather than the item, so data appears in the wrong row.

flashcards.front: What goes wrong with key={Math.random()}?
flashcards.back: Keys never match between renders, so React recreates every item and loses its state and DOM on each render.

flashcards.front: How do you deliberately reset a component's state when an ID changes?
flashcards.back: Render it with a different key, e.g. <Chat key={contact.id} />. React treats it as a new instance.

flashcards.front: setNumber(number + 1) is called three times in one click handler, starting at 0. Result?
flashcards.back: 1. Each call uses the same snapshot value 0, so each queues 'replace with 1'.

flashcards.front: setNumber(n => n + 1) is called three times in one handler, starting at 0. Result?
flashcards.back: 3. Each updater receives the previous queued value.

flashcards.front: setNumber(number + 5); setNumber(n => n + 1); setNumber(42) from 0. Result?
flashcards.back: 42. The queue is processed in order (5, then 6) and the final plain value replaces it.

flashcards.front: What does 'state as a snapshot' mean?
flashcards.back: A state variable is fixed for a whole render; handlers and timeouts created in that render see that value even after setState is called.

flashcards.front: Which rule applies to updater functions and reducers?
flashcards.back: They must be pure. Strict Mode calls them twice in development to expose impurity.

flashcards.front: What does lifting state up mean?
flashcards.back: Moving shared state to the closest common parent and passing it down with callbacks, so there is one source of truth.

flashcards.front: Why shouldn't you store fullName in state next to firstName and lastName?
flashcards.back: It is redundant: compute it during render. Storing it invites out-of-sync bugs and extra renders.

flashcards.front: Why does user.name = 'x'; setUser(user) not re-render?
flashcards.back: React compares with Object.is; it's the same object reference. Create a new object instead.

flashcards.front: What is an Effect for?
flashcards.back: Synchronising a component with an external system (network, browser API, non-React widget) because of rendering, not because of a specific user action.

flashcards.front: What does Strict Mode do to Effects in development?
flashcards.back: It runs one extra setup → cleanup cycle after mount, so missing cleanup shows up. It does not happen in production.

flashcards.front: How do you avoid a race condition when fetching in an Effect?
flashcards.back: Set a local ignore flag in the cleanup and only call setState if ignore is false.

flashcards.front: Why does an object created during render as an Effect dependency cause re-runs?
flashcards.back: It is a new object every render, so Object.is sees a change. Create it inside the Effect or depend on primitives.

flashcards.front: Where should code that runs because the user clicked 'Buy' go?
flashcards.back: In the event handler, not in an Effect that watches state.

flashcards.front: What are the rules for functions returned by useEffectEvent?
flashcards.back: Call them only from inside Effects, never list them as dependencies, and don't pass them to other components or hooks.

flashcards.front: Ref or state: which triggers a re-render when changed?
flashcards.back: State. Changing ref.current does not re-render, so don't use refs for values shown on screen or read them during render.

flashcards.front: Which components re-render when a context provider's value changes?
flashcards.back: All components that read that context below the provider, including memo-wrapped ones. Memoize the value and split contexts to limit this.

flashcards.front: Which provider does useContext read from?
flashcards.back: The closest provider above the calling component. A provider rendered in the same component doesn't count.

flashcards.front: What do useActionState's action arguments and return values look like?
flashcards.back: The action gets (previousState, formData) and returns the next state. The hook returns [state, formAction, isPending].

flashcards.front: Where must the useOptimistic setter be called?
flashcards.back: Inside an Action or Transition (form action or startTransition). Otherwise React warns and the value snaps back.

flashcards.front: What does use() require when reading a promise?
flashcards.back: A stable promise (e.g. created in a Server Component), a Suspense boundary for pending state and an error boundary for rejection; it can't be in try/catch.

flashcards.front: What does the React Compiler memoize, and what should you do with existing useMemo?
flashcards.back: It memoizes components and hooks automatically. Keep existing useMemo/useCallback; removing them can change compiled output.

flashcards.front: What changed for refs in React 19?
flashcards.back: Function components receive ref as a regular prop (forwardRef will be deprecated later), and ref callbacks can return a cleanup function.

flashcards.front: What does 'use client' mark?
flashcards.back: A boundary in the module dependency graph: that module and everything it imports become client code shipped to the browser.

flashcards.front: Default component type in the App Router?
flashcards.back: Server Component, unless it is under a 'use client' boundary.

flashcards.front: Can a Client Component render a Server Component?
flashcards.back: Not by importing it, but yes when the Server Component is passed in as children or another prop.

flashcards.front: Name three prop types that cannot cross from a Server to a Client Component.
flashcards.back: Ordinary functions (non-Server Functions), class instances, null-prototype objects, unregistered Symbols.

flashcards.front: Can a Date, Map or Promise be passed as a prop to a Client Component?
flashcards.back: Yes; all three are serializable by React.

flashcards.front: When are NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables resolved?
flashcards.back: Inlined into the client bundle at build time and frozen; dynamic lookups are not inlined.

flashcards.front: What does import 'server-only' do?
flashcards.back: Makes importing that module from client code a build error.

flashcards.front: Special file nesting order in a segment?
flashcards.back: layout > template > error > loading > not-found > page.

flashcards.front: Layout vs template on navigation?
flashcards.back: Layouts persist and do not re-render; templates get a fresh instance each navigation.

flashcards.front: What does a folder named (marketing) do?
flashcards.back: Route group: organizes routes or layouts without appearing in the URL.

flashcards.front: What does a folder named _lib do in app/?
flashcards.back: Private folder: excluded from routing.

flashcards.front: [...slug] vs [[...slug]]?
flashcards.back: Catch-all needs at least one segment; optional catch-all also matches the base route.

flashcards.front: What does each parallel route @slot need in Next 16?
flashcards.back: A default file.

flashcards.front: How do you read params in a Next 16 page?
flashcards.back: await props.params; synchronous access was removed.

flashcards.front: Which segment boundary catches an error thrown in that segment's layout?
flashcards.back: The parent segment's error file (or global-error for the root layout).

flashcards.front: Props of an error file in Next 16.3+?
flashcards.back: { error, retry }; error files must be Client Components.

flashcards.front: How is fetch deduplicated during a render?
flashcards.back: Identical fetch calls are memoized within a render pass.

flashcards.front: How do you dedupe a DB query used by several Server Components?
flashcards.back: Wrap it in React.cache, which dedupes per request.

flashcards.front: Fix for two independent awaits in a row?
flashcards.back: Start both promises, then await Promise.all (or split into Suspense-wrapped siblings).

flashcards.front: How does a Client Component read a server-started promise?
flashcards.back: With use(promise); it suspends to the nearest Suspense boundary.

flashcards.front: What does loading.tsx do?
flashcards.back: Wraps the segment's page in a Suspense boundary with that fallback.

flashcards.front: HTTP status once a streamed response has started?
flashcards.back: 200; notFound() later injects a noindex meta tag and redirect() becomes client-side.

flashcards.front: What is Partial Prerendering?
flashcards.back: A prerendered static shell with dynamic holes streamed in via Suspense.

flashcards.front: How is PPR enabled in Next 16?
flashcards.back: cacheComponents: true; experimental.ppr was removed.

flashcards.front: What replaced middleware.ts in Next 16?
flashcards.back: proxy.ts exporting a proxy function.

flashcards.front: Runtime of proxy.ts?
flashcards.back: Node.js only; setting runtime throws.

flashcards.front: What happens if proxy has no matcher?
flashcards.back: It runs on every request.

flashcards.front: Can route.ts and page.tsx share a segment?
flashcards.back: No.

flashcards.front: Status of the Edge runtime in Next 16?
flashcards.back: Deprecated; new routes should use Node.js, and Cache Components requires Node.

flashcards.front: What does 'use server' at the top of a file do?
flashcards.back: It marks every export of that module as a Server Function the client can call. Each export must be an async function.

flashcards.front: Can a Client Component define an inline Server Function?
flashcards.back: No. It imports one from a 'use server' module or receives one as a prop. Inline 'use server' functions are allowed in Server Components.

flashcards.front: How does the client invoke a Server Action in Next.js?
flashcards.back: With a POST request to the current page route, carrying the action ID and serialized arguments.

flashcards.front: Do multiple Server Action calls run in parallel?
flashcards.back: No. Next.js dispatches them sequentially per client, so Promise.all over actions does not parallelize them.

flashcards.front: What is progressive enhancement for a form action?
flashcards.back: A <form action={serverAction}> rendered by a Server Component submits even before JavaScript loads. In Client Components, submissions queue until hydration.

flashcards.front: What does useActionState return?
flashcards.back: [state, formAction, isPending]. Its signature is useActionState(action, initialState, permalink?).

flashcards.front: Which arguments does an action passed to useActionState receive?
flashcards.back: (prevState, formData): the previous state first, then the submitted FormData.

flashcards.front: Where must useFormStatus be called?
flashcards.back: In a component rendered inside the <form> whose status it reads, such as the submit button. It reads the parent form's pending state.

flashcards.front: Why prefer Zod safeParse over parse in an action?
flashcards.back: safeParse returns { success, data } or { success: false, error } instead of throwing, so you can return field errors as state.

flashcards.front: Expected error vs uncaught exception in a Server Action?
flashcards.back: Expected errors (bad input) are returned as values and shown with useActionState. Unexpected errors throw to the nearest error.js boundary.

flashcards.front: What does a production error.js see for a server error?
flashcards.back: A generic message plus error.digest; the original message is hidden to avoid leaking details.

flashcards.front: updateTag vs revalidateTag?
flashcards.back: updateTag (Server Actions only) expires and refreshes in the same request for read-your-own-writes. revalidateTag(tag, 'max') is stale-while-revalidate and also works in Route Handlers.

flashcards.front: What happened to revalidateTag(tag) with one argument in Next 16?
flashcards.back: It is deprecated. Pass a second argument such as 'max', or use updateTag inside a Server Action.

flashcards.front: Why must revalidation come before redirect()?
flashcards.back: redirect() throws to stop execution, so any code after it never runs.

flashcards.front: Where must the useOptimistic setter be called?
flashcards.back: Inside an Action or Transition. Outside one, React warns and the optimistic value immediately reverts.

flashcards.front: What happens to an optimistic value when the action fails?
flashcards.back: When the Action ends, the value converges back to the real value prop, so the optimistic change disappears without manual rollback.

flashcards.front: Name the four checks every Server Action should perform.
flashcards.back: Authenticate the session, authorize the specific resource, validate all input, and return only minimal data.

flashcards.front: How does Next.js protect Server Actions against CSRF?
flashcards.back: It compares the Origin header with Host or X-Forwarded-Host. Trusted proxy origins go in serverActions.allowedOrigins.

flashcards.front: Why is NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY needed on multi-instance deploys?
flashcards.back: Closed-over action variables are encrypted; every instance must share the same key to decrypt them.

flashcards.front: How do you stop a stale fetch response from overwriting newer results in an Effect?
flashcards.back: Set an ignore flag in the cleanup and skip setState when it is true; optionally abort the request with AbortController.

flashcards.front: When does a client data cache beat Server Component fetching?
flashcards.back: For data that must refresh while the page is open, rapid interactive queries, or remote data shared by many client components.

flashcards.front: Which request APIs make rendering depend on the request in Next.js?
flashcards.back: `cookies()`, `headers()`, `searchParams`, `draftMode()` (and non-generated `params`). In Next 16 they are async and must be awaited.

flashcards.front: With Cache Components, what happens to a component that reads `cookies()`?
flashcards.back: It must be inside `<Suspense>`. Its fallback goes into the prerendered static shell and the real content streams in as a dynamic hole.

flashcards.front: How do you safely use `Date.now()` or `Math.random()` in a Cache Components route?
flashcards.back: Call `await connection()` first and wrap the component in `<Suspense>`, or move the work inside a `use cache` boundary.

flashcards.front: How is Cache Components turned on, and what is its status in Next 16.4?
flashcards.back: `cacheComponents: true` at the top level of `next.config`. It is the recommended model, enabled by create-next-app since 16.4, and planned as the default in Next 17.

flashcards.front: What makes up the cache key of a `'use cache'` function?
flashcards.back: Build ID (or `deploymentId`), function ID, serialized arguments and closed-over values (plus an HMR hash in dev).

flashcards.front: Can you call `cookies()` inside a `'use cache'` function?
flashcards.back: No (error `next-request-in-use-cache`). Read it outside and pass the value as an argument, or use `use cache: private`.

flashcards.front: Where does plain `'use cache'` store entries by default?
flashcards.back: An in-memory LRU on each server instance. Entries do not persist across serverless invocations or deploys. Use `use cache: remote` for durable shared storage.

flashcards.front: What is special about `'use cache: private'`?
flashcards.back: It may read cookies, headers and searchParams (not `connection()`), results are cached in the browser only, it is excluded from the static shell and has no custom handlers.

flashcards.front: What do the three cacheLife values mean?
flashcards.back: **stale**: client may reuse without asking the server; **revalidate**: after this, serve cached and refresh in the background; **expire**: after this with no traffic, regenerate before serving.

flashcards.front: What are the values of the `'max'` and `'default'` cacheLife profiles?
flashcards.back: `default`: stale 5m, revalidate 15m, expire never. `max`: stale 5m, revalidate 30d, expire 1y.

flashcards.front: Which cacheLife settings make a cached entry a dynamic hole instead of being prerendered?
flashcards.back: `revalidate: 0` or an `expire` under 5 minutes. A stale time under 30 seconds is also excluded from prerendering.

flashcards.front: Is `fetch` cached by default without Cache Components?
flashcards.back: No. Opt in with `cache: 'force-cache'` or `next: { revalidate: n }`. `unstable_cache` covers non-fetch work.

flashcards.front: What does `revalidateTag(tag, 'max')` do, and where can it run?
flashcards.back: Marks the tag stale with stale-while-revalidate semantics. It runs in Server Functions and Route Handlers. The one-argument form is deprecated in Next 16.

flashcards.front: When should you use `updateTag` instead of `revalidateTag`?
flashcards.back: In a Server Action after the user's own mutation: it expires and refreshes in the same request (read-your-own-writes). It is not available in Route Handlers.

flashcards.front: What `Cache-Control` does a self-hosted Next.js app send for hashed static assets and for dynamic pages?
flashcards.back: Static assets: `public, max-age=31536000, immutable`. Dynamic pages: `private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate`.

flashcards.front: How should the LCP image be configured with next/image in Next 16?
flashcards.back: Not lazy: `loading="eager"` or `fetchPriority="high"`, or the `preload` prop. `priority` is deprecated.

flashcards.front: What does next/font do for performance and privacy?
flashcards.back: Downloads and self-hosts fonts at build time (no runtime requests to Google), defaults to `display: swap` and `preload: true`, and adjusts fallback metrics to reduce CLS.

flashcards.front: Name the next/script strategies and their constraints.
flashcards.back: `beforeInteractive` (root layout only), `afterInteractive` (default), `lazyOnload` (idle time), `worker` (experimental, not with the App Router).

flashcards.front: Default strategy for a SaaS marketing page vs a live trading ticker?
flashcards.back: Marketing: `use cache` with a long cacheLife and a tag invalidated by a CMS webhook. Ticker: no server cache; `await connection()` in Suspense plus client-side updates.

flashcards.front: Why can a cached per-tenant report leak data across tenants?
flashcards.back: The cache key is built from the arguments and closed-over values. If the tenant id is not one of them, every tenant shares one cache entry and can get another tenant's result. Request APIs like cookies() are not allowed inside use cache anyway, so read the tenant outside and pass it in.

flashcards.front: Core Web Vitals "good" thresholds?
flashcards.back: LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1, each measured at the 75th percentile of field data (mobile and desktop segmented).

flashcards.front: Core Web Vitals "poor" thresholds?
flashcards.back: LCP > 4 s, INP > 500 ms, CLS > 0.25. Values in between are "needs improvement".

flashcards.front: Which interactions does INP count?
flashcards.back: Clicks, taps and keyboard input. Not hover or scroll. It ignores the single highest interaction for every 50 interactions.

flashcards.front: The three phases of an INP interaction?
flashcards.back: Input delay, processing duration (event handlers and the render they trigger), and presentation delay (layout and paint).

flashcards.front: Why can Lighthouse not report INP, and what does it use instead?
flashcards.back: INP needs real user interactions. Lighthouse (lab) reports Total Blocking Time (TBT) as a proxy.

flashcards.front: How is a single layout-shift score computed?
flashcards.back: Impact fraction (union of the unstable area before and after) × distance fraction (how far it moved). Example: an element covering half the viewport moving down 25% gives 0.75 × 0.25 = 0.1875.

flashcards.front: How are layout shifts grouped into CLS?
flashcards.back: Into session windows (gaps under 1 s, at most 5 s per window); the worst window is the CLS. Shifts within 500 ms of user input are excluded.

flashcards.front: The four LCP subparts?
flashcards.back: TTFB, resource load delay, resource load duration and element render delay. Load delay and render delay should each be under about 10%.

flashcards.front: How do you mark the LCP image in next/image in Next 16?
flashcards.back: Use preload (replacing the deprecated priority), or loading="eager" / fetchPriority="high". next/image is lazy by default.

flashcards.front: How does next/font help CLS?
flashcards.back: It self-hosts fonts at build time (display: swap, preload: true by default) and uses adjustFontFallback to size the fallback so the swap shifts little.

flashcards.front: What does the React Compiler memoize, and should you delete existing useMemo?
flashcards.back: Components and hooks, automatically. Keep existing useMemo/useCallback: removing them can change compiler output.

flashcards.front: Is the React Compiler on by default in Next 16?
flashcards.back: No. reactCompiler: true is stable but opt-in, needs babel-plugin-react-compiler, and increases build time.

flashcards.front: useTransition vs useDeferredValue?
flashcards.back: useTransition marks a state update as non-blocking; useDeferredValue gives a lagging copy of a value. Neither has a fixed delay, and a Transition cannot control a text input value.

flashcards.front: Why might useDeferredValue not speed anything up?
flashcards.back: The slow child is not memoized, so it re-renders during the urgent render anyway. Wrap it in memo (or let the React Compiler memoize it).

flashcards.front: Where may dynamic(..., { ssr: false }) be used?
flashcards.back: Only in a Client Component. Using it in a Server Component is an error.

flashcards.front: What does import 'server-only' do?
flashcards.back: Makes it a build error to import that module from client code, keeping secrets and heavy server libraries out of the bundle.

flashcards.front: Common causes of hydration mismatches?
flashcards.back: Invalid HTML nesting, typeof window branches in render, Date/locale formatting, browser extensions, CSS-in-JS misconfiguration and CDN HTML minification.

flashcards.front: How far does suppressHydrationWarning reach?
flashcards.back: One level deep: only the element it is on. It is an escape hatch for unavoidable differences, not a fix.

flashcards.front: What is selective hydration?
flashcards.back: Each Suspense boundary hydrates independently, so a slow part of the page does not block the rest from becoming interactive.

flashcards.front: WCAG 2.2 Target Size (Minimum)?
flashcards.back: 2.5.8, level AA: pointer targets at least 24×24 CSS px (with exceptions such as adequate spacing).

flashcards.front: WCAG 2.2 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)?
flashcards.back: 2.4.11, level AA: a focused component must not be entirely hidden by author content such as sticky headers or banners.

flashcards.front: How should a React form announce "Saving…" and "Saved"?
flashcards.back: Update text inside a role="status" (aria-live="polite") region that is already in the DOM. This meets 4.1.3 Status Messages (AA) without moving focus.

flashcards.front: How does Next.js announce client-side route changes?
flashcards.back: A built-in route announcer reads the document title (then the first h1, then the pathname). Give every route a unique title.

flashcards.front: Which cookie options does the Next.js auth guide use for a session cookie?
flashcards.back: httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "lax", an expires value and path: "/".

flashcards.front: Stateless (JWT cookie) vs database sessions: main trade-off?
flashcards.back: Stateless needs no lookup per request but is hard to revoke early; database sessions store only an id in the cookie and make revocation easy at the cost of a lookup.

flashcards.front: Why is a layout not a safe place for auth checks?
flashcards.back: Layouts do not re-render on client navigation, and pages and Server Actions can be reached without them. Check in the Data Access Layer and in each action.

flashcards.front: What is proxy.ts appropriate for in authentication?
flashcards.back: Optimistic checks only, such as redirecting when no session cookie exists. Real authorization belongs in the data layer.

flashcards.front: What must every Server Action do?
flashcards.back: Authenticate the caller, authorize the specific resource, validate its input and return minimal data, because it is a public POST endpoint.

flashcards.front: What does SameSite=Lax still allow?
flashcards.back: Cookies are still sent on top-level GET navigations from other sites, so it is defense in depth only. Never mutate state on GET.

flashcards.front: Requirements of the __Host- cookie prefix?
flashcards.back: Secure, Path=/ and no Domain attribute.

flashcards.front: What does SameSite=None require?
flashcards.back: The Secure attribute.

flashcards.front: How does Next.js protect Server Actions against CSRF?
flashcards.back: POST only, and it compares the Origin header with Host / X-Forwarded-Host. Behind a proxy on another host, set serverActions.allowedOrigins.

flashcards.front: When is dangerouslySetInnerHTML acceptable?
flashcards.back: Only with trusted or sanitized HTML (for example via DOMPurify). React escapes normal JSX text; this prop bypasses that.

flashcards.front: What does a nonce-based CSP cost in Next.js?
flashcards.back: The nonce is generated per request in proxy, so affected routes render dynamically and cannot use static shells / Partial Prerendering.

flashcards.front: When are NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables resolved?
flashcards.back: At build time: they are inlined into the client bundle and frozen. Changing them requires a rebuild.

flashcards.front: What does import "server-only" do?
flashcards.back: Makes it a build error to import that module into client code.

flashcards.front: What do the Next.js docs recommend for testing async Server Components?
flashcards.back: End-to-end tests (for example Playwright), because Vitest/Jest tooling does not fully support async Server Components.

flashcards.front: Testing Library: preferred query and preferred interaction API?
flashcards.back: getByRole (with an accessible name), and user-event rather than fireEvent.

flashcards.front: Playwright: what replaces fixed sleeps?
flashcards.back: Web-first assertions such as await expect(locator).toBeVisible(), which retry until the condition holds or time out.

flashcards.front: How does a ReadableStream respect backpressure?
flashcards.back: Its pull() is called only when the internal queue has room (desiredSize > 0); piping propagates it. Enqueueing everything in start() ignores it.

flashcards.front: How do you cancel a streaming fetch from the client?
flashcards.back: Pass an AbortController signal to fetch and call abort() on Stop or in Effect cleanup; forward request.signal upstream on the server.

flashcards.front: What does output: 'standalone' leave out?
flashcards.back: public/ and .next/static are not copied into .next/standalone by default; copy them or serve from a CDN.

flashcards.front: Cache-Control for hashed /_next/static assets when self-hosting?
flashcards.back: public, max-age=31536000, immutable.

flashcards.front: What do multiple self-hosted instances need to share?
flashcards.back: A cache handler, a deploymentId for skew protection, and the same NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY.

flashcards.front: What are the two instrumentation.ts hooks?
flashcards.back: register(), run once when a server instance starts, and onRequestError(), called with server errors plus request and route context.

questions.scenario: A to-do list renders items.map((item, i) => <Row key={i} item={item} />). Each Row contains an uncontrolled <input> for notes. When the user deletes the first item, the notes typed in the old first row now appear next to the second item.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Wrap Row in memo so React skips re-rendering unchanged rows
Use a key that is generated with Math.random() on each render
Use a stable identifier from the item data, such as key={item.id}
Remove the key prop so React can infer identity from the item object
questions.explanation: Keys tell React which item is which across renders. With index keys, state and DOM stay attached to the position, so deleting an item shifts them onto the wrong data. A stable ID from the data keeps state with its item.
rationales: memo only skips re-renders when props are equal; it does not change how React matches positions to items.
Random keys never match between renders, so every row and its input would be recreated each render.
Correct. A stable, sibling-unique ID lets React move state and DOM along with the item.
Without a key React falls back to the index (and warns), which is exactly the current bug.

sources.title: Preserving and Resetting State — React Learn

questions.scenario: A developer writes function SignupForm() { const [step, setStep] = useState(1); function EmailField() { const [text, setText] = useState(''); return <input value={text} onChange={e => setText(e.target.value)} />; } return <><EmailField /><Stepper step={step} onNext={() => setStep(step + 1)} /></>; }. Clicking Next clears whatever was typed into EmailField.
questions.stem: Why does EmailField lose its text?
options: Strict Mode renders components twice, which discards local state
Each SignupForm render creates a new EmailField function, so React sees a different component type and resets its state
EmailField needs a key prop; without it React cannot preserve its state
The Rules of Hooks forbid calling useState in a nested function, so React ignores the state
questions.explanation: React preserves state only when the same component type stays at the same position. A component defined inside another is a new function on every parent render, so React unmounts and remounts it. Declare EmailField at the top level.
rationales: Strict Mode's double render in development does not discard state between real renders.
Correct. The nested definition gives React a new type at that position each render, resetting the subtree.
A single child at a fixed position doesn't need a key; the type change is the problem.
EmailField is a component and may use hooks; the issue is its identity, not a hooks rule violation.

questions.scenario: A messaging app renders <Chat contact={selected} />. Chat keeps a draft message in useState. When the user switches to a different contact, the previous draft remains in the text box, and the team wants it cleared.
questions.stem: Which approach does the React documentation recommend?
options: Add a useEffect in Chat that calls setDraft('') whenever contact changes
Store the draft in a ref so it isn't preserved across renders
Render <Chat key={selected.id} contact={selected} /> so React creates a fresh instance per contact
Render {isAlice ? <Chat contact={alice} /> : <Chat contact={bob} />} so each contact has its own component
questions.explanation: Changing the key tells React this is a different component instance, so it discards the old state and mounts a new one. An Effect that resets state works but renders once with the stale draft and adds complexity. A ternary of the same type at the same position still preserves state.
rationales: It works but is the discouraged pattern: it renders the stale value first and then re-renders.
Refs persist across renders too, and a displayed draft belongs in state.
Correct. A key derived from the contact ID resets Chat's whole subtree when the contact changes.
Both branches render Chat at the same position, so React preserves the state; only keys would separate them.

questions.scenario:
A component increments a module-level counter during render to number each card: let n = 0; function Card() { n = n + 1; return

Card #{n}

; }. In development, the cards show #2, #4 and #6 instead of #1, #2 and #3.
questions.stem: What is the best explanation and fix?
options: React 19 renders lists in reverse; sort the array before mapping
Card is impure because it mutates a variable outside the render; Strict Mode double-calls it to reveal this. Pass the number as a prop
Strict Mode has a bug with module variables; remove <StrictMode> from the root
The counter should be stored in a ref inside Card so it survives re-renders
questions.explanation: Components must not change variables that existed before rendering. Strict Mode calls component bodies twice in development precisely so that impure logic like this produces visibly wrong output. Computing the number from props makes the component pure.
rationales: React does not reverse render order; the doubling comes from impurity plus Strict Mode.
Correct. The render mutates preexisting state; pass the index or number as a prop.
Strict Mode is working as intended; removing it hides the impurity, which can still break in production features.
A per-instance ref cannot produce a sequence across cards, and writing refs during render is also discouraged.

questions.scenario: A <Counter /> component holds a count in useState. The parent can change in several ways between renders.
questions.stem: In which cases does Counter keep its count? (Select two.)
options: The parent renders {isFancy ? <Counter isFancy={true} /> : <Counter isFancy={false} />} and isFancy toggles
The parent renders {show && <Counter />}; show becomes false and then true again
The parent changes the wrapper around Counter from <div> to <section>
The parent re-renders and passes Counter a different color prop
questions.explanation: React keeps state while the same component type stays at the same position in the tree, regardless of prop changes. Removing a component destroys its state, and changing a parent element's type resets the whole subtree beneath it.
rationales: Correct. Both branches render Counter at the same position, so React treats it as the same instance.
Unmounting destroys the state; when it is shown again Counter starts from its initial value.
A different parent type at that position resets the entire subtree, including Counter.
Correct. Prop changes alone never reset state.

questions.scenario: A scoreboard button runs function handleBonus() { setScore(score + 1); setScore(score + 1); setScore(score + 1); }. Testers expect +3 but see +1.
questions.stem: Which change produces +3?
options: Store score in a ref and read ref.current in each call
Wrap the three calls in flushSync one at a time
Move the calls into a useEffect that depends on score
Call setScore(s => s + 1) three times
questions.explanation: Within one render, score is a fixed snapshot, so each call queues 'replace with score + 1'. Updater functions receive the previous queued value, so three updaters chain to +3. React batches them into a single render.
rationales: Displayed values belong in state; a ref would not trigger a render.
Each call still reads the same score snapshot from this render, so flushSync just renders score + 1 three times and the result is still +1; flushSync is also a costly escape hatch.
An Effect depending on score would create an update loop and is not how event-driven updates should work.
Correct. Updater functions compute from the latest queued state.

questions.scenario: Starting from number = 0, a click handler runs: setNumber(number + 5); setNumber(n => n + 1); setNumber(42);
questions.stem: What does the next render display?
questions.explanation: React processes the queue in order during the next render: replace with 5, then 5 + 1 = 6, then replace with 42. The last plain value overrides the earlier queued results.
rationales: 6 would be the result without the final setNumber(42).
The updater is not applied after 42; queue entries run in the order they were added.
1 ignores the first replacement value of 5.
Correct. The final 'replace with 42' wins.

questions.scenario: A form has a recipient select (state to) and a Send button whose handler calls setTimeout(() => alert('Sent to ' + to), 3000). A user clicks Send with Alice selected, then switches the select to Bob within three seconds. The alert says 'Sent to Alice'.
questions.stem: Which statement is accurate?
options: This is a bug in batching; React should have flushed the new state into the closure
The handler closed over the state snapshot from the render where it ran; if the latest value is needed later, read it from a ref
The alert is wrong because setTimeout runs outside React; wrapping it in startTransition fixes it
Adding to to a useEffect dependency array would update the variable inside the pending timeout
questions.explanation: A state variable never changes within a render; event handlers and timeouts see the values from the render that created them. This is expected behaviour and makes the message match what the user saw when clicking. If code needs the latest value at a later time, a ref is the documented escape hatch.
rationales: Batching is not involved; closures intentionally keep their render's snapshot.
Correct. State is a snapshot; refs provide a mutable 'latest value' box.
Transitions mark updates as non-urgent; they do not change what a closure captured.
An Effect cannot rewrite a variable already captured by an existing closure.

questions.scenario: An accordion has two <Panel> components, each with its own isActive state. Product now wants only one panel open at a time: opening one must close the other.
questions.stem: What is the recommended way to structure the state?
options: Move the active index to the common parent and pass isActive and an onShow callback to each Panel
Keep state in each Panel and use a useEffect in each to close itself when the other opens
Put the active panel in an app-wide context provider at the root
Store isActive in a module-level variable that both panels read
questions.explanation: When two components must change together, lift the state to their closest common parent and make the children controlled. This creates a single source of truth. Syncing with Effects or global stores adds complexity and moves state further from where it is used.
rationales: Correct. Lifting state up is the documented pattern for coordinated siblings.
Syncing duplicated state through Effects causes extra renders and can drift out of sync.
Context for two siblings puts state far from where it's used; props are simpler here.
Module variables don't trigger re-renders and are shared by every instance.

questions.scenario: A profile form keeps firstName and lastName in state, plus a fullName state that a useEffect updates whenever either name changes. Users notice a brief flash of the old full name.
questions.stem: What change best follows React's guidance?
options: Switch the Effect to useLayoutEffect so the update happens before paint
Store fullName in a ref and update it in the onChange handlers
Keep fullName in state but update it in the onChange handlers instead of an Effect
Remove the fullName state and compute const fullName = firstName + ' ' + lastName during render
questions.explanation: fullName is redundant state: it can be computed from existing state. Computing it during render removes the extra render pass and the possibility of the values drifting apart. Reserve useMemo for genuinely expensive calculations.
rationales: This hides the flash but keeps the redundant state and the extra render.
Refs don't trigger renders, so the displayed name could go stale.
Better than the Effect but still duplicates information that can be derived.
Correct. Derive values during render instead of storing and syncing them.

questions.scenario: A handler runs: function rename() { user.name = 'Ada'; setUser(user); }. The screen doesn't update.
questions.stem: Why, and what is the fix?
options: setUser is asynchronous; await it before reading user
React needs forceUpdate after mutating objects in state
The new value is the same object reference, so React bails out; call setUser({ ...user, name: 'Ada' })
Objects can't be stored in useState; split name into its own state variable
questions.explanation: React compares the next state with the current one using Object.is. A mutated object is still the same reference, so React treats it as unchanged. Treat state as read-only and create a new object.
rationales: setState doesn't return a promise, and awaiting doesn't change reference equality.
Function components have no forceUpdate; the correct fix is to create a new object.
Correct. A new object reference signals a change.
Objects are valid state; they must simply be replaced rather than mutated.

sources.title: Updating Objects in State — React Learn

questions.scenario: A chat component runs useEffect(() => { const c = createConnection(roomId); c.connect(); }, [roomId]); In development the console shows 'Connecting...' twice on mount and the server sees two open connections.
questions.stem: What should the developer do?
options: Return a cleanup that calls c.disconnect(), so setup → cleanup → setup leaves one connection
Use a ref flag to skip the second setup call
Remove <StrictMode> from the app root because it only affects development
Change the dependency array to [] so the Effect only runs once
questions.explanation: In development, Strict Mode runs one extra setup and cleanup cycle to reveal Effects that don't clean up. Adding a cleanup that disconnects makes the double run harmless, and the same cleanup is needed in production when roomId changes or the component unmounts. React's docs explicitly advise against using refs to prevent the extra run.
rationales: Correct. Cleanup that mirrors setup is the fix the stress test is designed to surface.
The docs advise against this; it hides the missing cleanup that will leak on roomId changes and unmounts.
This removes the check without fixing the leak.
[] still runs twice in Strict Mode and would ignore roomId changes.

questions.scenario: A search page fetches results in an Effect that depends on query. When users type quickly, the list sometimes shows results for an earlier query after the latest one has rendered.
questions.stem: Which change directly fixes this race condition?
options: Remove query from the dependency array and fetch only on mount
Debounce the input so fewer requests are sent
Switch to useLayoutEffect so the fetch starts before paint
Declare let ignore = false in the Effect, set it to true in the cleanup, and only call setResults when ignore is false
questions.explanation: Responses can arrive out of order, so a stale response may overwrite a newer one. The cleanup runs before the next Effect, marking the previous request as ignored. Debouncing reduces requests but doesn't guarantee ordering.
rationales: This breaks the feature: results would never update with the query.
Debouncing lowers the chance but responses can still arrive out of order.
Timing of setup doesn't affect when network responses arrive.
Correct. The ignore flag ensures only the latest request updates state.
