questions.scenario: In a chat component, const options = { serverUrl, roomId }; is declared in the component body and used in useEffect(() => { const c = createConnection(options); c.connect(); return () => c.disconnect(); }, [options]); The chat reconnects every time the user types in an unrelated input.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Wrap the Effect body in a try/catch to ignore duplicate connections
Build the options object inside the Effect and depend on [serverUrl, roomId]
Remove options from the dependency array and suppress the lint warning
Store options in state so it is preserved between renders
questions.explanation: An object created during render is a new reference on each render, so the dependency always looks changed. Creating it inside the Effect and depending on the primitive values means the Effect re-runs only when those values actually change.
rationales: Error handling doesn't stop the Effect from re-running.
Correct. Move the object into the Effect and depend on primitives.
Suppressing the linter leads to stale values when serverUrl or roomId really change.
Copying derived data into state adds redundant state and update logic.

questions.stem: Which of these are appropriate uses of an Effect? (Select two.)
options: Calling a non-React map widget's setZoomLevel(zoom) whenever the zoom prop changes
Computing a filtered list of todos from todos and filter state
Logging an analytics 'page visited' event when a page component is displayed
Sending the checkout POST request after the user clicks Buy
questions.explanation: Effects are for synchronising with external systems because a component rendered. Keeping a third-party widget in sync and logging a visit when a page is shown are both caused by display. Derived data belongs in render, and user-triggered requests belong in event handlers.
rationales: Correct. Controlling a non-React widget is synchronisation with an external system.
Compute this during render (with useMemo if it's expensive).
Correct. The event exists because the page was displayed, so an Effect fits.
The request happens because of a specific user action, so it belongs in the click handler.

sources.title: You Might Not Need an Effect — React Learn

questions.scenario: A chat room Effect shows a 'Connected!' notification styled with the current theme prop. Because theme is in the dependency array, toggling dark mode disconnects and reconnects the chat.
questions.stem: Which change is correct?
options: Remove theme from the dependency array and disable the lint rule for that line
Wrap the notification in useCallback with [theme] and add that callback to the dependencies
Move the notification into a function created with useEffectEvent and call it from inside the Effect, keeping only roomId as a dependency
Create the useEffectEvent function and add it to the dependency array so the linter is satisfied
questions.explanation: useEffectEvent separates non-reactive logic from the Effect, so the Effect can read the latest theme without re-synchronising when it changes. Effect Event functions must be called only from inside Effects and must never be listed as dependencies.
rationales: Suppressing the linter risks stale values and is not the documented fix.
The callback changes whenever theme changes, so the reconnect still happens.
Correct. Reactive roomId stays a dependency; theme is read through the Effect Event.
Effect Event functions have an intentionally unstable identity and must not be dependencies.

questions.scenario: A stopwatch component starts an interval in a click handler and needs the interval ID later so that the Stop button can call clearInterval. The ID is never shown on screen.
questions.stem: Where should the interval ID be stored?
options: In a ref created with useRef, because it persists across renders without triggering one
In useState, so that React re-renders whenever the ID is set
In a module-level variable next to the component
In a context provider so other components can stop the timer
questions.explanation: Refs are for values that need to survive re-renders but don't affect rendering output. Storing the ID in state causes a needless render. A module-level variable is shared by every instance of the component.
rationales: Correct. A ref is the documented tool for interval IDs and similar handles.
It works but triggers an unnecessary re-render for data that is never displayed.
All instances would share and overwrite the same ID.
Context is for sharing render data deeply; it adds complexity for a local handle.

questions.scenario: App holds a mousePosition state that updates on every pointer move and also renders <AuthContext value={{ user, login }}>. Dozens of components that only read user re-render on every mouse move, even though user hasn't changed. Several of them are already wrapped in memo.
questions.stem: What is the most effective fix?
options: Wrap even more of the consuming components in memo
Replace useContext with use(AuthContext) in the consumers
Convert user to a useReducer so its updates are batched
Memoize the provider value with useMemo (and login with useCallback), and move the fast-changing mouse state out of the provider's component
questions.explanation: An inline object is a new value on every render of App, and when a provider's value changes React re-renders every consumer, bypassing memo. Memoizing the value makes it change only when user or login changes, and colocating fast-changing state stops App from re-rendering on each move.
rationales: memo does not stop re-renders caused by a context value change.
use(Context) reads the same value and re-renders in the same way.
The problem is the new value object, not how user updates are batched.
Correct. A stable provider value plus colocated mouse state removes the storm.

questions.stem: Which statements about context in React 19 are accurate? (Select two.)
options: A component calling useContext reads from the closest provider above it, not from a provider it renders itself
You can render the context object directly as the provider, for example <ThemeContext value="dark">
A consumer re-renders only if the specific field it reads from the context value changed
Wrapping a consumer in memo prevents it from re-rendering when the context value changes
questions.explanation: useContext searches upward from the calling component and ignores providers in that same component. React 19 lets you use <Context value> as the provider. When the value changes, all consumers re-render regardless of which part they read, and memo doesn't block it.
rationales: Correct. Providers rendered by the calling component itself are not considered.
Correct. React 19 added <Context> as a provider; <Context.Provider> still works.
React compares the whole value with Object.is; there is no per-field subscription.
memoized components still re-render when a context they use changes.

questions.scenario: A task manager has many event handlers that each update a tasks array in slightly different ways, and bugs keep appearing. The team moves the logic into useReducer.
questions.stem: Which reducer implementation follows React's guidance?
options: case 'added': state.push(action.task); return state;
case 'added': return [...state, { id: action.id, text: action.text, done: false }];
case 'added': fetch('/api/tasks', { method: 'POST' }); return [...state, action.task];
case 'added': return [...state, { id: Date.now(), text: action.text, done: false }];
questions.explanation: Reducers must be pure: given the same state and action they return the same new state without side effects or mutation. IDs and requests belong in the event handler that dispatches. Strict Mode calls reducers twice in development to surface impurity.
rationales: Mutating and returning the same array means React sees no change.
Correct. A new array built only from state and action is pure.
Network requests are side effects and don't belong in a reducer.
Date.now() makes the result non-deterministic; generate the ID in the handler and pass it in the action.

questions.scenario: A developer writes const [state, formAction] = useActionState(async (formData) => { const qty = formData.get('qty'); ... }, { error: null }); and passes formAction to <form action>. At runtime, formData.get is not a function.
questions.stem: What is wrong?
options: useActionState only works with Server Functions, not client functions
formAction must be called inside startTransition even when passed to a form
The action's first argument is the previous state; the FormData is the second argument
The initial state must be null for the form data to be passed through
questions.explanation: useActionState calls the action with (previousState, formData) and uses the return value as the next state. The function here treats the previous state object as FormData. Changing the signature to (prevState, formData) fixes it.
rationales: useActionState accepts any async or sync function, not only Server Functions.
When passed to a form's action prop, React already runs it in a Transition.
Correct. The signature is (previousState, formData).
The initial state can be any value; it is passed as previousState on the first call.

questions.scenario: A comments list uses const [optimistic, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic(comments, (list, c) => [...list, c]). A button's onClick handler calls addOptimistic(newComment) and then await saveComment(newComment). React logs a warning, and the pending comment disappears immediately.
questions.stem: What should change?
options: Call addOptimistic inside an Action, for example from a form action or within startTransition together with the await
Store the optimistic comment in useState instead
Call addOptimistic after the await so the server has confirmed it
Wrap the component in <Suspense> so the optimistic value is kept while pending
questions.explanation: The useOptimistic setter must be called inside an Action or Transition. Outside one, React warns and the optimistic value reverts straight away. When the Action finishes, the optimistic value converges with the real comments in the same commit.
rationales: Correct. Running the update and the save inside an Action keeps the optimistic value until it settles.
Plain state loses the automatic revert-and-converge behaviour and needs manual rollback.
After the await the change is no longer optimistic, and it is still outside a Transition.
Suspense handles suspended reads, not optimistic state lifetimes.

questions.scenario: A Client Component renders const user = use(fetch('/api/user').then(r => r.json())); inside a try/catch block to show an error message. The component refetches endlessly and the catch never runs as expected.
questions.stem: Which approach aligns with the use() documentation?
options: Move the fetch into a useEffect and call use() on the stored state
Create the promise in a Server Component (or a cache) and pass it down; wrap the reader in <Suspense> and handle rejection with an error boundary
Keep the code but add a key to the component so React caches the promise
Replace try/catch with .catch() on the promise inside the render function
questions.explanation: Promises created during a Client Component render are recreated every render, so use() keeps suspending. use() cannot be wrapped in try/catch; rejections go to the nearest error boundary, and pending state shows the nearest Suspense fallback. Creating the promise on the server and passing it down gives a stable promise.
rationales: use() reads promises and context; it isn't designed to read state set by an Effect.
Correct. Stable promise plus Suspense and an error boundary is the documented pattern.
A key does not cache promises; each render still creates a new one.
The promise would still be recreated every render; the instability is the root issue.

questions.stem: Which changes are part of React 19's ref handling? (Select two.)
options: Function components can receive ref as a regular prop
forwardRef has been removed and now throws an error
A ref callback can return a cleanup function that React calls when the element is removed
Refs now trigger a re-render when ref.current is assigned
questions.explanation: React 19 passes ref to function components as a normal prop, and forwardRef is planned for deprecation in a future release rather than removed. Ref callbacks may return a cleanup function. Assigning ref.current still never triggers a re-render.
rationales: Correct. ref is a prop for function components in React 19.
forwardRef still works; the blog says it will be deprecated in a future release.
Correct. Ref callbacks can return cleanup, similar to Effects.
Refs remain non-reactive; use state for values that drive rendering.

questions.scenario: A team turns on the React Compiler in a large codebase. A developer proposes a cleanup PR that deletes every existing useMemo and useCallback, since 'the compiler handles memoization now'.
questions.stem: What is the best guidance?
options: Merge it; the compiler ignores manual memoization, so deleting it is harmless
Reject the compiler; it cannot coexist with manual memoization
Merge it only after converting all components to class components, which the compiler optimizes best
Keep the existing memoization (removing it can change compiled output) and write new code without it, while making sure code follows the Rules of React
questions.explanation: The React Compiler memoizes components and hooks automatically, but React's guidance is to leave existing useMemo and useCallback in place, because removing them can change the compiler's output. The compiler relies on code following the Rules of React, which its lint rules help enforce.
rationales: The compiler takes existing memoization into account; removing it can change the compiled output.
The compiler works alongside existing useMemo and useCallback.
The compiler targets function components and hooks, not class components.
Correct. Keep existing memoization, rely on the compiler for new code, and follow the Rules of React.

questions.scenario: A team adds 'use client' to app/products/layout.tsx because one header widget uses useState. The layout imports a heavy markdown renderer used to render product descriptions.
questions.stem: What is the main consequence, and the best fix?
options: Only the layout's own JSX ships to the client; imported modules stay on the server.
Nothing changes; layouts are always rendered on the server regardless of the directive.
The markdown renderer is now in the client bundle; move the directive to the header widget only.
The page fails to build because layouts cannot be Client Components.
questions.explanation: 'use client' marks a boundary in the module graph, so everything the layout imports becomes client code. Moving the directive to the interactive leaf keeps the renderer server-only.
rationales: Imported modules of a client module become client code too.
The directive does change where the module runs.
Correct: imports under the boundary ship to the client; a leaf boundary avoids that.
Layouts can be Client Components; it builds.

questions.scenario: A Server Component renders <ProductCard product={product} onSelect={() => track(product.id)} />, where ProductCard is a Client Component and product is an ORM class instance.
questions.stem: Which props will fail to serialize? (Select two.)
options: onSelect, an inline arrow function
product, a class instance
A Date stored on a plain object
A Promise of related products
questions.explanation: Ordinary functions and class instances are not serializable across the boundary. Dates, plain objects and Promises are supported.
rationales: Correct: only Server Functions may be passed as functions.
Correct: class instances must be mapped to plain objects.
Date is serializable.
Promises are serializable and can be read with use().

questions.scenario: A Client Component Modal needs to show a cart summary that queries the database. A developer tries to import the CartSummary Server Component inside modal.tsx.
questions.stem: What is the recommended pattern?
options: Add 'use server' to CartSummary so it can be imported by the client module.
Render <Modal><CartSummary /></Modal> from a Server Component, passing CartSummary as children.
Fetch the cart from a Route Handler inside a useEffect in Modal.
Remove 'use client' from Modal and use state anyway.
questions.explanation: A Client Component cannot import a Server Component, but it can render one passed as children or another prop. The server renders CartSummary and Modal only places it.
rationales: 'use server' marks Server Functions, not components to import into client code.
Correct: the composition pattern keeps CartSummary on the server.
Works but adds a client fetch and a round trip; not the recommended pattern.
State requires a Client Component.

questions.scenario: A lib/db.ts module reads DATABASE_URL and is meant to run only on the server. A new developer imports a helper from it into a Client Component; the build succeeds and the helper fails at runtime in the browser.
questions.stem: What prevents this class of mistake at build time?
options: Rename DATABASE_URL to NEXT_PUBLIC_DATABASE_URL.
Add 'use server' at the top of lib/db.ts.
Add import 'server-only' at the top of lib/db.ts.
Wrap the helper in React.cache.
questions.explanation: The server-only package turns any client import of the module into a build error. 'use server' would instead expose every export as a callable Server Function endpoint.
rationales: This would inline the secret into the client bundle.
This makes exports public Server Functions, a security risk for a DB module.
Correct: wrong-side imports become build errors.
React.cache dedupes; it does not restrict environment.

questions.scenario: A Docker image is built once and promoted to staging and production. The client shows NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE from staging even in production, where the container env has a different value.
questions.stem: Why?
options: Next.js caches environment variables in the router cache.
Containers cannot pass env vars to Next.js.
NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are inlined at build time and frozen into the bundle.
The variable must be read with process.env[name] to be public.
questions.explanation: NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are inlined at build time, so a promoted image carries the build-time value. Read runtime config on the server, or rebuild per environment.
rationales: There is no such env caching in the router cache.
Server code reads container env normally.
Correct.
Dynamic lookups are not inlined at all.

questions.scenario: An app protects /dashboard by checking the session in app/dashboard/layout.tsx and redirecting when it is missing. A security review flags this.
questions.stem: What is the most accurate concern?
options: Layouts run only at build time.
Layouts cannot call redirect().
The check runs twice per request, doubling database load.
Layouts do not re-render on navigation, so the check is not a reliable authorization point; verify near the data and in each page or action.
questions.explanation: The Next.js auth guide warns that layouts are preserved across navigations and do not re-render, so a layout check is not run for every child route render. Check authorization in a Data Access Layer close to the data.
rationales: Layouts render at request time when dynamic.
redirect() can be called in Server Components including layouts.
The problem is the opposite: it may not run.
Correct.

questions.scenario: A multi-step wizard at /signup/[step] keeps form progress in useState inside the shared wrapper. Product wants an enter animation and a fresh client state on every step.
questions.stem: Which file should host the wrapper?
options: template.tsx
layout.tsx
loading.tsx
default.tsx
questions.explanation: A template gets a new instance on each navigation, so state resets and effects re-run. A layout persists across navigations.
rationales: Correct.
Layouts persist, so state would not reset.
loading is a Suspense fallback, not a wrapper.
default is for parallel route slots.

questions.stem: A team wants /about and /pricing under a marketing root layout and /app/* under a separate app layout, without "marketing" appearing in any URL. Which structure does this?
options: app/[marketing]/about
app/@marketing/about
app/_marketing/about with app/_marketing/layout.tsx
app/(marketing)/about and app/(marketing)/pricing with app/(marketing)/layout.tsx
questions.explanation: Route groups in parentheses are omitted from the URL and can each have their own layout. Private folders are excluded from routing entirely.
rationales: A dynamic segment would capture a URL segment.
@ creates a parallel route slot.
Private folders opt out of routing, so the pages would not be reachable.
Correct.

questions.scenario: A docs site needs /docs, /docs/intro and /docs/api/hooks all served by one page file.
questions.stem: Which segment name works?
options: app/docs/[...slug]/page.tsx
app/docs/(slug)/page.tsx
app/docs/[slug]/page.tsx
app/docs/[[...slug]]/page.tsx
questions.explanation: An optional catch-all matches zero or more segments, so it also matches /docs. A plain catch-all requires at least one segment.
rationales: Does not match /docs itself.
A route group does not capture segments.
Matches exactly one segment.
Correct.

questions.scenario: After upgrading to Next 16 a page reads const { slug } = props.params and gets undefined / errors.
questions.stem: What change is required?
options: Wrap the page in Suspense.
Add export const dynamic = "force-dynamic".
Use useParams in the Server Component.
Make the page async and await props.params.
questions.explanation: In Next 16 params and searchParams are Promises and synchronous access was removed. They must be awaited.
rationales: Suspense does not resolve the promise for you.
Segment config does not change the params type.
useParams is a client hook.
Correct.

questions.scenario: app/dashboard/layout.tsx throws while loading user preferences. app/dashboard/error.tsx exists, but users see the root error UI instead.
questions.stem: Why, and what fixes it?
options: error.tsx does not wrap the layout of its own segment; add a boundary in the parent segment.
error.tsx must be a Server Component to catch layout errors.
The error file must be named layout-error.tsx.
Layouts never throw to error boundaries; use try/catch only.
questions.explanation: In the nesting hierarchy the error boundary sits inside the layout of the same segment, so it cannot catch that layout's errors. A boundary higher up (parent segment, or global-error for the root) catches it.
rationales: Correct.
error files must be Client Components.
No such convention exists.
Layout errors propagate to the nearest parent boundary.

questions.stem: Which statements about app/**/error.tsx in Next 16.3+ are correct? (Select two.)
options: It must be a Client Component ('use client').
It receives a retry function that refetches and re-renders the segment.
It also catches errors thrown in event handlers.
It must render its own <html> and <body>.
questions.explanation: error files are Client Components and receive { error, retry }. Event-handler errors are not caught by error boundaries, and only global-error renders its own html and body.
rationales: Correct.
Correct: retry became stable in 16.3; reset re-renders without refetching.
Error boundaries do not catch event-handler errors.
That requirement applies to global-error.

questions.scenario: A profile page runs: const user = await getUser(id); const orders = await getOrders(id); Neither call depends on the other and each takes ~400ms.
questions.stem: What is the best change?
options: Add 'use cache' to the page and keep the awaits.
Wrap the page in a template.tsx.
Move both calls into a useEffect.
Start both calls and await Promise.all([userP, ordersP]).
questions.explanation: Sequential awaits of independent requests create a waterfall. Starting both and awaiting Promise.all runs them in parallel.
rationales: Caching may help repeat requests but the cold path still waterfalls.
Templates do not affect fetching.
Moves fetching to the client and adds round trips.
Correct: total time drops to roughly the slower call.

questions.scenario: A layout, a page and a sidebar component each call getCurrentUser(), which runs a database query through the ORM (not fetch). Logs show three queries per request.
questions.stem: What dedupes the query per request?
options: Call getCurrentUser only in the layout and read it in pages via context.
Move the call into a Route Handler.
Nothing is needed; fetch memoization already covers it.
Wrap getCurrentUser in React.cache.
questions.explanation: fetch memoization only applies to fetch calls. React.cache dedupes arbitrary functions within a request.
rationales: Server Components cannot use context to share data this way, and layouts may not re-render.
Adds HTTP hops and still runs per caller.
The ORM query is not a fetch, so it is not memoized.
Correct.

questions.scenario: A page shows product details (fast) and reviews (slow, 2s). Currently the page awaits both before returning, so nothing displays for 2s.
questions.stem: Which approaches show the details immediately and stream reviews in? (Select two.)
options: Add a loading.tsx and keep awaiting both in the page.
Start the reviews promise in the page without awaiting, pass it to a Client Component wrapped in Suspense that calls use(promise).
Move the reviews fetch into a <Reviews> async component wrapped in <Suspense fallback={<Skeleton />}>.
Fetch reviews with await inside the layout instead.
questions.explanation: A Suspense boundary around the slow part lets the rest stream first; the boundary can wrap an async Server Component or a Client Component reading a promise with use(). loading.tsx alone wraps the whole page, so nothing of the page shows until both resolve.
rationales: The fallback replaces the entire page until both finish.
Correct: use() suspends to the nearest boundary.
Correct.
This blocks everything under the layout.

questions.scenario: A Client Component does const data = use(fetch("/api/stats").then(r => r.json())) directly in its body. It re-suspends endlessly.
questions.stem: What is the fix?
options: Wrap the use() call in try/catch.
Call use() only inside a condition.
Create the promise in a Server Component (or cache it) and pass it as a prop.
Move use() into a useEffect.
questions.explanation: Promises read with use() must be stable; a promise created during a client render is recreated each render. Create it on the server and pass it down.
rationales: use cannot be called in try/catch; use an error boundary.
Conditional calling is allowed but does not stabilize the promise.
Correct.
Hooks-like APIs cannot be called inside effects.

questions.scenario: A streamed product page calls notFound() inside a Suspense-wrapped component after the shell has already been sent. SEO reports the URL returns HTTP 200.
questions.stem: What actually happens?
options: notFound() is ignored inside Suspense.
The status is already 200 once streaming starts; Next injects a noindex robots meta tag instead.
Next rewrites the status to 404 at the end of the stream.
The browser receives a 404 header in a trailer.
questions.explanation: Headers are committed when streaming begins, so the status stays 200. notFound() mid-stream adds <meta name="robots" content="noindex">; call it before streaming to get a real 404.
rationales: The not-found UI is still rendered.
Correct.
The status cannot change after headers are sent.
No trailer mechanism is used.

questions.scenario: Streaming works locally, but behind the company Nginx reverse proxy users see the whole page appear at once.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Nginx buffers the response; send X-Accel-Buffering: no (or disable proxy buffering).
loading.tsx only works on Vercel.
Suspense is disabled in production builds.
Next disables streaming for HTTP/1.1.
questions.explanation: Proxies such as Nginx buffer responses by default, which defeats streaming. The Next.js streaming guide recommends X-Accel-Buffering: no.
rationales: Correct.
loading works self-hosted.
Suspense streaming works in production.
No such restriction.

questions.scenario: A team upgrading to Next 16 has experimental: { ppr: true } in next.config and export const experimental_ppr = true in several layouts.
questions.stem: How should they adopt Partial Prerendering now?
options: Set dynamic = "force-static" on each page.
Remove those and set cacheComponents: true at the top level.
Keep experimental.ppr; it is required alongside cacheComponents.
Add export const runtime = 'edge' to every PPR route.
questions.explanation: Next 16 removed experimental.ppr and experimental_ppr; PPR is opted into with top-level cacheComponents. Cache Components also requires the Node runtime.
rationales: That is segment config from the previous model and does not create dynamic holes.
Correct.
The flag was removed.
Cache Components needs the Node runtime.

questions.scenario: With cacheComponents enabled, a product page has a static description and a per-user "recommended for you" panel that reads cookies().
questions.stem: How should the page be structured so it still gets a prerendered static shell?
options: Mark the whole page 'use cache' and read cookies inside it.
Add 'use client' to the page.
Render the description normally and wrap the recommendations component in <Suspense>.
Read cookies() at the top of the page and pass values down.
questions.explanation: Request-time data must sit in a Suspense boundary so the rest can be prerendered as the shell and the dynamic part streams in. cookies() is not allowed inside a use cache scope.
rationales: cookies() inside use cache errors.
Client Components cannot read server cookies this way.
Correct: static shell plus a dynamic hole.
Reading cookies() at the top, outside any Suspense boundary, makes the whole page request-time, so no static shell is prerendered.

questions.scenario: A team upgrades to Next 16 and keeps middleware.ts for redirects and an auth-cookie check.
questions.stem: What is the recommended migration?
options: Move the logic into a Route Handler at app/middleware/route.ts.
Rename to proxy.ts with an exported proxy function; it runs on Node.js.
Move the logic into app/layout.tsx.
Keep middleware.ts and add runtime: "nodejs".
questions.explanation: Next 16 deprecates the middleware file and export in favor of proxy.ts exporting proxy, which runs on the Node runtime. Keeping middleware is only for teams that need to stay on Edge.
rationales: Route Handlers do not intercept other routes.
Correct.
Layouts do not run before routing and do not re-render on navigation.
The deprecated convention is not the recommended path.

questions.scenario: A proxy.ts reads the session cookie and redirects anonymous users from /account. Its matcher excludes /account/export for performance. A Server Action used on /account/export deletes data.
questions.stem: Which statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: Proxy cannot read cookies.
Proxy should only be an optimistic check; the action must verify the session and authorize the resource itself.
Server Actions are only callable from pages that proxy has approved.
Requests excluded by the matcher, including that page's actions, skip proxy entirely.
questions.explanation: Proxy runs only on matched requests and is meant for optimistic checks; every Server Action is a public endpoint that must authenticate and authorize. A matcher that excludes a path also skips that path's actions.
rationales: Reading a cookie is the typical optimistic check.
Correct.
Actions are reachable by POST regardless of proxy.
Correct.

questions.scenario: A proxy.ts sets export const config = { runtime: 'edge', matcher: ['/shop/:path*'] }.
questions.stem: What happens?
options: Proxy runs on Edge for /shop only.
The runtime key is ignored silently.
It throws: proxy runs on Node.js only and runtime cannot be configured.
Proxy runs twice, once per runtime.
questions.explanation: Proxy is Node-only and setting a runtime throws. Teams that must stay on Edge keep the deprecated middleware file.
rationales: Edge is not available for proxy.
It is not ignored.
Correct.
No such behavior.

questions.scenario: A Server Component page fetches its data by calling fetch("http://localhost:3000/api/products"), a Route Handler in the same app that queries the database.
questions.stem: What is the better design?
options: Call the database/data function directly from the Server Component.
Convert the Route Handler to proxy.ts.
Move the fetch to a useEffect in a Client Component.
Add a matcher so proxy caches the response.
questions.explanation: Server Components can query data directly, so calling your own Route Handler adds an unnecessary HTTP round trip. Route Handlers suit external consumers, webhooks and non-HTML responses.
rationales: Correct.
Proxy is not a data layer.
Adds client round trips and loading states.
Proxy does not cache responses.

questions.scenario: A developer creates app/feed/route.ts for an RSS GET endpoint next to the existing app/feed/page.tsx.
questions.stem: What is the problem?
options: Route Handlers only support POST.
Route Handlers must live under app/api/.
A route file cannot share a segment with a page file; move it (for example to app/feed.xml/route.ts).
RSS must be served from proxy.ts.
questions.explanation: Next.js does not allow route and page at the same route segment level. Route Handlers can live anywhere in app/ and support all HTTP methods.
rationales: GET and other methods are supported.
app/api is a convention, not a requirement.
Correct.
Proxy is for pre-routing logic.

questions.scenario: An older codebase sets export const runtime = "edge" on several routes. The team is enabling cacheComponents in Next 16.
questions.stem: What should they do with those exports?
options: Remove them: Cache Components requires the Node runtime, and the Edge runtime is deprecated.
Change them to runtime = "proxy".
Move them into next.config experimental.edge.
Keep them; Edge is required for streaming.
questions.explanation: Cache Components needs the Node.js runtime, and Next.js documents the Edge runtime as deprecated for new routes. Streaming works on Node.
rationales: Correct.
No such runtime.
No such config.
Streaming is supported on Node.

questions.scenario: A team wants a "subscribe" form to keep working for users on slow networks whose JavaScript has not loaded yet.
questions.stem: Which implementation gives progressive enhancement?
options: Attach an onSubmit handler that calls fetch("/api/subscribe") and calls preventDefault.
Call the Server Action from a useEffect once the component mounts.
Render the form in a Client Component and call the action from a button onClick.
Render <form action={subscribe}> from a Server Component, where subscribe is a Server Action.
questions.explanation: A form whose action is a Server Action and which is rendered by a Server Component submits as a normal HTML form before hydration. Handlers like onSubmit and onClick need JavaScript, so they do nothing until it loads.
rationales: onSubmit with preventDefault needs JavaScript; without it the handler never runs.
Effects only run on the client after hydration and are not a submission mechanism.
onClick handlers do nothing before hydration.
Correct: the HTML form posts to the action without JavaScript.

sources.title: Server Actions and Mutations — Next.js Docs

questions.scenario: A developer writes a Client Component with an inline async function marked 'use server' inside the component body.
questions.stem: What is the correct fix?
options: Move the function to a separate module marked 'use server' and import it into the Client Component.
Add 'use client' inside the inline function as well.
Wrap the inline function in useCallback.
Convert the function to a synchronous function.
questions.explanation: Client Components cannot define Server Functions inline. They import them from a 'use server' module or receive them as props from a Server Component.
rationales: Correct: a 'use server' module can be imported by Client Components.
'use client' marks a module boundary, not a function; it does not make an inline Server Function valid.
useCallback memoizes a client function; the code still runs on the client.
Server Functions must be async; a synchronous version is invalid.

sources.title: Server Actions and Mutations — Next.js Docs

questions.scenario: A dashboard calls three Server Actions inside Promise.all to load three widgets' data on mount. The widgets appear one after another and slowly.
questions.stem: What best explains this and fixes it?
options: Server Actions are cached; add revalidatePath to each call.
Next.js dispatches actions sequentially per client; fetch the data in Server Components (in parallel) instead.
Promise.all is not supported in Client Components; use a for loop.
The actions need the experimental parallel flag in next.config.
questions.explanation: Next.js queues Server Action calls and runs them one at a time per client, so Promise.all over actions does not parallelize. Actions are meant for mutations; reads belong in Server Components, where parallel fetching works.
rationales: Actions are not a read cache; revalidation does not change their dispatch order.
Correct: actions run sequentially, and data reads belong in Server Components.
Promise.all works in client code; the serialization comes from action dispatch.
No such flag exists for actions in the cited docs.

sources.title: Server Actions and Mutations — Next.js Docs

questions.scenario: A SubmitButton should show "Saving..." while its form's Server Action runs. The developer calls useFormStatus in the same component that renders <form>, and pending is always false.
questions.stem: Why?
options: pending is only true in development builds.
useFormStatus reads the status of a parent <form>, so it must be called in a component rendered inside the form.
useFormStatus only works with forms that use onSubmit.
useFormStatus must be wrapped in startTransition.
questions.explanation: useFormStatus returns the status of the parent form. The component that renders the form is not inside it, so the hook sees no form; move it into a child such as SubmitButton.
rationales: pending works in production too.
Correct: it must be rendered inside the form.
It works with action-based forms; onSubmit is not required.
It is a hook call, not a state update; startTransition is irrelevant.

questions.scenario: A signup action currently throws new Error("Email already used") when the email is taken. Users see the segment's error.js screen and lose what they typed.
questions.stem: What is the recommended change?
options: Wrap the whole page in a try/catch in the Server Component.
Catch the error in global-error.js and re-render the form.
Throw a notFound() instead so the user sees a 404.
Return the error as part of the action state and render it with useActionState.
questions.explanation: The Next.js error-handling guide models expected errors as return values shown through useActionState, and reserves error boundaries for uncaught exceptions. A duplicate email is expected, so it should be returned, not thrown.
rationales: A try/catch in the Server Component does not catch errors thrown later in an action invocation.
global-error.js replaces the whole root layout; it is for catastrophic errors.
A 404 misrepresents a validation problem.
Correct: expected errors are returned as state and shown inline.

questions.stem: A form uses const [state, formAction] = useActionState(updateName, { error: null }). Which signature must updateName have?
options: async function updateName(event: FormEvent)
function updateName(state: State): State (synchronous only)
async function updateName(prevState: State, formData: FormData)
async function updateName(formData: FormData)
questions.explanation: useActionState calls the action with the previous state as the first argument and the submitted FormData as the second. An action written with only a (formData) parameter would receive the state object in that slot instead of the form data.
rationales: Form actions receive FormData, not a DOM event.
The action may be async; Server Functions must be.
Correct: (prevState, formData).
This is the signature without useActionState; formData would actually receive prevState.

questions.scenario: An address form has HTML required attributes and a client-side regex for the postcode. The action writes formData values straight to the database.
questions.stem: What is the main risk and the right fix?
options: Move validation into a useEffect that runs before submit.
Add the same regex to a Proxy matcher.
Anyone can POST directly to the action, so validate on the server with a schema (for example Zod safeParse) inside the action.
No risk: browsers block submissions that fail HTML validation.
questions.explanation: Server Actions are reachable by direct POST, so client-side checks are UX only. The data security guide says to validate input inside every action; safeParse lets you return field errors instead of throwing.
rationales: Client-side code can still be bypassed.
Proxy matchers match paths; they do not validate form bodies.
Correct: validate on the server inside the action.
Browser validation is skipped by any direct request.

questions.scenario: After a user edits their profile through a Server Action, the page they land on still shows the old display name until a second reload.
questions.stem: Which call inside the action best gives the user their own write immediately?
options: revalidateTag('profile') with one argument
updateTag('profile')
revalidateTag('profile', 'max')
router.refresh() inside the action
questions.explanation: updateTag is the Server Action API for read-your-own-writes: it expires the tag and refreshes it in the same request. revalidateTag with 'max' is stale-while-revalidate, so the next read can still be stale, and the single-argument form is deprecated.
rationales: Deprecated in Next 16 and does not guarantee fresh data on the next read.
Correct: expires and refreshes within the same request.
Stale-while-revalidate may serve the old value once more.
router.refresh is a client router method and is not available inside a server action.

questions.scenario: A headless CMS calls a webhook Route Handler when an article is published.
questions.stem: Which API should the handler use to invalidate cached article data?
options: revalidateTag('articles', 'max')
redirect('/articles')
updateTag('articles')
useOptimistic in the handler
questions.explanation: updateTag is limited to Server Actions, so a Route Handler uses revalidateTag(tag, 'max'), which marks the data stale and refreshes it in the background. That is fine for readers who did not make the change.
rationales: Correct: stale-while-revalidate invalidation from a Route Handler.
redirect does not invalidate any cache.
updateTag cannot be used in Route Handlers.
useOptimistic is a client hook.

questions.stem: An action ends with redirect("/posts") followed by revalidatePath("/posts"). The posts page shows stale data after creating a post. What is wrong?
options: redirect() is not allowed in Server Actions.
revalidatePath only works in Route Handlers.
redirect() throws, so revalidatePath never runs; call revalidation before redirect.
revalidatePath needs the "layout" type for static paths.
questions.explanation: redirect works by throwing, so code after it never runs. Revalidate first, then redirect.
rationales: redirect is commonly used at the end of Server Actions.
revalidatePath works in Server Functions as well.
Correct: the revalidation line is unreachable.
The type argument is needed for dynamic patterns, and it is not the cause here.

sources.title: Server Actions and Mutations — Next.js Docs

questions.scenario: A like button updates a counter with useOptimistic. The developer calls setOptimistic(count + 1) in onClick, then awaits the Server Action outside any Transition. The count flickers back immediately and React logs a warning.
questions.stem: What fixes it?
options: Store the optimistic count in useState instead.
Call setOptimistic and the action inside startTransition (or from a form action).
Add count to a useEffect dependency array.
Call setOptimistic after the action resolves.
questions.explanation: The useOptimistic setter must be called inside an Action or Transition. Outside one, React warns and the value reverts at once; inside one, it holds until the Action finishes and then converges with the real value.
rationales: useState would require manual rollback and loses the convergence behaviour.
Correct: run the update inside a Transition or Action.
Effects do not create Transitions.
Setting it after the response defeats the optimistic purpose.

questions.scenario: A team relies on useOptimistic to show a new comment immediately.
questions.stem: Which statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: If the server write fails, the optimistic comment disappears when the Action finishes, because the value converges with the real prop.
Optimistic updates make server-side revalidation unnecessary.
The Server Action should still revalidate the comments data so the real value includes the new comment.
useOptimistic persists the optimistic value to the server cache.
questions.explanation: When the Action ends, the optimistic value converges with the real value, so a failed write reverts without manual rollback. Optimistic UI is purely client-side; the server must still revalidate so the real data includes the change.
rationales: Correct: the value converges back to the real data.
Without revalidation, the real value never includes the change and the comment vanishes.
Correct: revalidation makes the real value catch up.
useOptimistic is local UI state only.

questions.scenario: A deleteInvoice(id) action is only rendered on an admin-only page. The action deletes the row by id without further checks.
questions.stem: What is the most important problem?
options: The action should be moved to a Client Component to hide it.
Action IDs are encrypted, so attackers cannot call it.
None: users without access never see the button.
The action is a public POST endpoint; it must verify the session and authorize this user for this invoice inside the action.
questions.explanation: The data security guide treats Server Actions as public endpoints that can be called directly. Encrypted IDs and hidden buttons are not access control, so the action must authenticate and authorize the specific resource itself.
rationales: Client code is visible to everyone, so moving it hides nothing.
Encrypted IDs reduce exposure but do not check who is calling.
Hiding UI does not prevent a direct POST.
Correct: authenticate and authorize inside the action.

questions.scenario: An updateComment(commentId, text) action checks that a session exists, then updates the comment with that id.
questions.stem: Which vulnerability remains?
options: CSRF, because Next.js performs no origin checks.
Hydration mismatch.
Cross-site scripting, because React escapes nothing in actions.
Insecure direct object reference: any logged-in user can edit any comment by sending its id.
questions.explanation: Authentication proves who the user is but not that they may edit this comment. Each action must also authorize the specific resource, for example by checking ownership.
rationales: Next.js compares Origin and Host for Server Actions.
Hydration is unrelated to authorization.
XSS concerns rendering output, not the authorization gap here.
Correct: authorization of the specific resource is missing.

questions.scenario: Admin routes are protected by a proxy.ts whose matcher covers /admin/:path*. A Server Action used on /settings changes user roles.
questions.stem: Which statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: The action must verify the session and the caller's admin role itself.
The proxy check does not cover the action, because the request goes to /settings, which the matcher excludes.
Proxy is the recommended place for full authorization of every action.
Layouts re-check auth on every navigation, so a check in the /settings layout is enough.
questions.explanation: Actions are posted to the page route, so a matcher that excludes the path also skips the action. The docs treat Proxy as an optimistic check and say layouts do not re-render on navigation, so authorization belongs inside the action.
rationales: Correct: the action authorizes itself.
Correct: the matcher does not include /settings.
Proxy is for optimistic checks, not full authorization.
Layouts do not re-render on navigation, so their checks are not reliable.

questions.scenario: An app runs on several instances behind a load balancer. Some users intermittently get errors from Server Actions that capture variables in closures.
questions.stem: Which setting most directly addresses this?
options: Set the same NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY on every instance.
Switch the actions to the Edge runtime.
Increase serverActions.bodySizeLimit.
Disable CSRF origin checks.
questions.explanation: Next.js encrypts variables captured by action closures. Every instance needs the same encryption key, otherwise a request encrypted by one instance cannot be decrypted by another.
rationales: Correct: a shared key lets every instance decrypt.
The Edge runtime is deprecated and does not change key handling.
Body size is unrelated to decryption across instances.
Disabling origin checks weakens security and does not fix decryption.

questions.scenario: A product page shows a list that is the same for all visitors and changes a few times a day.
questions.stem: What is the best default for loading it?
options: Fetch it in useEffect in a Client Component on every visit.
Load it through a Server Action called on mount.
Fetch it in a Server Component (with appropriate caching) and render it into the HTML.
Poll it every second with a client data library.
questions.explanation: The Next.js fetching guide makes Server Components the default way to read data: it arrives in the HTML and needs no client JavaScript. Client fetching or polling adds work without benefit for slow-changing shared data.
rationales: Delays content until after hydration and adds client work.
Actions are for mutations and are dispatched sequentially.
Correct: server fetching is the default for this kind of data.
Polling is wasteful for data that changes a few times a day.

questions.scenario: A search-as-you-type box fetches results in a useEffect keyed on the query, with no cleanup. When a user types fast, results for an earlier query sometimes replace the results for the final query.
questions.stem: Which changes fix this? (Select two.)
options: Set an ignore flag in the Effect cleanup and skip setState when it is true.
Wrap the fetch in useMemo.
Abort the in-flight request in the cleanup with an AbortController.
Remove query from the dependency array.
questions.explanation: Responses can arrive out of order, so a stale one can overwrite fresh results. React documents an ignore flag in cleanup to drop stale responses, and AbortController cancels the outdated request itself.
rationales: Correct: React's documented fix for fetch race conditions.
useMemo is for computing values during render, not for async side effects.
Correct: cancels the obsolete request.
The Effect would stop re-running and the results would never update.

sources.title: You Might Not Need an Effect — React Learn

questions.scenario: A notifications panel must stay fresh while the page is open, refetch when the tab regains focus, and be shared by three client components.
questions.stem: Which approach fits best?
options: Moving the whole app to Client Components.
A client-side data cache library (SWR or React Query style) for that panel, with server rendering for the rest of the page.
A Server Action called every few seconds from each component.
Rendering the panel in the root layout so it re-renders on navigation.
questions.explanation: Client caches suit data that must refresh while the page is open and is shared across client components. The rest of the page can stay server-rendered, which the Next.js fetching guide treats as the default.
rationales: Giving up server rendering for one live widget is unnecessary.
Correct: a scoped client cache for live, shared data.
Actions are sequential mutations, not a polling mechanism.
Layouts do not re-render on navigation.

questions.scenario: A client component calls the dispatch function from useActionState inside a button onClick (not via a form action prop). React warns and isPending never becomes true.
questions.stem: What is the fix?
options: Call the dispatch from useEffect instead.
Convert the action to a synchronous function.
Pass the dispatch to useFormStatus.
Wrap the dispatch call in startTransition.
questions.explanation: When the dispatch from useActionState is called outside a form or action prop, it must be wrapped in startTransition. Form action props do this automatically.
rationales: Effects do not create Transitions and add needless re-renders.
Being synchronous does not fix the missing Transition.
useFormStatus takes no arguments; it reads the parent form.
Correct: manual dispatch needs a Transition.

questions.scenario: A team on Next 16 without Cache Components has a product listing page that was fully static. A developer adds a "sort by" control that reads `searchParams` in the page component.
questions.stem: What is the effect on how the route is rendered?
options: The build fails until the page exports a revalidate value.
Only the sort control is rendered dynamically; the rest stays static.
Nothing changes, because searchParams are resolved at build time.
The whole route is now rendered dynamically at request time.
questions.explanation: In the previous model, using a request-time API such as searchParams opts the entire route into dynamic rendering. Splitting a page into a static shell and dynamic holes is what Cache Components adds. searchParams are only known per request, and no revalidate export is required.
rationales: Nothing requires a revalidate export; the route simply becomes dynamic.
Per-component static/dynamic splitting is the Cache Components model, not the previous one.
searchParams come from each request URL and cannot be known at build time.
Correct: request APIs make the whole route dynamic in the previous model.

sources.title: Caching without Cache Components — Next.js Docs

questions.scenario: With `cacheComponents: true`, a product page renders a static description and a `<Recommendations>` component that reads `cookies()` to personalize results. `next build` reports an error about request data accessed outside a boundary.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Add `export const dynamic = "force-dynamic"` to the page.
Wrap `<Recommendations>` in `<Suspense>` with a skeleton fallback.
Add `'use cache'` to `<Recommendations>` so the cookie read is cached.
Move the cookies() call into the root layout.
questions.explanation: With Cache Components, components that read runtime data must sit inside a Suspense boundary: the fallback goes into the static shell and the personalized content streams in. Reading cookies inside use cache is not allowed. Moving the read up the tree makes more of the page request-dependent, which is the opposite of the goal.
rationales: Segment configs like dynamic belong to the previous model and would throw away the static shell.
Correct: the Suspense boundary turns the component into a dynamic hole and keeps the rest prerendered.
cookies() cannot be called inside a use cache scope (next-request-in-use-cache).
Reading request data higher up makes more of the tree dynamic and does not fix the boundary problem.

questions.stem: What is the correct way to cache this report per tenant?
options: Keep the code as is; Next.js adds the session cookie to the cache key automatically.
Read the tenant id outside the function and pass it as an argument: `getReport(tenantId)`.
Replace `'use cache'` with `React.cache` so the result is shared across requests.
Switch to `cacheLife('seconds')` so a wrong tenant's data is only shown briefly.
questions.explanation: Request APIs such as cookies() cannot be read inside a use cache scope, and the cache key is built from the function's arguments and closed-over values. Passing the tenant id as an argument both avoids the forbidden read and makes each tenant a separate cache entry. React.cache only dedupes within one request, and a shorter lifetime does not prevent cross-tenant leaks.
rationales: Cookies are not read into the key; they are not even allowed inside the scope.
Correct: the id becomes part of the cache key, one entry per tenant.
React.cache dedupes per request; it is not a cross-request cache.
Shortening the lifetime still leaks data; the key is the problem.

questions.scenario: A Next 16 app is deployed to a serverless platform with several instances. Functions use plain `'use cache'`. The team notices the cache hit rate is low and cached values vanish after each deploy.
questions.stem: What explains this, and what should they consider?
options: The default storage is an in-memory LRU per instance that does not survive deploys; consider `'use cache: remote'` or a shared cache handler.
The cache is stored in the browser; switch to `'use cache: private'` to store it on the server.
cacheLife defaults to zero; set any profile to make entries persist.
Serverless platforms disable use cache; switch to unstable_cache.
questions.explanation: Plain 'use cache' stores entries in an in-memory LRU, which does not persist across serverless invocations and is not carried over across deploys. 'use cache: remote' (or a shared cacheHandlers implementation when self-hosting) provides durable shared storage. 'use cache: private' is the browser-only variant, not a server store.
rationales: Correct: per-instance memory explains both symptoms.
It is the reverse: 'use cache: private' is the browser-only variant.
The default profile has a 15-minute revalidate and no expiry; it is not zero.
use cache is not disabled on serverless; it just uses per-instance memory by default.

questions.stem: A cached function uses `cacheLife('days')`. Twenty-six hours after the entry was created, a request arrives. What happens?
options: The request waits while the entry is regenerated, then gets fresh data.
The request gets the cached value and a fresh value is generated in the background.
The entry has expired, so the route errors until it is rebuilt.
The cached value is served and never refreshed until the next deploy.
questions.explanation: The days profile revalidates after 1 day and expires after 1 week. Past the revalidate window but before expiry, Next.js serves the cached value and refreshes it in the background (stale-while-revalidate). Blocking regeneration only happens after the expire time.
rationales: Blocking regeneration applies only after expire (1 week for days).
Correct: between revalidate and expire, stale-while-revalidate applies.
Expiry does not cause errors, and 26 hours is well within a week.
The revalidate window triggers a background refresh; it does not wait for a deploy.

questions.stem: Which cacheLife configurations cause a cached entry to be left out of the prerendered shell and treated as dynamic? (Select two.)
options: `revalidate: 0`
An `expire` value under 5 minutes
The `'max'` profile
The `'hours'` profile
questions.explanation: Per the cacheLife rules, revalidate: 0 or an expire under 5 minutes turns the entry into a dynamic hole rather than prerendering it. The max and hours profiles have long revalidate and expire times and are prerendered normally.
rationales: Correct: revalidate 0 makes the entry dynamic.
Correct: an expire under 5 minutes is too short to prerender.
max revalidates after 30 days and expires after a year; it is prerendered.
hours revalidates after 1 hour and expires after 1 day; it is prerendered.

questions.scenario: A marketing site pulls pages from a headless CMS. Editors publish a few times a week and expect changes live within a minute. Traffic is high.
questions.stem: Which approach best fits?
options: Cache pages with `cacheLife('seconds')` so changes appear quickly.
Render every page dynamically with `await connection()`.
Cache with a long cacheLife and `cacheTag('cms')`, and have a CMS webhook Route Handler call `revalidateTag('cms', 'max')`.
Cache with a long cacheLife and call `updateTag('cms')` from the CMS webhook Route Handler.
questions.explanation: When you know when data changes, tag-based on-demand revalidation lets content stay cached for a long time and refresh right after a publish. revalidateTag runs in Route Handlers; updateTag is limited to Server Actions. Very short lifetimes or fully dynamic rendering waste work on a high-traffic site whose content rarely changes.
rationales: A seconds-level lifetime re-renders constantly for content that changes a few times a week.
Fully dynamic rendering discards caching entirely for mostly static content.
Correct: long cache plus webhook-driven tag invalidation.
updateTag can only be called from Server Actions, not Route Handlers.

questions.scenario: In a project management app, a user renames a project through a Server Action. The project list is cached with `cacheTag('projects')`. After the action, users sometimes still see the old name until they reload again.
questions.stem: What change gives the user their own write immediately?
options: Call `revalidateTag('projects')` with one argument.
Call `revalidatePath('/', 'layout')` after `redirect()`.
Call `updateTag('projects')` in the Server Action.
Set `cacheLife('seconds')` on the project list.
questions.explanation: revalidateTag(tag, 'max') uses stale-while-revalidate, so the response can still contain stale data. updateTag, available only in Server Actions, expires and refreshes the tag in the same request so the user reads their own write. The one-argument revalidateTag is deprecated, and redirect() throws, so anything after it never runs.
rationales: The one-argument form is deprecated in Next 16 and still has no read-your-own-writes guarantee.
redirect() throws, so code after it never runs; purging everything is also excessive.
Correct: updateTag gives read-your-own-writes in Server Actions.
Short lifetimes do not guarantee the next response is fresh and cost cache efficiency.

questions.stem: A team self-hosts Next.js behind a CDN. Which statements about the default Cache-Control headers are accurate? (Select two.)
options: Hashed files under /_next/static are sent with `public, max-age=31536000, immutable`.
Dynamically rendered pages are sent with `private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate`.
Dynamic pages are sent with `public, s-maxage=31536000` so the CDN caches them.
Static assets are sent with `no-store` so the CDN always fetches the latest build.
questions.explanation: The self-hosting guide documents immutable one-year caching for hashed static assets, since their names change with their content, and private/no-store headers for dynamic pages so shared caches do not store them. Caching dynamic pages publicly at a CDN could serve one user's page to another.
rationales: Correct: hashed assets are safe to cache forever.
Correct: dynamic pages must not be stored by shared caches.
Dynamic pages are private; public long-lived caching would be unsafe.
Hashed assets are immutable, not no-store.

questions.scenario: Lighthouse flags a late LCP on a landing page. The LCP element is a hero rendered with `<Image src="/hero.jpg" width={1600} height={900} alt="" />` using default props.
questions.stem: What change most directly addresses the LCP?
options: Add `loading="eager"` or `fetchPriority="high"` (or `preload`) to the hero image.
Add the `priority` prop, the recommended way in Next 16.
Remove width and height so the image can render at natural size.
Replace next/image with a CSS background image.
questions.explanation: next/image lazy-loads by default, which delays the LCP image. Marking it eager or high priority (or using the preload prop) makes the browser fetch it early. priority is deprecated in v16, and removing dimensions would introduce layout shift.
rationales: Correct: the LCP image should not be lazy.
priority is deprecated in Next 16 in favour of preload.
Dimensions reserve space; removing them causes CLS and does not speed loading.
CSS background images are discovered late and lose optimization; this tends to make LCP worse.

questions.scenario: A site loads Google Fonts via a `<link>` tag in the root layout. Users notice text jumping when the font arrives, and the privacy team objects to browsers contacting a third-party font host.
questions.stem: What is the best change?
options: Add `font-display: block` so text never renders with the fallback.
Load the font with next/script using `beforeInteractive`.
Use `next/font/google`, which self-hosts the font at build time and adjusts fallback metrics.
Preconnect to the Google Fonts domain to speed it up.
questions.explanation: next/font downloads fonts at build time and serves them with the app, so the browser makes no requests to Google. It uses display swap by default and adjustFontFallback to reduce layout shift. Preconnecting still contacts the third party, and block display hides text instead of fixing the shift.
rationales: Blocking hides text during load and does not address the third-party request.
next/script is for JavaScript, not stylesheets or font files.
Correct: self-hosting addresses privacy, and fallback adjustment reduces CLS.
Preconnect speeds the request up but still contacts the third party and does not prevent the shift.

questions.scenario: A SaaS dashboard loads a support chat widget, an analytics tag and a consent manager that must run before the page becomes interactive.
questions.stem: Which assignment of next/script strategies is most appropriate?
options: All three with `beforeInteractive` in the root layout.
Consent: `lazyOnload`; analytics: `beforeInteractive`; chat: `worker`.
Consent: `beforeInteractive` in the root layout; analytics: `afterInteractive`; chat: `lazyOnload`.
All three with `worker` to keep them off the main thread.
questions.explanation: beforeInteractive is for truly critical scripts and must be placed in the root layout; afterInteractive (the default) suits analytics; lazyOnload defers non-critical widgets to idle time. The worker strategy is experimental and does not work with the App Router.
rationales: Loading everything before hydration bloats the critical path.
Consent would load too late, and worker is unavailable in the App Router.
Correct: each script matches its urgency.
worker is experimental and not supported with the App Router.

questions.scenario: A team is planning rendering for a new B2B SaaS app with Cache Components enabled: a public pricing page, a dashboard with a fixed sidebar and per-user widgets, a per-user settings page whose data changes rarely, and a live incident feed.
questions.stem: Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Render all four pages dynamically to avoid stale data.
Pricing: dynamic; dashboard: 'use cache' around the whole page including the session read; settings: CDN-cached by URL; incident feed: cacheLife('max').

Pricing: 'use cache' with a tag; dashboard: static shell with per-user widgets in Suspense; settings: cache keyed by user id passed as an argument (or 'use cache: private'); incident feed: uncached via await connection() with client-side updates.
Cache everything for one hour with one shared tag and revalidate it on every write.
questions.explanation: The strategy should match each page: public content is cached and invalidated by tag, dashboards keep a static shell with dynamic holes, per-user data is cached only with the user in the key or in the browser, and real-time data skips the server cache. Caching a session read or CDN-caching per-user pages by URL risks leaking data, and a long cache on a live feed shows outdated incidents.
rationales: Rendering everything dynamically gives up cheap, fast caching for public and shell content.
Session reads are not allowed in use cache, URL-keyed CDN caching leaks per-user pages, and max is wrong for live data.
Correct: each page type gets the strategy that fits its freshness and privacy needs.
One shared tag invalidates everything on every write and still serves stale live data.

questions.stem: Which statements about `'use cache'` are accurate? (Select two.)
options: It can only be applied to async functions or components.
Its cache key includes the serialized arguments and closed-over values.
It can be used in Proxy (proxy.ts) to cache responses.
Inside it, `React.cache` shares results with the surrounding request.
questions.explanation: 'use cache' applies at file, component or function level and only on async functions. Its key combines the build ID, function ID, serialized arguments and closed-over values. It has no effect in Proxy, and React.cache is isolated inside use cache.
rationales: Correct: only async functions can be cached.
Correct: arguments and closures are part of the key.
use cache has no effect in Proxy.
React.cache is isolated inside use cache scopes.

questions.scenario:
A team on Next 16 without Cache Components expects a product API call to be cached, but logs show it runs on every request:

```ts
const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/products')
```
questions.stem: Why, and how do they cache it for ten minutes?
options: fetch caching requires `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'`.
fetch is cached by default but only in production; deploy to see caching.
External URLs cannot be cached; wrap it in a Route Handler.
fetch is not cached by default; pass `{ next: { revalidate: 600 } }` or `cache: 'force-cache'`.
questions.explanation: In the previous model, fetch is not cached by default. You opt in per request with cache: 'force-cache' or next: { revalidate: seconds }, the latter giving time-based revalidation. force-dynamic does the opposite and forces dynamic rendering.
rationales: force-dynamic forces dynamic rendering, the opposite of caching.
The default is uncached in all environments.
External fetches can be cached with the opt-in options.
Correct: opt in per fetch; next.revalidate sets a time window.
