questions.scenario: A product page with Cache Components shows a "Deal ends in" countdown computed with `Date.now()` in a Server Component. The build reports an error about non-deterministic values during prerendering.
questions.stem: Which fix keeps the rest of the page in the static shell?
options: Disable cacheComponents for the project.
Add `'use cache'` to the page component so Date.now() runs once at build time and is reused indefinitely.
Read `headers()` first to force the whole page dynamic.
Move the countdown into a component that calls `await connection()` before `Date.now()`, wrapped in `<Suspense>`.
questions.explanation: Non-deterministic values such as Date.now() need await connection() plus a Suspense boundary (or a deliberate cache boundary). Isolating the countdown makes only that piece a dynamic hole. Caching the whole page would freeze the countdown, and forcing the page dynamic or disabling Cache Components throws away the static shell.
rationales: Disabling the feature avoids the error but loses partial prerendering.
Caching freezes the time value, which breaks a countdown.
Making the whole page dynamic gives up the shell for one small widget.
Correct: only the countdown becomes request-time work.

questions.scenario: A personalized "recently viewed" panel reads a cookie. The team wants to avoid refetching it on every client navigation but must never store it in a shared server cache.
questions.stem: Which option fits?
options: Plain `'use cache'` reading cookies() inside the function.
`'use cache: remote'` keyed by URL.
A CDN rule caching the page for 5 minutes.
`'use cache: private'` on the panel's data function.
questions.explanation: 'use cache: private' is allowed to read cookies, headers and searchParams, and its results are cached in the browser only and excluded from the static shell. Remote and CDN caches are shared, and plain use cache forbids cookie reads.
rationales: Plain use cache does not allow cookies() inside the scope.
Remote caches are shared server storage and the URL does not identify the user.
A shared CDN cache would serve one user's panel to others.
Correct: browser-only caching that may read cookies.

questions.scenario: A self-hosted Next.js app runs on four instances behind a load balancer. A CMS webhook calls `revalidateTag`, but only some users see updated content afterwards.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The CDN is caching /_next/static files; set them to no-store.
The webhook must call revalidateTag four times, once per instance.
revalidateTag only works on Vercel; switch to revalidatePath.
Each instance has its own cache; configure a shared cache handler that implements tag refresh so invalidation reaches every instance.
questions.explanation: With per-instance in-memory caches, a webhook that hits one instance only invalidates that instance. The self-hosting guide calls for a shared cacheHandler / cacheHandlers implementation with tag refresh support in multi-instance setups. Hashed static assets are immutable by design and are not the cause.
rationales: Hashed assets change name per build; caching them is correct.
The load balancer decides which instance receives each call, so repeating it is unreliable.
revalidateTag is not platform-specific, and revalidatePath has the same per-instance issue.
Correct: a shared cache handler makes invalidation global.

questions.stem: Without Cache Components, how do you make a GET Route Handler that returns a static sitemap cached rather than run on every request?
options: Add `'use client'` to the route file.
Nothing; GET Route Handlers are cached by default.
Export `const dynamic = 'force-static'` from the route file.
Return the response with a `revalidateTag` header.
questions.explanation: In the previous model, GET Route Handlers are not cached by default; export const dynamic = 'force-static' opts in. With Cache Components, GET handlers follow the same prerender model as pages instead.
rationales: 'use client' has no meaning for Route Handlers.
GET handlers are not cached by default.
Correct: force-static opts the handler into static caching.
revalidateTag is a function, not a response header.

sources.title: Caching without Cache Components — Next.js Docs

questions.scenario: An app uses `cacheLife('minutes')` on a nested cached function inside an outer cached component that sets no cacheLife of its own.
questions.stem: How does the outer cache's lifetime behave?
options: It inherits the shorter inner lifetime.
It keeps the 'default' profile regardless of inner caches.
It takes the longest lifetime of any inner cache.
The inner cacheLife is ignored when nested.
questions.explanation: An outer cache that sets no cacheLife uses the default profile (15-minute revalidate). Inner caches with shorter lifetimes reduce it, so here the inner minutes profile (1-minute revalidate) propagates outward; longer inner lifetimes cannot extend it. The minutes profile is not short-lived enough (expire is 1 hour) to trigger the nested short-lived cache error.
rationales: Correct: shorter inner lifetimes propagate outward.
Shorter inner lifetimes do propagate when the outer cache sets none.
Longer inner lifetimes cannot extend the outer cache.
Inner cacheLife values take part in the outer calculation.

questions.scenario: A marketing page built with the App Router shows a large hero photo rendered with next/image using only src, alt, width and height. Field data shows LCP at 3.8 s, and the waterfall shows the hero request starting after most scripts.
questions.stem: Which change most directly addresses the late hero image request?
options: Add preload (or loading="eager" / fetchPriority="high") to the hero next/image
Wrap the hero in a Suspense boundary with a skeleton fallback
Switch the hero to a CSS background-image loaded from a stylesheet
Add the priority prop together with loading="lazy" to keep it in sync with other images
questions.explanation: next/image lazy-loads by default, so the LCP image is discovered late, which inflates resource load delay. In Next 16, preload replaces the deprecated priority prop, and loading="eager" or fetchPriority="high" also make the browser fetch it early. A Suspense fallback or CSS background makes discovery later, not earlier.
rationales: Correct. It removes the lazy-load delay for the LCP element.
The hero would only paint when the boundary resolves, which delays LCP further.
Background images in CSS are discovered even later, after the stylesheet is parsed.
priority is deprecated in v16, and combining it with lazy loading is contradictory.

questions.scenario: A dashboard reports these 75th-percentile field values for mobile: LCP 2.3 s, INP 260 ms, CLS 0.05.
questions.stem: How should the team classify these results?
options: CLS needs improvement because any value above 0 indicates layout shifts
All three are good, because the median user is under every threshold
LCP and CLS are good; INP needs improvement
INP is poor because it is above 200 ms
questions.explanation: Good thresholds are LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms and CLS ≤ 0.1, and poor begins above 4 s, 500 ms and 0.25. INP at 260 ms sits between the two INP thresholds, so it needs improvement. Classification uses the 75th percentile, not the median.
rationales: CLS up to 0.1 is good.
Core Web Vitals use the 75th percentile, and 260 ms INP is above the good threshold.
Correct. 2.3 s and 0.05 are good; 260 ms is between 200 and 500 ms.
Poor INP starts above 500 ms; 260 ms is "needs improvement".

questions.scenario: Clicking a category tab on a product page sets state that re-renders a grid of 3,000 cards synchronously. INP traces show the processing-duration phase is about 400 ms, and the tab highlight only appears when the grid finishes.
questions.stem: Which change best improves INP while keeping the same features?
options: Move the category filter into a Server Action so the browser does no work
Set the selected tab urgently and update the grid category inside startTransition, rendering fewer cards at once
Add a 300 ms debounce before handling clicks on the tabs
Wrap the click handler in useCallback so the tab buttons receive a stable function
questions.explanation: The long processing phase comes from the synchronous re-render of a huge grid. Marking the grid update as a Transition lets React paint the urgent tab change first and render the grid in an interruptible background render, and reducing the rendered DOM cuts the remaining work. Stabilizing the handler or debouncing does not remove the work, and a server round trip adds latency before the next paint.
rationales: A network round trip does not make the next paint faster, and the grid still has to re-render.
Correct. The urgent update paints first and the expensive render becomes non-blocking.
Debouncing delays the response to the click, which makes the interaction feel slower.
The handler identity is not the cost; the grid render is.

questions.scenario: A news article page has CLS of 0.31. Investigation shows ads that load into the article without reserved space, author avatars rendered with plain tags without width or height, and an accordion that expands when the reader clicks it.
questions.stem: Which two changes will reduce CLS? (Select two.)
options: Animate the accordion expansion more slowly
Lazy-load the ads with loading="lazy" while keeping the slots unsized
Reserve fixed-size slots for the ads before they load
Give the avatars dimensions, for example by using next/image with width and height
questions.explanation: Unexpected shifts come from content that arrives without reserved space, so sizing the ad slots and the images removes them. The accordion shift happens right after a click, and shifts within 500 ms of user input are excluded from CLS. Lazy-loading unsized slots only moves the shift later in the visit.
rationales: Input-driven shifts within 500 ms are already excluded, so this is not the source of the score.
The slot still has no size, so content still shifts when the ad appears.
Correct. Reserved space means the ad no longer pushes content down.
Correct. Dimensions let the browser reserve the image box before it loads.

questions.scenario: A cookie banner is injected at the top of the page well after load, with no user input nearby. Before the shift, the article content occupies the top half of the viewport; the banner pushes it down by 25% of the viewport height, so the union of its old and new positions covers 75% of the viewport. No other shifts occur.
questions.stem: What CLS does this single shift produce, and how is it rated?
options: 0.25, rated poor
0.1875, rated needs improvement
1.0, rated poor
0.1875, rated good because it happens only once
questions.explanation: A layout-shift score is impact fraction × distance fraction. The impact fraction is the union of the unstable content's visible area before and after the shift (50% + 25% = 75% of the viewport), and the distance fraction is how far it moved (25% of the viewport height), so the score is 0.75 × 0.25 = 0.1875. That is above the 0.1 good threshold and not above the 0.25 poor threshold, so it needs improvement. Frequency does not change the rating; one large shift is enough.
rationales: 0.25 is only the distance fraction; it must be multiplied by the impact fraction.
Correct. 0.75 × 0.25 = 0.1875, which falls between 0.1 and 0.25.
The fractions are multiplied, not treated as a full-page shift.
The value is right but the rating is not; good requires 0.1 or less.

questions.scenario: A team says its checkout page "has great INP" because Lighthouse in CI scores 98. Real users still complain that tapping "Pay" feels laggy.
questions.stem: What is the best explanation and next step?
options: INP is only measured on desktop, so mobile complaints do not affect it
Run Lighthouse more times and use the best score as the INP value
Lighthouse measures INP accurately; the complaints are caused by slow networks and can be ignored
Lighthouse cannot measure INP, so it reports Total Blocking Time as a proxy; collect field INP from real users
questions.explanation: INP depends on real user interactions over a visit, so it is a field metric. Lighthouse runs in the lab with no interactions and reports TBT as a proxy for main-thread blocking. Field data, segmented by mobile and desktop at the 75th percentile, shows the real INP.
rationales: Core Web Vitals segment mobile and desktop; both are measured.
Repeating a lab run still never measures a real interaction.
Lighthouse does not interact with the page, so it cannot produce INP.
Correct. TBT is a lab proxy; real interactions are needed for INP.

questions.scenario: A Next 16 app enables reactCompiler: true. A developer opens a pull request that deletes every useMemo and useCallback across 400 files, arguing the compiler now makes them redundant.
questions.stem: What should the reviewer recommend?
options: Merge it, but also wrap every component in memo to be safe
Merge it; the compiler memoizes every function in the codebase, so the hooks are dead code
Reject it; the compiler only works if every component still uses useMemo
Keep the existing hooks, rely on the compiler for new code, and use useMemo/useCallback only as escape hatches
questions.explanation: The React Compiler auto-memoizes components and hooks, so new code rarely needs manual memoization. The React docs advise keeping existing useMemo and useCallback because removing them can change the compiler output, and using them as escape hatches when precise control matters, such as Effect dependencies. Wrapping everything in memo by hand defeats the point of the compiler.
rationales: Manual memo everywhere duplicates what the compiler does and the mass deletion is still risky.
The compiler memoizes components and hooks, not every function, and removal can change its output.
The compiler does not require manual memoization; it adds memoization itself.
Correct. This matches the guidance for adopting the compiler.

questions.scenario: A search page uses const deferred = useDeferredValue(query) and renders <input value={query} .../> plus <Results query={deferred} />. Results is a plain function component that filters 20,000 items. The project does not use the React Compiler. Typing is still janky.
questions.stem: What is the most likely reason?
options: Results is not memoized, so it re-renders during the urgent render as well
The input should read the deferred value instead of query
useDeferredValue only works inside Server Components
useDeferredValue waits a fixed 500 ms, which is too long for typing
questions.explanation: On each keystroke the parent re-renders urgently with the old deferred value. Without memo, Results re-renders anyway and does its 20,000-item filter in the urgent render, so nothing is deferred. Wrapping Results in memo lets it skip the urgent render and only re-render in the background with the new deferred value.
rationales: Correct. The slow child must be memoized for the deferral to help.
The input must stay urgent; binding it to the lagging value would make typing feel broken.
It is a client hook used in components that hold state.
useDeferredValue has no fixed delay; it renders in the background once the urgent render finishes.

questions.scenario: An admin table renders 10,000 rows, each with several cells and buttons. The rows are already wrapped in memo and props are stable, but scrolling and clicking a row checkbox still produce long presentation delays.
questions.stem: Which change addresses the remaining cost?
options: Add useCallback to every row handler
Virtualize the table so only rows in or near the viewport are in the DOM
Move the table into a Server Component
Wrap each row in its own Suspense boundary
questions.explanation: Memoization already removed the React re-render cost; what remains is a very large DOM that makes style, layout and paint slow, which shows up as presentation delay. Virtualization keeps only the visible rows mounted, shrinking the DOM. A Server Component would still send the same 10,000 rows of HTML to the browser.
rationales: Props are already stable; more memoization does not shrink the DOM.
Correct. Fewer DOM nodes means less layout and paint work per interaction.
The browser still has to lay out all the rows, and the checkboxes need client interactivity.
Suspense controls loading states, not how many nodes stay mounted.

questions.scenario: To make a filter box feel faster, a developer writes onChange={e => startTransition(() => setText(e.target.value))} for a controlled <input value={text} />, where text also drives an expensive list.
questions.stem: What is wrong with this approach, and what is the better pattern?
options: startTransition must be replaced by setTimeout so the update runs later
The input should be uncontrolled and read with a ref during render
A Transition cannot control a text input value; keep setText urgent and defer the list with a separate Transition state or useDeferredValue
Nothing; Transitions are the recommended way to control text inputs
questions.explanation: The React docs state that a Transition cannot be used to control a text input, because the input must reflect each keystroke synchronously. The fix is to keep the input state urgent and derive the expensive part from a deferred value or from a second state updated in a Transition. Reading refs during render is not a valid way to drive rendering.
rationales: A timeout delays the work but does not make it interruptible, and the input still lags.
Reading refs during render breaks the rendering model and does not trigger updates.
Correct. Split urgent input state from the expensive, deferred render.
The docs specifically call out text inputs as something Transitions cannot control.

questions.scenario: A Client Component dashboard imports a 400 KB charting library at the top of the file, but the chart only appears inside a modal that few users open.
questions.stem: Which approach reduces the JavaScript users download up front?
options: Add 'use client' to the chart file a second time to split it
Load the chart component with next/dynamic (or React.lazy) when the modal opens
Add useMemo around the chart data
Move the import into a useEffect body as a regular static import
questions.explanation: A static import puts the library in the dashboard bundle for every visitor. next/dynamic or React.lazy create a separate chunk that loads only when the component renders, so most users never download it. Memoization or repeating the directive does not change what is bundled.
rationales: The directive marks a client boundary; it does not create a lazy chunk.
Correct. Code splitting moves the library into an on-demand chunk.
useMemo affects render work, not bundle contents.
Static imports cannot be placed inside a function; a dynamic import() would be needed, which is what next/dynamic wraps.

questions.scenario: A Server Component page.tsx contains const Map = dynamic(() => import('./Map'), { ssr: false }) because the map library touches window. The build fails.
questions.stem: What is the correct fix?
options: Move the dynamic(..., { ssr: false }) call into a Client Component and render that component from the page
Replace ssr: false with suppressHydrationWarning on the map container
Wrap the dynamic call in a try/catch
Add export const dynamic = "force-dynamic" to the page
questions.explanation: Using ssr: false with next/dynamic inside a Server Component is an error, because Server Components never run in the browser. The pattern is to create a small Client Component that performs the dynamic import with ssr: false and render it from the server page. Route segment config and suppressHydrationWarning do not affect this rule.
rationales: Correct. ssr: false is only allowed inside Client Components.
suppressHydrationWarning silences one-level text and attribute mismatches; it does not stop server code touching window.
This is a build-time rule, not a runtime exception to catch.
Rendering mode does not make ssr: false valid in a Server Component.

questions.scenario: A lib/db.ts module reads a database password from process.env.DB_PASSWORD and imports a large ORM. A developer accidentally imports a helper from it into a 'use client' component. The bundle grows and the password variable is undefined in the browser.
questions.stem: What is the best way to stop this from happening again?
options: Wrap the helper in a useEffect so it only runs on the client
Add 'use server' to lib/db.ts so every export becomes safe to import
Rename the variable to NEXT_PUBLIC_DB_PASSWORD so it works on the client
Add import 'server-only' at the top of lib/db.ts so any client import fails the build
questions.explanation: Everything a 'use client' module imports joins the client bundle. The server-only package turns a wrong-side import into a build error, keeping the ORM and secrets out of the browser. A NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix would inline the secret into client JavaScript at build time.
rationales: The module would still be bundled for the client.
'use server' exposes exports as callable Server Functions, which are public endpoints; it is not an import guard.
That would publish the password in the client bundle.
Correct. It makes the mistake a build-time error.

questions.scenario: A Client Component renders {new Date().toLocaleString()} in the page header. In production, hydration warnings appear for users in other time zones.
questions.stem: Which two changes are appropriate fixes? (Select two.)
options: Render a stable placeholder on the server and set the formatted time in useEffect after mount
Add suppressHydrationWarning to the <span> because the timestamp difference is expected
Add suppressHydrationWarning to <html> so it applies to the whole tree
Branch on typeof window during render to choose between server and client output
questions.explanation: Date and locale formatting differ between server and browser, so the first client render does not match the HTML. Setting the value after mount keeps the first render identical, and suppressHydrationWarning on the element itself is the documented escape hatch for unavoidable differences like timestamps. It only works one level deep, and a typeof window branch is itself a listed cause of mismatches.
rationales: Correct. The server and first client render match; the real value arrives after mount.
Correct. Placed on the element whose text differs, it silences this expected difference.
It only applies one level deep, so it does not reach the span.
Branching on typeof window during render produces different server and client markup.

questions.scenario:
A product card renders

, and ProductSpecs returns a
with a list. Development shows a hydration error on every product page, even though no values depend on time or the browser.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause?
options: React requires every list item to use suppressHydrationWarning
ProductSpecs needs to be a Server Component

Invalid HTML nesting: a
inside a

is repaired by the browser, so the DOM no longer matches
The page is missing a loading.tsx file
questions.explanation:
Browsers do not allow block elements like
inside

; the parser closes the paragraph early, so the server HTML turns into a different DOM than React expects. Invalid nesting is the first cause listed in the Next.js hydration error docs. The fix is to use a

wrapper or valid inline content.
rationales: Keys and lists are unrelated; suppressing warnings would hide a real bug.
Server or client rendering does not change the invalid nesting.
Correct. The parsed DOM differs from React's tree, causing the mismatch.
Loading UI has no effect on markup validity.

questions.scenario: A product page streams its static shell immediately. The hero image is rendered by a component that first awaits personalized recommendations, and that component is wrapped in <Suspense fallback={<HeroSkeleton />}>. LCP is 4.6 s while TTFB is fast.
questions.stem: Which change most improves LCP?
options: Render the hero image in the shell outside the Suspense boundary and stream only the personalized part
Add a second nested Suspense boundary around the image
Disable streaming so the whole page is sent at once
Make HeroSkeleton larger so it becomes the LCP element
questions.explanation: The Next.js streaming guide notes that an LCP element inside a Suspense boundary cannot paint until that boundary's content is swapped in, so a slow data await delays LCP even with a fast TTFB. Keeping the LCP element outside or above Suspense boundaries lets it paint with the static shell, while the slow personalized content still streams in. Gaming the metric with a skeleton or blocking the whole page does not improve real loading.
rationales: Correct. The hero paints with the shell instead of waiting for data.
The image would still sit behind the outer boundary that waits for data.
Blocking on the slow data delays everything, including TTFB.
The real hero still appears late and the skeleton then shifts layout; this hides the problem.

questions.scenario: A settings form uses a Server Action. While pending, a "Saving…" text appears next to the button, then "Saved". Screen-reader users report hearing nothing, and the team does not want to move focus.
questions.stem: What should the team do to meet WCAG 2.2 AA?
options: Use an alert() dialog when saving completes
Add a tooltip to the button that says the form is saving
Move focus to the message each time it changes
Render the messages inside a role="status" (aria-live="polite") region that is present in the DOM before the message changes
questions.explanation: Success Criterion 4.1.3 Status Messages (AA) requires status messages to be programmatically determinable so assistive technology can present them without receiving focus. A persistent live region with role="status" announces content changes politely. Moving focus or using alert() interrupts the user and is not required.
rationales: A modal alert interrupts the user and blocks interaction.
Tooltips are not announced on content change.
The criterion targets messages that do not take focus; moving focus disrupts the user.
Correct. The live region announces the text changes without moving focus.

questions.scenario: An app has a sticky footer bar with promotional content. Keyboard testing shows that when tabbing through a long form, some focused fields end up completely hidden behind the footer.
questions.stem: Which WCAG 2.2 success criterion does this fail, and at what level?
options: 2.4.13 Focus Appearance, level AA
2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), level AA
2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), level AAA
4.1.1 Parsing, level A
questions.explanation: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) is a new AA criterion in WCAG 2.2: a focused component must not be entirely hidden by author-created content such as sticky headers or footers. Focus Appearance (2.4.13) is AAA and about the indicator itself. 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete and removed in 2.2.
rationales: Focus Appearance is AAA and covers the indicator's size and contrast, not obstruction.
Correct. Fully hiding the focused field behind a sticky bar fails this AA criterion.
Target Size (Minimum) is AA and covers pointer target size.
4.1.1 Parsing was removed from WCAG 2.2.

questions.scenario: A team is planning an accessibility audit against WCAG 2.2 level AA and wants to list the criteria that are new in 2.2 and apply at AA.
questions.stem: Which two of these belong on that list? (Select two.)
options: 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum)
2.4.13 Focus Appearance
4.1.1 Parsing
2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)
questions.explanation: WCAG 2.2 added 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) and 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) at level AA, along with 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) and 2.5.7 Dragging Movements. 2.4.13 Focus Appearance is new but AAA. 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete and removed in 2.2.
rationales: Correct. New in 2.2 at AA.
New in 2.2, but level AAA, so outside an AA audit scope.
Removed in WCAG 2.2, not added.
Correct. New in 2.2 at AA, with a 24×24 CSS px minimum.

questions.scenario: A custom dropdown is built from <div onClick={toggle}> elements styled to look like buttons. Keyboard users cannot open it, and screen readers announce it as plain text.
questions.stem: What is the most robust fix?
options: Add a title attribute describing the dropdown
Add tabIndex={0} to the div and keep the click handler only
Use a native <button> for the trigger (with aria-expanded) and native elements for the options where possible
Add role="button" and leave the existing styling
questions.explanation: A native <button> provides the role, keyboard focus and Enter/Space activation for free, and aria-expanded communicates the open state. A div with only tabIndex or role still lacks keyboard activation unless you reimplement it. A title attribute does not give the element a role or keyboard behaviour.
rationales: A title is not a substitute for a role or keyboard support.
It becomes focusable but still has no role and does not respond to Enter or Space.
Correct. Semantic HTML gives role, focus and keyboard behaviour natively.
The role is announced but keyboard activation must still be built by hand.

questions.scenario: A dashboard app checks the session in `app/(dashboard)/layout.tsx` and redirects anonymous users to `/login`. A penetration test shows that an anonymous user can still call the `deleteProject` Server Action and read `/dashboard/reports` data after client-side navigation in some cases.
questions.stem: What is the most robust fix?
options: Move the session check into the root layout so it runs higher in the tree.
Add a server-only Data Access Layer with verifySession() and call it from every data function and inside each Server Action, including an ownership check.
Add a proxy.ts matcher for /dashboard/:path* and rely on it as the single authorization gate.
Convert the layout to a Client Component that checks a session cookie in useEffect.
questions.explanation: Layouts do not re-render on navigation and do not guard Server Actions, which are public POST endpoints. The Next.js guide recommends verifying the session in a server-only Data Access Layer close to the data, and authorizing each action.
rationales: A higher layout has the same problem: layouts are not re-run on every navigation and do not wrap action calls.
Correct: checks at the data layer and in each action cannot be bypassed by navigation or by calling the action directly.
Proxy is meant for optimistic checks; a matcher that excludes a path also skips its actions, so it should not be the only gate.
A client-side check runs after data is already sent and can be bypassed entirely by calling the server directly.

questions.scenario: A team stores a signed JWT session in a cookie. Security review asks for the cookie settings that reduce theft by injected scripts and keep the cookie off plain HTTP, while still letting users arrive logged in from links in emails.
questions.stem: Which cookie configuration fits best?
options: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax, Path=/ and an expiry.
Secure, SameSite=None, readable by JavaScript so the client can attach it as a header.
HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, without Secure so local HTTP testing works.
Store the JWT in localStorage and send it in an Authorization header instead of a cookie.
questions.explanation: HttpOnly keeps the value out of document.cookie, Secure restricts it to HTTPS, and Lax still sends the cookie on top-level GET navigations such as clicking an email link. This matches the options used in the Next.js authentication guide.
rationales: Correct: these are the options the Next.js guide uses, and Lax allows top-level navigations from links.
A script-readable cookie can be stolen by XSS, and SameSite=None widens cross-site sending unnecessarily.
Omitting Secure lets the cookie travel over plain HTTP, and Strict would drop it when arriving from an email link.
localStorage is readable by any script on the page, so an XSS bug exposes the token.

questions.scenario: An app keeps a legacy Route Handler `GET /api/account/close` that closes the signed-in user's account. Session cookies are SameSite=Lax. A developer argues CSRF is impossible because of SameSite.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: SameSite=Lax still sends cookies on top-level GET navigations, so a link on another site could trigger the close.
Because it is a Route Handler, Next.js applies the same Origin/Host check it uses for Server Actions.
The state change should move to a POST (for example a Server Action) with an authenticated, authorized check, keeping SameSite as defense in depth.
Adding HttpOnly to the cookie prevents cross-site requests from carrying it.
questions.explanation: Lax only blocks most cross-site subrequests; top-level GET navigations still carry the cookie, which is why state must never change on GET. OWASP treats SameSite as defense in depth, and the Origin check Next.js performs is specific to Server Actions, so custom Route Handlers need their own protection.
rationales: Correct: top-level GET navigations are exactly what Lax still allows.
The built-in Origin comparison applies to Server Actions; custom Route Handlers must be audited and protected manually.
Correct: use a non-GET method with explicit auth checks and keep SameSite as an extra layer.
HttpOnly only hides the cookie from JavaScript; it does not affect whether the browser attaches it to requests.

questions.scenario: Behind a corporate reverse proxy, forms that call Server Actions fail in production with an origin mismatch, while they work locally. The proxy forwards to the app on a different host name.
questions.stem: What is the appropriate fix?
options: Disable CSRF protection for Server Actions in next.config.
Switch the forms to GET so the Origin header is not checked.
Add the proxy's public origin to serverActions.allowedOrigins.
Set the session cookie to SameSite=None so cross-origin requests succeed.
questions.explanation: Next.js compares the Origin header with Host or X-Forwarded-Host for Server Actions. When a proxy changes the host, the documented fix is to list the trusted origin in serverActions.allowedOrigins.
rationales: There is no reason to turn off the protection; the documented setting exists for this case.
Server Actions are POST-only, and moving mutations to GET would create a CSRF hole.
Correct: allowedOrigins tells Next which additional origins are trusted.
Cookie SameSite has nothing to do with the server-side Origin/Host comparison and would weaken defenses.

questions.scenario: A CMS lets editors write rich-text bios that are stored as HTML and rendered on public profile pages with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. The team also has a strict CSP.
questions.stem: What is the primary defense against stored XSS here?
options: The CSP alone, since it blocks inline scripts.
Sanitize the HTML with a vetted sanitizer such as DOMPurify before rendering, keeping CSP as defense in depth.
Wrap the component in an error boundary so malicious markup fails to render.
Render the bio inside a Client Component, because React escapes it there.
questions.explanation: dangerouslySetInnerHTML bypasses React's escaping, so untrusted HTML must be sanitized first. OWASP positions CSP as defense in depth, not the primary control.
rationales: CSP reduces impact but is a second layer; event-handler attributes and policy gaps can still be exploited.
Correct: sanitizing untrusted HTML is the primary control, with CSP as an extra layer.
Error boundaries handle rendering errors; malicious HTML renders without throwing.
dangerouslySetInnerHTML inserts raw HTML in Client Components too; React only escapes ordinary JSX text.

questions.scenario: A marketing site relies on static shells and Partial Prerendering for speed. Security asks for a nonce-based Content-Security-Policy generated in proxy.ts on every route.
questions.stem: What trade-off should the team expect, and what alternative does the Next.js guide mention?
options: No trade-off: nonces are embedded at build time, so static pages keep working.
Nonces only work for API routes, so pages need no CSP.
The site must switch to the Edge runtime because proxy cannot set headers.
Nonce CSP forces those routes to render dynamically, losing static shells; for static pages, hash-based SRI (experimental) is the alternative.
questions.explanation: A nonce must be unique per request, so pages using it must render at request time and are incompatible with static shells / PPR. The Next.js CSP guide offers experimental Subresource Integrity with hashes as an option for static content.
rationales: A nonce baked in at build time would be the same for every visitor, which defeats its purpose.
CSP is for documents; nonces apply to the scripts in pages.
Proxy runs on Node in Next 16 and can set headers; the Edge runtime is deprecated.
Correct: per-request nonces mean dynamic rendering; SRI hashes are the static-friendly option.

questions.scenario: A developer sets `NEXT_PUBLIC_PAYMENTS_SECRET` so that a Client Component can call a payments API directly. They plan to rotate the value per environment by changing the variable on the running server.
questions.stem: Which TWO problems does this plan have? (Select two.)
options: NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are inlined into the client bundle, so the secret is exposed to every visitor.
NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are encrypted in the bundle, so the client cannot read them.
NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are frozen at build time, so changing the variable on the server has no effect until a rebuild.
Next.js refuses to start when a NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable contains the word SECRET.
questions.explanation: The Next.js environment variables guide says NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are inlined at build time into JavaScript sent to the browser. That both exposes the value and freezes it; secrets belong in non-prefixed variables used only on the server.
rationales: Correct: anything prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_ ships to the browser.
They are inlined as plain values, not encrypted.
Correct: the value is fixed at build time.
There is no such name check; it is the developer's responsibility.

questions.scenario: A `lib/billing.ts` module reads `process.env.STRIPE_KEY` and is imported by a Server Component. A teammate later imports one of its helpers into a Client Component, and the build passes.
questions.stem: What change makes this mistake fail fast in the future?
options: Add import 'server-only' at the top of lib/billing.ts.
Rename the variable to NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_KEY so it is consistent on both sides.
Add 'use server' to every helper in the module.
Wrap the helpers in React.cache.
questions.explanation: The server-only package makes importing the module from client code a build error. Non-public env vars are not exposed to the client anyway, but server-only stops the module and its logic from being bundled there.
rationales: Correct: server-only turns a wrong-side import into a build error.
This would expose the key to the browser.
'use server' would turn the helpers into publicly callable Server Functions, which is a different and riskier change.
React.cache dedupes calls during a render; it does not restrict where code runs.

questions.scenario: A team writes Vitest + React Testing Library tests for every component. The tests for `app/orders/page.tsx`, an async Server Component that awaits a database call, are flaky and hard to set up.
questions.stem: What do the Next.js testing docs recommend?
options: Mock React internals so the async component resolves synchronously.
Convert the page to a Client Component so it can be tested with Testing Library.
Cover async Server Components with end-to-end tests (for example Playwright), and unit-test the data and validation functions directly.
Skip testing Server Components because they cannot fail at runtime.
questions.explanation: The Next.js testing guide notes that async Server Components are new to the React ecosystem and current unit-test tools do not fully support them, so it recommends E2E tests for them. The plain async functions they call can still be unit-tested.
rationales: Mocking React internals is brittle and not a supported approach.
Changing the architecture to fit a test tool loses server rendering benefits.
Correct: E2E for async Server Components, unit tests for their underlying logic.
Server Components can fail like any code; they need test coverage.

questions.scenario: A component test uses `container.querySelector('.btn-primary')` and `fireEvent.click`. It broke twice this month after styling changes, although the feature still worked.
questions.stem: Which rewrite follows Testing Library's guidance?
options: Add data-testid to every element and query by test id.
Query with getByRole('button', { name: /save/i }) and interact via user-event.
Snapshot the whole component tree and compare it on each run.
Use getByText on the CSS class name.
questions.explanation: Testing Library's query priority puts accessible queries such as getByRole first and test ids last, so tests resemble how users find elements. user-event simulates full interactions and is recommended over fireEvent.
rationales: Test ids are the last resort in the query priority and do not check accessibility.
Correct: role plus accessible name survives styling changes, and user-event is more realistic.
Snapshots break on any markup change, which is the problem being solved.
getByText matches visible text, not class names.

questions.scenario: A Playwright test for checkout fails intermittently. It clicks "Pay", calls `page.waitForTimeout(3000)`, then reads `textContent` of the confirmation element and compares it.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Increase the timeout to 10 seconds.
Run the tests serially in one shared browser context so state is warm.
Retry the whole test three times in CI and ignore single failures.
Use a role-based locator with a web-first assertion such as await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText(/paid/i).
questions.explanation: Playwright's web-first assertions wait and retry until the condition holds, which removes timing guesses. The best-practices guide recommends user-facing locators and isolated tests over fixed sleeps and shared state.
rationales: A longer sleep is slower and still a guess.
Sharing state across tests reduces isolation and creates order dependencies.
Retries hide the flakiness without fixing its cause.
Correct: auto-retrying assertions on user-facing locators.

questions.scenario: A chat page calls `POST /api/chat`, a Route Handler that streams a model response. Users who close the tab mid-answer still consume full model tokens, and memory spikes when the client is slow.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes address these problems? (Select two.)
options: Pass request.signal to the upstream model fetch so a client disconnect cancels the upstream request.
Read the whole upstream response into a string first, then return it in one Response.
Produce the stream from a pull-based source or by piping the upstream body, so data is only produced as the consumer reads it.
Switch the Route Handler to the Edge runtime, which never buffers.
questions.explanation: Forwarding the request's AbortSignal lets cancellation propagate upstream. ReadableStream pull sources and pipes respect backpressure through the queue's desiredSize, whereas enqueueing everything eagerly buffers in memory.
rationales: Correct: the abort signal propagates cancellation to the upstream call.
Buffering the whole answer removes streaming and increases memory use.
Correct: pull/pipe-based streams honor backpressure.
The Edge runtime is deprecated in Next 16 and does not by itself solve cancellation or backpressure.

questions.scenario: A client streams text with a `reader.read()` loop and calls `setAnswer(answer + chunk)` for each chunk. The final answer only contains the last chunk, and occasionally shows broken characters for non-English text.
questions.stem: Which change fixes both issues?
options: Convert each chunk with String.fromCharCode(...value).
Wrap each setAnswer in flushSync and create a new TextDecoder per chunk.
Store the answer in a ref and never update state.
Use setAnswer(a => a + decoder.decode(value, { stream: true })) with one TextDecoder for the whole stream.
questions.explanation: The async loop closes over the answer value from the render that started it, so each non-updater set replaces the text with that stale value plus one chunk; an updater function appends to the latest state. A single TextDecoder with { stream: true } keeps multi-byte characters that are split across chunks intact.
rationales: fromCharCode on bytes does not decode UTF-8 and breaks non-ASCII text.
flushSync does not fix the stale closure, and new decoders per chunk lose partial characters.
A ref without state updates means the UI never shows partial output.
Correct: updater function for stale state, streaming decode for split characters.

questions.scenario: Streaming responses arrive all at once in production but stream correctly with `next dev` locally. The app is self-hosted behind Nginx.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Route Handlers cannot stream in production builds; use a Server Action instead.
React batches streamed chunks in production; disable StrictMode.
Nginx is buffering the response; disable proxy buffering for that route (for example with X-Accel-Buffering: no).
The Content-Type must be application/json for streaming to work.
questions.explanation: Proxies such as Nginx buffer responses by default, which holds the stream until it completes. The Next.js streaming and self-hosting guidance points to disabling buffering, for example with the X-Accel-Buffering: no header.
rationales: Route Handlers can return streaming Response bodies in production.
StrictMode is development-only and unrelated to network buffering.
Correct: proxy buffering is a documented cause.
Content type does not control buffering; plain text is fine for a text stream.

questions.scenario: A team builds with `output: 'standalone'` and copies only `.next/standalone` into a Docker image. Pages load but CSS, client JavaScript and images from `public/` return 404.
questions.stem: What is missing?
options: standalone mode requires an adapter to serve assets.
public/ and .next/static are not copied into the standalone folder by default; copy them in or serve them from a CDN.
The image must run next dev to serve static files.
standalone disables static assets; use output: 'export' instead.
questions.explanation: The output docs state that standalone output produces a minimal server with traced dependencies but does not copy public or .next/static. They are expected to be copied manually or handled by a CDN.
rationales: No adapter is required; the minimal server.js can serve assets once they are present.
Correct: those two folders must be added.
next dev is for development and not appropriate in production.
Static export would remove server features the app relies on; the issue is just missing files.

questions.scenario: A team wants to deploy to a plain static file host. The app uses Server Actions for a contact form, reads cookies for a theme preference, and uses `proxy.ts` for locale redirects.
questions.stem: What is the correct assessment of `output: 'export'` for this app?
options: It works unchanged; Next.js converts actions and proxy into client code at export time.
It works if every page is marked with export const dynamic = "force-static".
Only images need to change, because the default image loader is unavailable.
Those features need a server, so the app needs a Node server, container or platform adapter, or those features must be redesigned.
questions.explanation: The static exports guide lists features that are unsupported in export mode, including Server Actions, cookies, proxy and rewrites/redirects. An app that depends on them needs one of the server-based deployment options.
rationales: Server-side features are not converted to client code; they are unsupported.
Segment config cannot make request-time features work without a server.
Image optimization is one limitation, but not the only one affecting this app.
Correct: these features require a running server.

questions.scenario: A self-hosted app is scaled from one to four instances behind a load balancer. Afterwards, revalidated data appears on some requests but not others, and some form submissions fail with "Failed to find Server Action" right after deploys.
questions.stem: Which configuration addresses both symptoms?
options: Run each instance with a different build so caches warm independently.
Sticky sessions on the load balancer only.
Disable caching with no-store on every fetch and redeploy more slowly.
A shared cache handler for all instances, a deploymentId for skew protection, and the same NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY everywhere.
questions.explanation: The default cache is in memory per instance, so revalidation on one instance does not reach the others without a shared handler. The self-hosting guide also calls for a deploymentId and a consistent action encryption key so clients and instances agree on actions across versions.
rationales: Different builds make skew worse, since action ids and assets differ.
Sticky sessions mask the cache problem partly but do not share revalidation or fix version skew.
Turning off caching gives up performance and does not address action skew.
Correct: these are the multi-instance requirements in the self-hosting guide.

questions.scenario: Users report a generic "An error occurred in the Server Components render" message in production. The team wants these server errors sent to their error tracker with the route that failed.
questions.stem: What is the most direct approach?
options: Wrap every Server Component body in try/catch and call the tracker from each.
Export onRequestError from instrumentation.ts to forward errors with request and route context, and correlate with the error.digest shown to users.
Rely on the browser console, since production shows the full server stack trace.

rationales: Possible, but repetitive and easy to miss; the framework provides a central hook.
Correct: the instrumentation hook plus the digest for correlation.
Production hides server error details from the browser.
The error prop in production carries a generic message and digest, not the server stack.
